he is also able to comfort all sentient beings who fear birth and death, acting as their kinsman and friend;
he is adorned with immeasurable virtues such as great compassion and the like.

These—Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Tathāgatas—are the true sons of my father; within this Bhadrakalpa, they shall attain Buddhahood and shall be the most preeminent among all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Using various merits as diverse and wondrous fragrances, he perfumes the pure waters of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* with which he bathes himself; he dons the raiment of shame and remorse, takes the pure *dharmadhātu* as the jewel in his topknot, and adorns his head with the vast garlands of the spheres of activity traversed by all Buddhas, bound together by the exquisite white silk of liberation.

Furthermore, they adorn themselves with the various jewels of merit, such as the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) and the acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).
Taking loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as their precious sandals, they are able to cover the three realms.
The three kinds of sublime conduct, which perfect the causes of the noble ones, serve as its parasol.
It establishes the adamantine seat of meditative concentration, protected and sustained by the Buddhas and celestial sages of antiquity.
They enter into the four foundations of mindfulness, which are reverently upheld by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
they sit upon the seat spread by previous buddhas and realize the state of omniscience, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

In order that the lineage of the Triple Gem may never be severed, he turns the wheel of Dharma and strikes the Dharma-bell and drum; the sublime sound of the Dharma pervades the triple world, causing all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans to clearly understand the Four Noble Truths through the wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
It cannot be turned back by any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, Brahmās, humans, non-humans, or anyone else in all the worlds.

Desiring to benefit and bring peace and happiness to the immeasurable devas and humans of the world, and to enable them to attain supreme and vast benefit, that which had never been turned before is now being turned.
“Good son! I have accomplished this foremost wheel of the Buddha.

By means of this wheel, I know as they truly are what is possible and what is impossible in this world and the next; I dwell in peace, free from alarm and fear, subduing all devas, Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, and I turn the Great Brahma-wheel to fulfill the Great Brahma-conduct.”
I should dwell in this world of defilement during this age of the five corruptions, standing amidst the great assembly to roar the true lion’s roar.

I shall extinguish the five deeds of immediate retribution of all sentient beings, and so forth, up to their various unwholesome roots; I shall crush and destroy the vajra-like, continuous afflictions of all classes of living beings, and establish the wondrous fruit of liberation in which all outflows are forever exhausted. According to their inclinations, I shall settle all capable sentient beings in the stage of non-retrogression within the Three Vehicles.

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration and first ascends the throne; having assumed the imperial office, he examines the royal paths of the past, future, and present. Among the various wheels of kingly affairs, by means of his wisdom that skillfully observes the retribution of causes and effects, he establishes all ministers and assistants as appropriate, extending [his governance] to the three kinds of wheels of action for the people—both ignorant and wise—throughout the kingdoms and cities.”
By means of this wheel of karma, the people throughout the land enjoy its benefits throughout the long night;
all manner of pleasing requisites and increasing joys and pleasures are provided, capable of extinguishing all enemies and evil associates.
What are the three types of wheels of activity?
First is the wheel of activity for establishing sovereign emperors, which refers to skillfully training in military formations and combat to defeat enemy forces and nurture the populace.

Second, he establishes the wheel of activity for fields and dwellings, meaning he skillfully instructs them in building houses and farming, so that they may attain security and have sufficient food and drink.

Third, he establishes the wheel of activity for wealth and treasures, meaning he skillfully instructs them in commerce, industry, and various arts, so that they may obtain all kinds of rare curiosities and resources to enjoy as they wish, thereby increasing their happiness.
"Noble son! A Kṣatriya, a great king consecrated by coronation, accomplishes this second wheel of kingship.
By means of this wheel, he dwells in peace and happiness within his own realm; he is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, well-guarding his person and causing his lifespan to increase."
“Good son! Thus, when the Tathāgata first attained the fruit of Buddhahood and acquired unsurpassed wisdom, he observed the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
By means of the wisdom that skillfully observes the causal retribution of all karmic phenomena and their experiences, he establishes the three wheels of karma for all sentient beings to be converted.

Through these wheels of karma, he ensures that the Three Jewels, the spiritual lineage, and the Eye of Dharma do not perish throughout the long night, and that the unsurpassed True Dharma flourishes and circulates widely.

May all sentient beings long experience the various forms of peace, happiness, and bliss of rebirth in the heavens and nirvana; and may all the heterodox and erroneous doctrines of outsiders be unable to overcome my eye of the True Dharma, while I am able to lawfully refute those erroneous doctrines.
Good son! What are the three kinds of wheels of karma?
The first is the wheel of karma for establishing the cultivation of meditative concentration.
Second, establishing the wheel of activity for recitation and study;
third, establishing the wheel of activity for cultivating merit. "Good son!
What is the Tathāgata’s wheel of action consisting of the cultivation of meditative concentration?
There are ten kinds of concentration. What are these ten?

That is to say, one correctly contemplates that the sixfold objects of the conscious body have the grasping at "I" and "mine" as their cause; karma serves as the fertile field, ignorance acts as the covering, craving provides the moisture, and it lacks autonomy, being established in dependence upon others and bound to various conditions.
In order to sever and extinguish the three kinds of flows—karma, afflictions, and suffering—one observes in this way: what is the flow of karma?
It refers to the various formations performed by sentient beings.
If these conditioned phenomena arise with ignorance and craving as their causes, thereby producing the various realms of existence, they are called the "flow of afflictions.
If, through the afflictions, consciousness acts as the cause and the various conditions harmonize, name-and-form arises.
With name-and-form as cause and through the conjunction of various conditions, the six sense bases arise.

With the six sense bases as cause and through the conjunction of various conditions, contact arises; following contact, feeling arises; and subsequently, birth, old age, death, and so forth arise in succession—this is called the stream of suffering.
Thus, these three streams grow by having karma as their fertile field, ignorance as their cause, and craving as their moisture.

To dry them up, one regards the five aggregates of clinging—which have karma as their fertile field, ignorance as their cause, and craving as their moisture—through these three streams as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; as dull and motionless; as like a magical illusion, a flame, the moon reflected in water, or what is seen in a dream; as empty and devoid of anything existing; as signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unproduced, imageless, tranquil, secluded, and without origination.

By observing the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) in this manner, one becomes compliant with the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatākṣānti*), the patience of signlessness (*animittakṣānti*), and the patience of wishlessness (*apraṇihitakṣānti*).

Desiring to conform to these, one observes the five aggregates of clinging and further skillfully cultivates the meditation on inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*); this is the cultivation of maintaining mindfulness of coming and going.
"How does one, by means of mindfulness, observe the inhalation and exhalation as they truly are?
It is by observing them correctly through counting, following, settling, observing, transforming, and purifying."
It should be understood that, in this context, counting performs two functions:
first, it serves as the basis for subduing discursive thoughts; second, it enables the grasping of the characteristics of inhalation and exhalation.
It performs two kinds of activities:
first, based on renunciation, it abandons all discursive thoughts; second, it is able to correctly apprehend the characteristics of inhalation and exhalation.
Calm abiding (śamatha) performs two kinds of activities:
First, it can manifest the cessation of inhalation and exhalation; second, it can abide in superior samādhi.
Contemplation performs two kinds of functions:
first, it can manifest the exhaustion of inhalation and exhalation; second, it can abide in the mind and mental factors while observing them through distinct analysis.
It can perform two kinds of activities:
first, it can skillfully relinquish the aggregates of grasping; second, it can skillfully enter the stages of the noble ones.
Purity can perform two kinds of activities:
First, the ability to abandon the fetters; second, the ability to purify views.
By practicing these six kinds of skillful means in the contemplation of inhalation and exhalation, one is then able to accord with the contemplation of the five aggregates of clinging.
Why is this so? The intrinsic nature of such inhalation and exhalation is called the aggregate of appropriation consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-upādānaskandha*).
The experiencing of such inhalation and exhalation is called the aggregate of appropriation consisting of sensation (*vedanā-upādānaskandha*).
Thus, the grasping of the signs of inhalation and exhalation is called the aggregate of grasping at perception (*saṃjñā-upādānaskandha*).
Thus, the formative activity of inhalation and exhalation is called the aggregate of grasping at formations (*saṃskāra-upādānaskandha*).
Thus, the discernment of inhalation and exhalation is called the aggregate of appropriation through consciousness (*vijñānopādānaskandha*).
These five aggregates of appropriation thus described are each distinct and dissimilar from one another; they are ever-new and not old, without abiding, without accumulation, and ineffable.
Observing the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) in this way can eliminate the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*).

If one can thus ultimately observe the exhaustion of these three types of formations, one will then be able to ultimately observe the grasping at "I" and "mine" regarding the sixfold objects of this conscious body; thereby, ignorance, craving, causes, fields, coverings, and moisture—all will be completely exhausted.
In this way, the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness all reaches fulfillment.
Even up to the cultivation of the noble eightfold path, all reach fulfillment.
In this manner, even up to the cultivation of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all reach fulfillment.

In this manner, up until the point that they cultivate the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvākāra-anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and so forth, they achieve complete perfection in all respects.

Thus, by practicing and maintaining mindfulness of coming and going while entering the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), they are called sentient beings who abide in the ultimate meaning of the True Dharma; they are called those who truly practice meditative absorption; they are called those who truly make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the three periods of time; they are called the heart-sons of all Buddhas, born from the mouth of the Buddha, accomplished through this Dharma, and transformed by this Dharma.
There may be some bodhisattvas who, practicing in this manner, gradually regress until they exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*) and become arhats endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

There may be other bodhisattvas who, practicing in this manner, gradually advance until their merit is perfected and they become great bodhisattvas, even reaching the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) and the perfection of the cultivation of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*); such persons shall before long attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

“Good son! By means of this wisdom regarding the causal retribution received from such karmic dharmas, I observe the Dharma-eye of all Buddhas of the three periods of time establishing sentient beings, and cause them to practice these ten kinds of wheels of karma for cultivating meditative concentration.”
"Good son! This is called the Tathāgata’s wheel of action for cultivating meditative concentration. Good son!"
What is the Tathāgata’s wheel of activity for recitation?

It refers to those bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or likewise faithful sons of good family or daughters of good family, whose roots of virtue are slight and thin, who rely upon conventional truth, and whose faculties have not yet matured.
I shall establish such sentient beings so that they may practice recitation, being diligent and untiring during both the first and last watches of the night.

If there are sentient beings who seek unsurpassed wisdom, I shall establish them in the pure Mahāyāna, causing them to read it themselves or to teach others to read it; to recite it themselves or to teach others to recite it; to explain it themselves or to teach others to explain it; and to study it themselves or to teach others to study it within the Mahāyāna, for the sake of eliminating the multitude of great afflictions within their own bodies and those of others, and for the sake of realizing unsurpassed wisdom.
It is for the sake of eliminating the suffering of all sentient beings;
it is for the sake of causing them to enter the city of fearlessness.
If there are sentient beings who seek the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, I shall establish them in the various dharmas of dependent origination and cause them to study and recite them.

If there are sentient beings who seek the Śrāvaka vehicle, I shall establish them in hundreds of thousands of verses of the four Āgamas, hundreds of thousands of verses of the Vinaya Piṭaka, and hundreds of thousands of verses of the Abhidharma and its Vibhāṣā, causing them to practice and recite them.
"Good son! This is called the Tathāgata’s wheel of practice through recitation. Good son!"
What is the Tathāgata’s wheel of cultivating meritorious deeds?

It refers to those sentient beings whose faculties are dull and obtuse, who have not planted roots of goodness, whose wisdom is feeble and inferior, who are indolent and lose mindfulness, who are stained by attachment to various articles of enjoyment and requisites, and who remain far removed from virtuous friends.

I shall establish such sentient beings so that they may perform meritorious deeds; that is to say, I shall cause them to cultivate and carry out the services due to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as those due to their preceptors and instructors.
"Noble son! This is called the Tathāgata’s wheel of cultivating meritorious deeds. Noble son!"
I have thus accomplished this second wheel of the Buddha.

By means of this wheel, through my unsurpassed knowledge of the karma of the three times, I know, as they truly are, the causes and the karmic retributions for all the actions and the experiences of all sentient beings.

According to what is appropriate for each case, he establishes the wheel of the three karmas to mature all sentient beings to be converted, enabling them to dwell in peace and security, to be free from alarm and fear, and to be without dread; he subdues all celestial Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, turns the Great Brahma-wheel, and accomplishes the Great Brahma-conduct, truly and as it is understanding the causes and retributions of sentient beings.

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration and has perfected skillful wisdom; he observes all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, as well as their various merits, extensive learning, valor, and artistic skills.”

If there are sentient beings who are rich in merit, have perfected skillful wisdom, and are diligent, courageous, firm, and non-regressive, adorning themselves with various forms of merit, this consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste shall, according to what is appropriate for them, bestow precious jewels, wealth, grain, fields, houses, slaves, and servants.

Within his own realm, if there are sentient beings whose virtue and skill are slight and whose meritorious achievements are meager, this consecrated Kṣatriya great king provides them with appropriate and modest relief and assistance.

Within his own realm, if there are sentient beings whose merit is meager, who lack diligence, are indolent and lazy, have lost right mindfulness, lack compassion, do not know how to repay kindness, feel no dread toward the sufferings of future lives, are submerged in the mud of household life, and accumulate various evil deeds—this consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste shall, according to what is appropriate for them, impose various punishments. These may include verbal instruction, harsh treatment, or reprimand; the confiscation of various precious jewels and resources; the seizure of their means of enjoyment and property; or punishment with whips and staves, imprisonment in dungeons, the severing of limbs, or decapitation. In such ways, he inflicts immeasurable punishments according to what each individual deserves.

"Good son! A Kṣatriya, an anointed great king, who accomplishes this third wheel of kingship, by means of this wheel, causes his own realm to increase in peace and happiness; he is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, well protects his person, and increases his lifespan."
“Good son! Thus the Tathāgata has accomplished skillful means and possesses the wisdom that knows the faculties and dispositions of beings.

If any disciples, being devoid of the wisdom of merit, wisdom, and skillful means, as well as generosity, self-discipline, and tranquility—having lost mindfulness and their minds being distracted—come into my presence and take refuge in me, I thoroughly know their faculties, their inclinations, their latent tendencies, and their resolute convictions.”
According to what is appropriate for each case, I teach the Vinaya rules for discipline and punishment.

If there are sentient beings whose natures are perverse and who are unable to uphold the various precepts (śikṣāpada), I perform many actions in order to ensure that my holy teaching endures for a long time: I may establish disciplinary measures of "remembrance" (smṛti-daṇḍa); or I may use verbal instruction to terrify and rebuke them; or I may temporarily expel them; or I may cause them to be subdued and to return with sincere prostrations; or I may not speak with them nor share in their benefits; or I may apply the "grass-spreading" (tṛṇaprastāraka) penance; or I may even carry out formal excommunication (pravarjana).

By means of my wondrous wisdom, I know the faculties, inclinations, latent tendencies, and resolutions of all sentient beings and individuals; accordingly, I mete out punishment so that they may all shatter the vast accumulation of meaningless darkness, exhaust the torrential floods of afflictions, attain the bliss of rebirth in heaven and nirvana, and so that those individuals who travel upon evil paths may be tamed. Thus, according to what is appropriate for each, I teach the Dharma of remedial punishment.

I observe the distinctions between the Black Teaching and the Great Teaching, and according to what is appropriate for each, I bestow upon them the methods for punishing those who practice evil paths.
With my sublime wisdom, I know that these sentient beings are fully endowed with superior faith and reverence, as well as a purely virtuous intention.

According to what is appropriate for each, he explains various distinctions among the categories of wholesome qualities, causing them to practice and study, until all their roots of goodness are brought to full completion and they enter the city of fearlessness.

“Good son! I have accomplished this third wheel of the Buddha; by means of this wheel, I know the various faculties, inclinations, latent tendencies, and resolute convictions of all sentient beings and individuals, as well as their karmic actions, dharmas, and experiences.”
According to what is appropriate for each, they bring benefit and happiness, attaining peaceful dwelling, freedom from alarm, and fearlessness.

They declare of themselves: "I occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage; I turn the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all celestial Māras, external paths, and heterodox arguments, and I roar the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly."

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has been consecrated by coronation; he knows that within his own realm there are immeasurable sentient beings and individuals who take refuge in various false deities and non-Buddhist paths, giving rise to false faith and false views, studying false prohibitions and precepts, and clinging to the cultivation of false signs of good and bad fortune, thereby undergoing all kinds of unbeneficial suffering.

Once the Great King had understood this, he summoned them repeatedly, awakening and instructing them by means of the righteous laws with which his predecessor had governed the kingdom; he taught and exhorted them to abandon perverted faiths and perverted views, and to practice and study the upright, ancient laws of the former king.

He causes all sentient beings within his own realm to have a single destination, a single refuge, a single intention, and a single desire; they are all in harmony, collectively relying upon the true Dharma of the former kings, receiving and listening to his edicts, and complying with them in their practice. Thus, the entire land is unified, and everyone performs what ought to be done.

At that time, the Kṣatriya Great King, consecrated by coronation, frequently assembled with his ministers to enjoy fine delicacies together, experiencing various pleasures, amusements, and excursions; they harbored no mutual suspicion or duplicity, and all consulted one another to manage the affairs of state.

“Good son! A Kṣatriya, a great king who has received the consecration, accomplishes this fourth royal wheel. By means of this wheel, he causes his own realm to increase in peace and happiness; he is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, well-protects his person, and increases his lifespan.”
“Good son! Thus the Tathāgata, having accomplished skillful means, possesses the wisdom that knows the knowledge of resolute belief (*adhimukti*).

He sees that all beings in the world have various false refuges, false views, and false intentions; they delight in and cling to the practice of false dharmas and the performance of false karmas, and by these causes and conditions, they undergo immeasurable suffering.”

Having seen this, the Tathāgata repeatedly summoned them before the great assembly and, through the various causal dharmas—namely, the past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, the Three Jewels, the lineage of causes and effects, the six *pāramitās*, the causal basis of *yoga*, and the three types of restraint—he awakened and revealed them, bringing joy and consolation while exhorting and instructing the entire gathering.

He causes them to be liberated from all inverted views and establishes them in right view, placing them upon the ancient, upright path of the ten wholesome actions. Together with all sentient beings, they repeatedly practice in concert, practicing in accordance with the Dharma through skillful means that draw forth the natural outflow of cause and effect.

For the sake of all sentient beings, the fourfold assembly shall harmonize and together cultivate all sublime virtuous deeds; they shall then sport together in the four foundations of mindfulness, finding joy and delight within the samādhis, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and the various factors of enlightenment. In order to cause the holy teaching to abide long in the world and to ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels remains unbroken, they shall further sport together in the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, finding joy and delight within those various superior samādhis, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and the various factors of enlightenment.
“Son of good family!
I have accomplished this fourth wheel of the Buddha.
By means of this wheel, I know the various inclinations, the destinations and intentions, and the karmic experiences of all sentient beings and individuals.”
According to what is appropriate for each, they bring benefit and happiness, attaining peaceful dwelling, freedom from alarm, and fearlessness.

They declare of themselves: "I occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage; I turn the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all devas, Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, and I roar the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly."

“Good son! It is like a great Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated with the coronation rite, who knows that within his own realm or in other realms there are immeasurable sentient beings and individuals who are addicted to and insatiable for their own wealth and beauty, and who greedily seek and pursue the wealth and beauty of others.”

Even if one establishes solid city walls, villages, outposts, kingdoms, towns, and royal palaces—and to speak at length—down to the use of shells and parrots as defensive implements, ensuring that nothing is lost.

"Noble son! A Kṣatriya king who has been consecrated as a Great King, having accomplished this fifth royal wheel, by means of this wheel causes his own realm to increase in peace and happiness; he is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, well protects his person, and causes his lifespan to increase."
“Good son! Thus the Tathāgata has accomplished skillful means and possesses the wisdom that knows all natures.

He knows all evil Māras, the ninety-five kinds of heterodox outsiders, and the immeasurable other sentient beings deluded by Māras and outsiders who are insatiably addicted to their own wealth and beauty, who greedily pursue and crave the wealth and beauty of others, and who harbor deep hatred and jealousy toward myself and my assembly.”

In order to harm me, they prepared exquisite delicacies mixed with poison, placed fire pits in darkness while falsely laying out beds and seats, or pushed down mountain rocks, or released mad elephants, or drew their swords in pursuit; they scattered filth and dust upon me, slandered me for practicing lust, insulted me as a eunuch, or claimed I was a non-human spirit, or said I was a magical illusion—using all such evils to revile and disparage me.
They also gave rise to immeasurable varieties of slander, abuse, and insults against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Out of envy toward my resident śrāvaka disciples, they further incited various forms of defamation.

Having known this, the Tathāgata—well-guarding the six sense faculties, relying upon the four Brahma-abodes, and possessing the four analytical knowledges—proclaims the essential points of the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, establishing them in the three pure gates of liberation.
By means of such knowledge of all natures—both mundane and supramundane—I truly understand, as they are, the various and immeasurable distinctions among the natures of all sentient beings.
According to what is appropriate for each, I bring them benefit.
"O son of good family!

I have accomplished this fifth Buddha-wheel; by means of this wheel, through the knowledge of all natures—both mundane and supramundane—I know the various and immeasurable distinctions among the natures of sentient beings and individuals (pudgala).”
According to what is appropriate for each, they bring benefit and happiness, attaining peaceful dwelling, freedom from alarm, and fearlessness.

They declare of themselves: "I occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage; I turn the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all devas, Māras, heterodox teachers, and false doctrines, and I roar the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly."

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has been consecrated by coronation, having established all secure city walls, villages, watchtowers, kingdoms, towns, and royal palaces—extensively described up to including *śāra* birds and parrots as defensive equipment—and then residing within his own palace, surrounded by his kinsmen, queens, and court ladies, sporting with the various pleasures of the five desires and indulging the six sense faculties in manifold joys.”

"Noble son! A Kṣatriya, a great king consecrated by coronation, who accomplishes this sixth royal wheel—by virtue of this wheel—he causes his own realm to increase in peace and happiness; he is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, well-protects his person, and increases his lifespan."

“Good son! In this way, the Tathāgata, together with the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the great śrāvakas, having established all matters concerning the defense of the firm holy teachings, immediately manifests entry into the first dhyāna, up to manifesting entry into the fourth dhyāna; he manifests entry into the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, and so on, as extensively explained, up to manifesting entry into the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and likewise manifests entry into all concentrations practiced by the Buddhas.”

Once he had entered this meditative absorption, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, and others—who constantly harbored poisonous, evil, and harmful intentions toward sentient beings, lacking compassion or pity, and seeing no fear in the suffering of future lives—[were transformed].

When they see me enter the samādhi of the conduct of all Buddhas, they all conceive great joy toward me; they give rise to pure faith in the Three Jewels, and all produce the most supreme joy and pure faith, honoring and respecting me with such unprecedented devotion.
They feel shame and remorse for all their evils, confessing them from the depths of their hearts, repenting their transgressions, and vowing to sever them forever.
By these causes and conditions, in a single instant, immeasurable and innumerable obstacles of affliction, obstacles of karma, and obstacles to the Dharma are all completely extinguished;
immeasurable and innumerable provisions of merit and wisdom are all brought to fulfillment;
one turns away from birth and death and proceeds toward nirvana, upholding the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata.

“Good son! I have accomplished this sixth Buddha-wheel. By means of this wheel, the Tathāgata sports in the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of subtle and profound meditative concentrations—dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis—and by turning in accordance with pure wisdom, he extinguishes the immeasurable afflictions of all sentient beings.”
According to what is appropriate for each, they bring benefit and happiness, enabling beings to dwell in peace, to be free from alarm, and to be without fear.

They declare of themselves: "I occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage; I turn the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all devas, Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, and I roar the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly."

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration, leading his various ministers and the fourfold army, traveling around to inspect all the cities, towns, villages, mountains, rivers, valleys, streams, gardens, parks, fields, marshes, ponds, pools, wildernesses, groves, and military outposts within his own kingdom.”

Wherever they may be located within the various regions of the realm, those places are perilous and fraught with many hardships, unfit for administration; they are filled with suspicion and fear, and are capable of harboring external enemies and wicked associates who have fled there to hide.

This consecrated great king of the kṣatriya caste, according to his power and capability, employs skillful means to establish various repairs and solid defenses, ensuring that all regions are level and free from hardship, fit for administration, and devoid of doubt or fear; he wards off external enemies and evil associates, preventing them from seeking refuge or hiding within his borders.
He pacifies all the people of his own country so that they are all freed from manifold sufferings and experience various forms of happiness. Noble son,
when a consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste accomplishes this seventh royal wheel, by means of this wheel, he causes peace and happiness to increase within his own realm.
He is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, skillfully guarding the body and increasing one’s lifespan. “Good son!

Thus the Tathāgata, with his Buddha-eye, knows as they truly are all sentient beings and individuals who possess minds of greed, hatred, and delusion; he knows as they truly are the various differences in the afflictions, illnesses, and behavioral tendencies of these sentient beings.”

Having known this, the Tathāgata gives rise to the power of immeasurable diligence, valor, and skillful means; according to what is appropriate for each, he bestows various sublime medicines of meditative cultivation, causing all sentient beings to practice with diligence so as to eliminate the disease of afflictions.
If there are sentient beings for whom the practice of impurity is suitable to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers the medicine of practicing impurity;
if there are sentient beings for whom the practice of the Brahma-abodes is suitable to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers the medicine of practicing the Brahma-abodes;

if there are sentient beings for whom the practice of dependent origination is suitable to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers the medicine of practicing dependent origination.

If there are sentient beings for whom it is appropriate to cultivate mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers to them the medicine of cultivating mindfulness of breathing;

if there are sentient beings for whom it is appropriate to cultivate the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*) to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers to them the medicine of cultivating the three gates of liberation;

if there are sentient beings for whom it is appropriate to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers to them the medicine of cultivating meditative concentration.

If there are sentient beings for whom the cultivation of the formless realms is appropriate to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers the medicine of cultivating the formless realms;

if there are sentient beings for whom even the cultivation of various samādhis, such as the Śūraṅgama, is appropriate to eliminate the disease of afflictions, he immediately administers the medicine of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata bestows such Dharma-medicine upon all sentient beings, so that none of those beings to be converted shall be bound or captured by the four Māra-enemies.
I shall not allow any sentient beings who are to be converted to turn their backs on the vehicles of humans and devas and head toward the various evil destinies;
nor shall I allow the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Dharma-eye and the lineage of the Three Jewels to be swiftly destroyed.
For this reason, the Tathāgata bestows such medicinal teachings upon all sentient beings.
"O son of good family!

I have accomplished this seventh Buddha-wheel. By means of this wheel, through the wisdom of supreme and universal conduct, I bestow various medicinal teachings upon all living beings, causing them to diligently practice and train so as to eliminate the disease of afflictions, attaining peaceful dwelling, freedom from alarm, and fearlessness."

Claiming for himself the exalted position of a Great Sage, he turns the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all devas, Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, and utters the true lion’s roar in the midst of the great assembly.

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has been consecrated with the coronation rite, who recollects his own and others’ ancestral lineage from the past, as well as such matters as his being a newborn infant and his childhood play.”

That is to say, one recollects oneself and others in such a place at the time of initial birth: being bathed, held in one's arms, nursed with milk, and having one’s limbs massaged; continuing even until the times of play and laughter, or playing with ashes and dust, or wandering about in various ways with attendants, or practicing the arts and crafts, or engaging in various kinds of work and enterprises, or traveling to other lands and lodging there day and night, or serving a king, or managing royal affairs, or being a crown prince, or ascending the throne to attain great sovereignty and experience all manner of pleasures, with a vast reputation spreading throughout every direction.

Having reflected on these matters, he established the true Dharma followed by his predecessors, nurtured all the people of the realm, and protected his own country without encroaching upon the territories of others.
"Good son! A Kṣatriya, an anointed great king, who accomplishes this eighth royal wheel, by means of this wheel, causes his own kingdom to increase in peace and happiness."
He is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, skillfully guarding the body and increasing its lifespan. "Good son!
In this way, the Tathāgata, while in the midst of a great assembly, recollects the immeasurable varieties of events experienced by himself and others throughout past lives."

That is to say, one recollects one lifetime, or two, or three, up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lifetimes; or one recollects an eon of formation, or an eon of destruction, or immeasurable eons of formation and destruction. One recalls that in the past, one dwelt in such a place, had such a name, belonged to such a clan, was of such a caste, ate such food, experienced such feelings of suffering and pleasure, had such a lifespan, remained for such a duration, and reached such a limit of the lifespan; having passed away from that place, one was reborn here, and having again passed away from here, one was reborn there.

Recalling such matters from past lives—immeasurable and boundless—he establishes the True Dharma according to the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings, thereby bringing them benefit.

“Good son! I have accomplished this eighth wheel of the Buddha; by means of this wheel, I bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, enabling them to dwell in peace and stability, to be free from alarm and fear, and to attain fearlessness.”

He proclaims himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, turning the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all the celestial Māras, external paths, and heterodox arguments, and uttering the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

“Good son! It is like a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration, who, according to his reflection and observation, examines the sentient beings, lineages, skills, and various undertakings within his own kingdom, as well as their deaths here and births there, and the differences in the excellence or inferiority of their causes and effects.

He knows that those sentient beings are born into such families; he knows whether their bodies are courageous and robust or timid and weak; whether they have already studied or not yet studied the various arts and crafts; whether they perform their tasks well or poorly; and whether they are wealthy or poor, noble or lowly, handsome or ugly.
In such categories, until the end of their lives, some die because their own karma is not yet exhausted;
some die because their own karma has already been exhausted; some die through execution for violating the king’s law;
some die from mutual slaughter and injury; some die from being whipped, flogged, or beaten; and some die from imprisonment and confinement in dungeons.
Or they die because of practicing arts and crafts; or they die because of being wounded or killed in battle;
or they die because of fighting, quarreling, or physical assault; or they die because of greed and stinginess regarding wealth and treasures;
or they die because of indulgence in sensual desire; or they die because of anger, resentment, and bitter indignation; or they die because of exhaustion.
They die exhausted and worn out; they die from the exhaustion of hunger and thirst;
some die with fault, others die without fault; some die in old age, some die in middle age, and some die in youth;
some die having performed various kinds of wholesome deeds, and some die having performed various kinds of unwholesome deeds.
He knows that those sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, proceed to a happy destination.
He knows that those sentient beings who practice unwholesome deeds will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, proceed to an unhappy destination.
Having understood this matter, he further reflected to himself:
"I shall apply right effort to cultivate wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind;
I shall employ various skillful means, practice, generosity, self-mastery, and tranquility."
"At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he shall go to a happy destination and not fall into an evil realm.
Having reflected thus, this Kṣatriya great king, consecrated by coronation, with courage and diligence, cultivates the three kinds of wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind;

he constantly practices giving, being without stinginess regarding all that he possesses—food and drink, clothing, elephants, horses, and mounts, bedding, medicine, dwellings, lamps, and other requisites, as well as slaves, servants, various precious treasures, and even his own head, eyes, hands, feet, and life itself.

Furthermore, they abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, abstain from harsh speech, abstain from divisive speech, abstain from frivolous chatter, abstain from all covetousness, abstain from all ill will, and abstain from all wrong views.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, this consecrated Kṣatriya great king shall obtain ten kinds of meritorious benefits.

What are the ten? First, he will possess great renown; second, he will possess great wealth and treasures; third, he will possess exquisite physical marks; fourth, he will possess many followers; fifth, he will have little illness and little affliction; sixth, his friends and kinsmen will be wise and learned; seventh, those who are upright and practice correctly will draw near to him and offer him support; eighth, his broad and beautiful reputation will spread throughout the ten directions; ninth, deities of great majesty and power will constantly follow and protect him; and tenth, when his body perishes and his life ends, he shall be reborn in the heavens, dwelling eternally in a land of bliss within the happy realms.
"Noble son! A Kṣatriya, an anointed great king, who accomplishes this ninth royal wheel—by means of this wheel, he causes his own realm to increase in peace and happiness."
He is able to subdue all enemies and evil associates, skillfully guarding the body and increasing one’s lifespan. “Good son!
In this way, the Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, all matters concerning the death and rebirth of sentient beings.”

That is to say, knowing things as they truly are: if sentient beings engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones and possess wrong views; then, due to the causes and conditions of such karma of wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the various evil destinies—whether born in hell, or born among animals, or born as hungry ghosts.

If there are sentient beings who have accomplished good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones; who are endowed with right view and the karmic causes of right view; then, at the breaking up of the body after death, they ascend to the various happy realms—whether being born among the devas, or born among human beings, or exhausting all outflows.

Having thus known this as it truly is, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for those sentient beings; with valor and diligence, he manifests the three miraculous transformations to cause those beings to take refuge in the Buddha-dharma, instructing and establishing them in mundane and supramundane faith.
What are the three?
First, the manifestation of supernormal powers;
second, the manifestation of prophetic declaration.
Third is the manifestation of instruction and admonition.

By means of these three kinds of manifested power, he exhorts and inspires sentient beings, providing instruction and establishing them in mundane and supramundane faith, so that they may attain liberation from birth and death within all realms of existence.

“Good son! I have accomplished this ninth Buddha-wheel; by means of this wheel, I bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, enabling them to dwell in peace and security, to be free from alarm, and to be without fear.”

He proclaims himself to occupy the exalted position of a Great Sage, turning the Wheel of the Buddha, crushing all Maras, celestial demons, heterodox paths, and false doctrines, and uttering the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

“Good son! It is like a great Kṣatriya king who has received the consecration, who relinquishes his royal throne in order to eliminate the various physical ailments of immeasurable sentient beings throughout the four continents.”
Having bathed his body and head with various fragrant waters, he put on fresh, clean garments and sat upright in contemplation.
Toward all sentient beings, his mind was impartial, guarding and mindful of them with loving-kindness and compassion.
In order to bring liberation from all illnesses, one should offer various kinds of incense, flowers, music, and other ritual implements to worship all the deities of great majesty and power.
At that time, all the emperors of the gods, the emperors of the nāgas, and even the emperors of the mahoraga spirits, having learned of these matters, said to one another:

"This consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste possesses all meritorious virtues and great majestic power; he ought to become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) and rule over the four continents."

"We ought to go together to establish him, restore him to the royal throne, and have him govern the four continents, so that all sentient beings may be free from illness and dwell in peace and happiness.

Then, from the various celestial emperors down to the emperors of the *mahoraga* spirits, they immediately went together and established the consecrated Kṣatriya Great King as a Wheel-Turning Monarch (*cakravartin*), endowing him with the seven treasures and governing the four great continents, attaining sovereignty over them all.

He will be endowed with a thousand sons, valiant, robust, and handsome, capable of crushing his enemies. He shall rule over the great earth as far as the limits of the ocean; punishments shall cease, weapons and staves shall not be raised, and all shall practice the True Dharma, universally enjoying peace and happiness.

"Noble son! A Kṣatriya, an anointed great king, who accomplishes such a tenth royal wheel—by virtue of this wheel—he establishes all sentient beings within the four great continents and the eighty-four thousand minor islands in the ten paths of wholesome action. He well protects their bodies, causes their lifespans to increase, and ensures that when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall be reborn among the devas and experience various sublime pleasures."

“Good son! Thus, when the Tathāgata was formerly in the stage of a bodhisattva, he knew that his own body and the bodies of others possessed immeasurable kinds of afflictions as diseases; he bathed his body with the perfumed water of meditative concentration, washed his head with the great kindness and great compassion of the Dharma of Truth, and donned the garment of shame and remorse.”

All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, through their various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), diligence (*vīrya*), skillful means (*upāya*), wisdom-mind (*jñāna-citta*), and compassionate protection, all spoke these words: "O Great Being!..."
This is a precious vessel adorned with great merit and wisdom!

It is capable of containing all three kinds of non-protection, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it is capable of attaining the unsurpassed knowledge of omniscience, and is fully endowed with great loving-kindness and great compassion.

Always delighting in the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, this leader among merchants seeking the Buddha-jewel can rescue sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth and death and bestow upon them the great bliss of nirvāṇa.

We, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall with truthful words grant him his vow, enabling him to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, to attain the unsurpassed Dharma, and to become a Great Dharma King.
At that time, relying on the power of merit and wisdom through courageous diligence, I realized the Four Noble Truths as they truly are and attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
“Good son! Just as a wheel-turning monarch rules over the four great continents and attains mastery over them all,

so too does the Tathāgata attain mastery over the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, the four Brahma-abodes, the four analytical knowledges, the contemplation of the four noble truths, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the knowledge of all modes.”
Just as a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with the seven treasures,
so too does the Tathāgata achieve the seven kinds of jewels of the factors of enlightenment.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch is fully possessed of a thousand sons who are brave, strong, and handsome, capable of subduing enemies, so it is with the Tathāgata.

Thus, for the Tathāgata, there were the great śrāvakas, beginning with Ājñātakauṇḍinya and ending with Subhadra Sauraka, who were born from the mind of the Buddha, born from the mouth of the Buddha, and transformed by birth from the Dharma; having attained a portion of the Buddha’s Dharma, their outflows were forever exhausted, and they were named "the Valiant."
Possessing the four Brahma-abodes is called being "handsome"; such a person is able to subdue all celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, heterodox arguments, and enemies.
Like a Wheel-Turning King, their transformative influence extends to eighty-four thousand minor islands.

In this manner, the Tathāgata, within this one vast and high Buddha-field, attains mastery in manifesting transformative teachings through his voice throughout a hundred koṭis of Jambudvīpas, a hundred koṭis of Aparagoyānīdvīpas, a hundred koṭis of Pūrvavidehadvīpas, a hundred koṭis of Uttarakuru-dvīpas; throughout a hundred koṭis of great oceans, a hundred koṭis of Sumeru mountains, a hundred koṭis of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and so on up to a hundred koṭis of the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; and throughout a hundred koṭis of the Great Cakravāḍa mountain ranges.

“Good son! I have accomplished this tenth Buddha-wheel; by means of this wheel, I know as it truly is that the outflows (āsrava) of myself and others are forever exhausted. Thus, I bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, attaining peaceful dwelling, freedom from alarm, and fearlessness.”

Claiming for himself the exalted position of a Great Sage, he turns the Wheel of the Buddha, subdues all devas, Māras, externalists, and heterodox arguments, and utters the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.

“Good son! Having accomplished these ten kinds of Buddha-wheels through the power of my original vows, I dwell in this buddha-field of the five turbidities and evil world. All sentient beings therein have diminished all pure and wholesome dharmas; they are destitute of all the seven treasures of the noble ones; they are far removed from all wise and sagacious sages; and they are shrouded by the net of eternalism and nihilism.
They constantly delight in riding the chariots of the various evil realms and see no fear in the sufferings of future lives.”

They constantly dwell in the pervasive and heavy darkness of ignorance, possessing the ten unwholesome karmas, committing the five deeds of immediate retribution, slandering the True Dharma, reviling the noble ones, abandoning all wholesome dharmas, and being endowed with all unwholesome dharmas;
yet, because I have accomplished these Ten Wheels of the Buddha within them, I abide in peace, am free from alarm, and possess fearlessness.

He proclaims himself to occupy the exalted station of a Great Sage, turning the Wheel of the Buddha, subduing all devas, Māras, and non-Buddhist heretics with their false doctrines, and destroying the adamantine, solid afflictions of all sentient beings.
"According to their inclinations, we shall establish all sentient beings who possess power, causing them to abide in the stage of non-retrogression within the Three Vehicles.

At that time, the entire assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, all Śrāvakas, all devas and nāgas—and so on, including all the gaṇas of kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans—were all filled with great joy. Together they cried out, "Excellent! They rained down a great rain of incense, a great rain of flowers, a rain of various jewels, and a rain of great garments; the entire great earth shook in every way.

Upon hearing this exposition of the ten kinds of Buddha-wheels, within that assembly, eighty-four hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, there were immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained various dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and patiences.
Moreover, there were immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who first gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings who attained the realization of the fruits [of the path].
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Two.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: On Practice Without Dependence, Part One.

At that time, in the assembly, there was a Great Brahmā named Devagarbha—who had long cultivated roots of goodness, dwelt in the tenth stage, and was fully endowed with the virtues of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. He rose from his seat, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and spoke in verse:
“O Ocean of Wisdom, Treasury of Merit, I now ask about my doubts;
may you, O Ocean of Wisdom, deign to listen and dispel my lingering uncertainties for me.
We now thirst and long for the flavor of the sublime Dharma, the Treasury of Virtue.”
"And the most supreme meaning and flavor—may the entire assembly desire to hear them.
The Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā Deva Tiṣya, saying:
"The Tathāgata now permits you to ask as you wish; I shall answer according to your questions and cause your heart to rejoice."
The Great Brahmā said:
“Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
He asked in verse:
"One who possesses sharp wisdom and cultivates meditative concentration, abiding in heedfulness—
does such a person abide in the ultimate truth?"
Do you rely upon birth and death?
Or do you diligently recite and study the meaning of the Dharma day and night in order to cross the ocean of afflictions?
Is it for falling back into the evil realms?
Diligently and valiantly cultivate merit; Is it for certain progression toward Nirvana?
Or while dwelling within birth and death, Will you fall back into the evil realms?
O wise Kṣatriya, having accomplished the ten wheels,
will you sink into the midst of birth and death,
or shall you ascend to the fruit of Buddhahood?
“The defiled mind is difficult to subdue, being disturbed by various afflictions;
by what means can one purify that mind through the practices of meditative concentration, merit, and recitation?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great Brahmā Devakūṭa, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! You possess skillful eloquence to inquire about this meaning;

you have already exerted yourself in this Dharma, you have attained perfection regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and in the presence of as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, you have diligently applied the three karmas, caused the True Dharma to flourish, and succeeded to the lineage of the Triple Gem.”
Now, for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings, you have again questioned the Tathāgata regarding this profound meaning. "Good son!

There is a great prophetic teaching named 'Practice Without Dependence. All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones of the past, in order to bring sentient beings to maturity, to cause them to cultivate weariness toward and detachment from the phenomena of birth and death, to cause them to sever and abandon karma and afflictions, and to cause the three vehicles to be swiftly perfected, proclaimed and maintained this great prophetic teaching of Practice Without Dependence."

Now, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions likewise proclaim and maintain this Great Prophecy of the Practice Without Support for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, for the sake of causing them to grow weary of and renounce the phenomena of birth and death, for the sake of causing them to sever and eliminate karma and afflictions, and for the sake of causing the three vehicles to be swiftly perfected.

All future Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will likewise proclaim and uphold this Great Prediction Dharma of the Practice Without Support, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, for the sake of causing them to cultivate revulsion toward the phenomena of birth and death, for the sake of causing them to sever and eliminate karma and afflictions, and for the sake of causing the three vehicles to be swiftly perfected.
In the presence of all the Tathāgatas of the past, you have already fully heard this Dharma of the Great Prophecy of the Practice Without Support.

Now, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, for the sake of causing them to feel weary of and detach from the phenomena of birth and death, for the sake of causing them to sever the afflictions of karma, and for the sake of causing the three vehicles to be swiftly perfected, I proclaim and uphold this Dharma of the Great Prophecy of the Practice Without Support.
"You should listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
At that time, the Great Brahma Heaven Deity Tianzang said:
“Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
“I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, “Great Brahmā!
There are ten kinds of practices that lack reliance.

If a practitioner of meditative concentration possesses even one of these practices, they will still be unable to accomplish the roots of goodness of the desire realm; even if they have previously accomplished them, they will immediately fall away and lose them. How much less could they possibly accomplish the meditative concentrations of the form or formless realms, or even achieve any one of the three vehicles?
What are these ten?
First, there is a class of people in the world who, though desiring to cultivate meditative concentration, lack the necessary resources and are distracted by the toil of seeking them.
Second, there is another class who, though desiring to cultivate meditative concentration, violate the precepts and engage in various evil deeds.

Third, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, hold inverted views, falsely cling to notions of good and bad fortune, and possess bodies and minds that are rigid and stubborn.

Fourth, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, have restless and agitated minds, do not accord with the noble ones, and possess faculties that are light and fickle.
Fifth, there is another class who, though desiring to cultivate meditative concentration, use divisive speech to create discord and confusion between others.
Sixth, there is another class who, though desiring to cultivate meditative concentration, use harsh and abusive speech to revile and insult the noble ones.
Seventh, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, engage in frivolous speech and false speech.
Eighth, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, harbor greed and envy toward the gains and honors obtained by others, and their minds find no joy therein.
Ninth, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, harbor anger and resentment toward sentient beings, their minds constantly filled with indignation and wrath.
Tenth, there is another class who, though wishing to cultivate meditative concentration, harbor wrong views that deny cause and effect.
Mahābrahmā! You should know that these are called the ten kinds of practices devoid of reliance.

If a practitioner of meditative concentration possesses even one of these practices, they will still be unable to accomplish the roots of goodness of the desire realm; even if they were previously accomplished, they would immediately fall away and lose them. How much less could they possibly accomplish the meditative concentrations of the form or formless realms, or even achieve any of the three vehicles?
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
There are ten kinds of practices that lack a basis.

If a practitioner of meditative concentration engages in even one of these practices, they will ultimately be unable to achieve any *samādhi*; even if they should previously have achieved them, they will soon fall away and lose them."
What are the ten? First, attachment to worldly activities;
second, attachment to idle discourse.
Third, delighting in and attachment to sleep;
fourth, delighting in and attachment to seeking and acquisition;
fifth, delighting in and attachment to beautiful forms.
Sixth, attachment to exquisite sounds;
seventh, attachment to fragrant scents;
eighth, attachment to delicious flavors.
Ninth, they delight in and are attached to subtle tactile sensations.
Tenth, they delight in and are attached to discursive thought and investigation.
Great Brahmā!
One should know that these are called the ten types of practices lacking a basis.

If a practitioner of meditative concentration engages in even one of these practices, they will ultimately be unable to achieve any samādhis; even if they were previously achieved, they will soon fall away and lose them.

If one is unable to achieve the various samādhis, then even though one has accumulated a collection of other wholesome dharmas, such things may occur: on account of seeking the enjoyment of offerings given in faith, one gives rise to unwholesome minds and mental factors, thereby committing transgressions against kings, ministers, and others; or one may be reviled, beaten, or have one's limbs, hands, and feet severed.

Due to these causes and conditions, they may either contract a grave illness and suffer for a long time, or their lives may end prematurely as they are reborn in one of the three evil destinies, even as far as the Avīci Hell—just like Udraka, Arāḍa, Tiṣya, Kūpālaka, Devadatta, and others of their kind—who fell away from meditative concentration and even descended into the Avīci Hell, undergoing immeasurable kinds of unbearable great suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya, saying:

"I authorize you to provide the foremost dwellings, the foremost bedding and seating, and the foremost food and drink for those bhikṣus who practice meditation in the forest hermitages (āraṇya). They shall be exempted from all monastic duties."

Why is this so? Because if those who practice meditative concentration lack the necessary material provisions, they will immediately give rise to all manner of unwholesome minds and mental factors; they will be unable to achieve the various *samādhis*, and may even fall into the Avīci Hell, where they undergo immeasurable kinds of unbearable, great suffering.

For a practitioner cultivating meditative concentration, if they possess the necessary material conditions, those samādhis not yet accomplished will be accomplished; if they have already been accomplished, they will never be lost. By means of this, one does not give rise to any unwholesome dharmas, ranging extensively from unwholesome thoughts and investigations up to rebirth in the heavens and the realization of nirvāṇa.

A practitioner of meditative concentration who has not yet attained the various *samādhis* should abandon sleep during the first and last watches of the night, training with diligence, remaining far removed from clamor and bustle, being content with few desires, free from attachment, and completely distancing themselves from all greed, hatred, anger, concealment, malice, harm, pride, arrogance, stinginess, envy, divisive speech, harsh words, falsehood, frivolous talk, and all human amusements, dissipation, and negligence.

A practitioner such as this should receive the praise, prostration, reverence, service, and offerings of hundreds of thousands of nayutas from Śakra, Brahmā, the Four World-Protecting Kings, the Wheel-Turning Kings, and others—not to mention from kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, and śūdras.
Even those who have not yet attained meditative concentration should still receive this praise, prostration, respect, service, and offerings; how much more so those who have already attained samādhi!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Cultivating meditative concentration can sever delusions— a task no other practice can accomplish.
Therefore, the cultivation of concentration is supreme; the wise should offer it their veneration."
At that time, the Great Brahmā Deva Gaganagañja said:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!

Regarding those who have gone forth from home within the Buddha-dharma—whether they be Kṣatriyas, great ministers, or state counselors—if their bodies are beaten with whips, staves, and the like; or if they are imprisoned, or reviled, or have their limbs severed, or have their lives cut short—is this indeed appropriate?"
"Is it not improper?
The Buddha addressed the Great Brahmā Devakūṭa, saying: "Good son!

If any sentient beings go forth in my Dharma, even to the extent of shaving off their hair and beards and donning a fragment of the saffron robe—whether they uphold the precepts, violate them, or fall as low as being without precepts at all—then all devas, humans, asuras, and others, even according to the worldly right dharma, ought not to strike their bodies with whips or rods, nor imprison them, nor revile them, nor dismember their limbs, nor take their lives; how much less so by means of what is contrary to the dharma?

Why is this? With the exception of those who uphold the precepts and possess great learning among those who have gone forth within my Dharma, if there are those who break the precepts and practice various evil dharmas—whose inner nature is rotten like a foul snail, who are not truly śramaṇas yet claim to be śramaṇas, who are not truly practitioners of the holy life yet claim to be practitioners of the holy life, and who are constantly overcome by various afflictions, being ruined, corrupted, and overturned.

Even such evil bhikṣus who have broken their precepts are still able to show and guide all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans to the immeasurable treasure-trove of precious merits.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Those who have gone forth within my Dharma, even if they have broken their precepts, should inspire ten kinds of sublime reflections in sentient beings upon seeing their physical appearance, whereby those beings shall obtain an immeasurable accumulation of the jewels of merit."
What are these ten? They are as follows:

among those who have gone forth in my Dharma, even if they have violated their precepts, there may be sentient beings who, upon seeing them, give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, profound reverence, faithful respect, and sublime reflection. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they will ultimately never turn to believe in the teachers, scriptures, or assemblies of non-Buddhist paths; furthermore, they will be able to enter the great city of Nirvana, which is free from all fears.

Or, having seen this, they may give rise to the thought of the sublime nature of the noble precepts; by reason of this cause and condition, they are able to abstain from taking life, abstain from taking what is not given, abstain from sexual misconduct, abstain from false speech, and abstain from drinking intoxicants which lead to heedlessness, and even go so far as to enter the great city of Nirvana, free from all fears.

Some, having seen this, give rise to the thought of giving and sublime reflections; by reason of these causes and conditions, they attain great wealth and status, and through drawing near to, making offerings to, and correctly following those who have reached the goal and practice rightly, they are even able to enter the city of Great Nirvāṇa, which is free from all fears.

Some, upon seeing this, give rise to thoughts of patience, gentleness, uprightness, and sublime reflection; by these causes and conditions, they are able to distance themselves from divisive speech, harsh words, frivolous chatter, and anger, and even enter the great city of Nirvana, which is free from all fears.

Some, upon seeing this, give rise to the thought of renouncing the household life and cultivate superior reflections through diligent practice; by these causes and conditions, they are able to abandon the ways of the home and enter the homeless state, practicing with valor and diligence all sublime conducts, even unto entering the great city of Nirvāṇa, which is free from all fears.

Or, having seen this, they give rise to the thought of distancing themselves from all distracted minds and cultivate the sublime contemplation of meditative concentrations and attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*); by reason of these causes and conditions, their hearts delight in mountain forests and forest hermitages (*aranyaka*), and they diligently practice various meditative disciplines day and night, until they are able to enter the great city of Nirvāṇa, which is free from all fear.

Some, having seen this, give rise to thoughts of wisdom and sublime reflection; by reason of these causes and conditions, they joyfully listen to, hear, read, and recite the True Dharma, even unto the point of being able to enter the Great City of Nirvana, which is free from all fears.

Or, having seen [him], they may give rise to thoughts of the excellence of roots of goodness for renunciation planted in past lives, offer gentle words of consolation, and even prostrate at his feet. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall be born into families of great power and noble status; immeasurable sentient beings will all look up to them with reverence, and they will eventually be able to enter the great city of Nirvāṇa, which is free from all fears.

“Good son! Those who have gone forth within my Dharma, even if they have broken their precepts and conduct, will cause sentient beings to give rise to these ten kinds of sublime reflections upon seeing their physical form; such beings shall obtain an immeasurable accumulation of the jewels of merit.”

Therefore, it is absolutely improper for any Kṣatriya king, minister, or counselor to strike their bodies with whips or staffs, or to imprison them, or to revile them, or to dismember their limbs, or to take their lives.
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!

If there are those who have gone forth in reliance upon me, yet violate the precepts and engage in evil conduct, being internally rotten like a foul snail, who are not truly śramaṇas though they call themselves śramaṇas, and are not truly practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya) though they call themselves practitioners of the holy life; they are constantly overcome by various afflictions (kleśa), ruined, and overturned."

In this way, although a bhikṣu may have violated the prohibitions and engaged in various evil deeds, he acts as a spiritual friend to all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, showing them the way to the immeasurable treasury of merit.

Thus, although such a bhikṣu is not a true vessel of the Dharma, he shaves his hair and beard and wears the saffron robes; his deportment and dignified conduct are identical to those of the noble sages.

Because of seeing him, the various roots of goodness of immeasurable sentient beings all attain growth, and he is further able to reveal to immeasurable sentient beings the correct path to rebirth in the higher realms, birth as a deva, and nirvāṇa.

Therefore, regarding those who have gone forth under me—whether they uphold the precepts, violate them, or even lack them entirely—I do not permit wheel-turning monarchs, other kings, or various ministers to subject their bodies to flogging with whips or canes, or to imprison them, or to revile them, or to dismember their limbs, or to take their lives, according to secular law; how much less so by unlawful means!

“Mahābrahmā! Although such a bhikṣu of broken precepts and evil conduct is called a ‘corpse’ within my Dharma and Vinaya, he still possesses the residual power of the virtue of his renunciant precepts.”

For example, after the life of a cow or a musk deer has ended, although they are the corpses of insentient animals, the cow possesses its medicinal bile and the musk deer its fragrance; these can bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

A bhikṣu who has broken his precepts is likewise; although he is called a "corpse" within my Dharma and Vinaya, because he still possesses the residual power of the virtue of his renunciant precepts, he can bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

“Mahābrahmā! It is like a merchant who enters the great ocean, slaughters a certain class of immeasurable sentient beings, plucks out their eyes, and combines them with madana fruits, pounding and sifting them to produce an eye-remedy jewel.”

If there are sentient beings who are blind and sightless, even those born blind from the womb, by applying this precious medicinal ointment to their eyes, all their ailments will be removed and they will obtain clear, pure vision.

A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is likewise; although within my Dharma and Vinaya he is called a corpse, he still possesses the outward appearance and deportment of one who has gone forth. Even those immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who merely catch a glimpse of him obtain the pure eye of Dharma and wisdom, let alone those who are able to proclaim the True Dharma for others!
"Mahābrahmā! It is like burning incense: although its substance is consumed, its fragrance remains pervasive, perfuming others with its scent.
A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is just like this; because he has broken the precepts, he is not a field of merit."

Although they are constantly consumed by the offerings of the faithful day and night, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life fall into the three evil realms, they bring great benefit to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, causing them all to hear the fragrance of rebirth in heaven and of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Mahābrahmā!
All laypeople should protect, revere, and make offerings to such bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct.
I absolutely do not permit householders to strike their bodies with whips or staves, or to imprison them, or to revile them, or to dismember their limbs, or to take their lives.
I permit only that the pure community of monks may, at the time of the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇa*, expel such a person and drive him out.
He shall not be permitted to receive or use any gifts bestowed upon the Saṃgha of the four quarters, including food, drink, or requisites;
regarding all matters of the śramaṇa’s *vinaya*, he shall be expelled and not allowed to remain within the assembly.
"I do not permit the application of whips or staves, nor binding, nor the taking of life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Though the *campaka* flower may wither and fade, It still surpasses all other flowers."
"Even bhikṣus who have broken their precepts and committed evil deeds are superior to all the hosts of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, Great Brahmā,
there are five great sins of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma)."
What are the five?
First, intentionally killing one's father.
Second, intentionally killing one's mother.
Third, intentionally killing an arhat;
