fourth, with perverted views, causing a schism in the Saṃgha of śrāvakas;
fifth, with an evil mind, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
These five types are called the great sinful karmas of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
If a person commits even one of these five acts of immediate retribution, they are ineligible for renunciation and the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one were to cause such a person to leave the household life or receive full ordination, the preceptor would commit an offense, and that person should be expelled from my Dharma.

Even though such a person possesses the outward appearance and deportment of one who has left the household life, I do not permit anyone to strike them with a whip or staff, imprison them, revile them, dismember their limbs, or take their life.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of fundamental sins that approximate the great evil karma of the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*). What are these four?
First, to kill a *pratyekabuddha* with an unwholesome mind; this is the fundamental sin of the great evil karma of taking life."
Second, to engage in sexual misconduct with an Arhat bhikṣuṇī is the fundamental sin among the great sinful karmas of sexual misconduct.
Third, to plunder or damage the property of the Triple Gem that has been offered is the fundamental sin among the great sinful karmas of taking what is not given.
Fourth, to destroy a harmonious Saṃgha through perverted views is a fundamental sin among the great evil karmas of false speech.
If a person commits even one of these four fundamental sins that approximate the immediate [ānantarya] offenses, they are ineligible for renunciation or the reception of full ordination.
If one causes such a person to go forth or receive full ordination, the preceptor incurs an offense; they should be expelled from my Dharma.

Even though such a person has gone forth and received full ordination and possesses the outward marks and deportment of a monk, I do not permit anyone to strike them with a whip or staff, imprison them, revile them, dismember their limbs, or take their life.

"In this way, there are cases where there is a root offense that is not an immediate offense; there are cases where there is an immediate offense that is not a root offense; there are cases where there is both a root offense and an immediate offense; and there are cases where there is neither a root offense nor an immediate offense."
What are those that are called both root transgressions and ānantarya offenses?

They refer to cases within my teaching where one who has previously gone forth and received full ordination intentionally kills another who has already reached the culmination [of the path] and seen the truths; such are called both root transgressions and ānantarya offenses.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya of mine, such individuals should be swiftly expelled.
What is defined as a root offense that is not an immediate (ānantarya) offense?

It refers to one who, within my Dharma, has already gone forth and received full ordination, yet intentionally kills another ordinary person (pṛthagjana), even down to employing means such as giving someone poison to cause an abortion; this is called a root offense that is not an immediate offense.
This person should not dwell together with the Saṃgha, nor should they be permitted to enjoy any of the offerings made to the Saṃgha from the four quarters.
What is meant by an "immediate offense" (ānantarya) that is not a "root offense" (mūlāpatti)?

That is to say, if there is a person who has received the three refuges, or the five precepts, or the ten precepts, yet commits any one of the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), this is called an immediate offense (*ānantarya-karma*) rather than a fundamental offense (*mūla-āpatti*).
Such a person is unfit for renunciation and the reception of full ordination.
If one causes them to renounce or receive full ordination, the preceptor incurs an offense; they should be expelled from my Dharma.
What are those that are neither root transgressions nor ānantarya crimes?

They refer to cases where a person, having either received the three refuges or the five precepts, conceives doubts regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; or turns to non-Buddhist paths to take as their guide; or clings to various signs of good or bad fortune, whether few or many, to perform sacrifices to ghosts and spirits.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, regarding the true Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas—whether it be the true Dharma associated with the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the true Dharma associated with the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the true Dharma associated with the Mahāyāna—slanders and obstructs it, neither believing nor accepting it themselves, and causes others to feel aversion and turn away from it; or if they hinder others from reading, reciting, or copying it, even to the extent of creating obstacles for a single verse of the true Dharma: such a person is said to have committed a grave and evil karmic deed that is neither a root offense nor an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), yet is extremely heavy and near to an immediate transgression.
Such a person, if they have not yet repented and eliminated such great sinful karma, is unfit for renunciation or the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one allows them to renounce or receive full ordination, the preceptor incurs an offense; they should be expelled from my Dharma.
If they have already renounced or received full ordination and commit such an offense, provided they do not repent, they should be swiftly expelled from this Vinaya of my Dharma.

Why is this? These two kinds of people practice the destruction of the eye of the True Dharma; they practice the concealment and extinction of the lamp of the True Dharma; they practice the severing of the lineage of the Triple Gem. They cause gods and humans to practice what is meaningless, unbeneficial, and painful, leading them to fall into the various evil destinies.
These two types of persons slander the True Dharma and revile the noble ones themselves, and they also cause others to slander the True Dharma and revile the noble ones.
At the end of their lives, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell, where they will suffer for kalpas, beyond all remedy.
"Furthermore, Great Brahmā!
There are proscriptive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) that lack a basis for practice, and there are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) that lack a basis for practice;
within those natural offenses, there are some fundamental [offenses] that lack a basis for practice."
What is the fundamental practice of non-reliance?

It refers to when a bhikṣu commits a root offense by engaging in unchaste conduct; or commits a root offense by intentionally killing an ordinary person; or commits a root offense by stealing property that does not belong to the Triple Gem; or commits a root offense by speaking a great falsehood.

If there is a bhikṣu who commits any one of these four kinds of root offenses, he shall undergo disciplinary subjugation regarding all activities performed by the bhikṣus; furthermore, it is not permitted for him to enjoy any of the requisites given to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
Furthermore, one must not apply whips or canes, nor imprison them, nor revile them, nor dismember their limbs, nor take their lives.
This is called the practice of non-reliance regarding the fundamental grave offenses among natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Why are they called root offenses?

It is because if anyone commits these four dharmas, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the various evil destinies; since these are the root offenses for those evil destinies, they are therefore called root offenses.

For what reason are the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), the proximate immediate transgressions, the root offenses, and so forth, called extremely grave and heavy sinful karmas and practices devoid of refuge?
O son of good family!
For example, just as a ball of iron, a ball of lead, or a ball of tin, once thrown into the air, never remains suspended for even a moment but must swiftly fall to the ground;

so too it is with these two kinds of offenders: those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and the four root offenses proximate to them, as well as those who slander the True Dharma or harbor doubts regarding the Triple Gem.

If a person commits any one of these eleven offenses, at the dissolution of the body after death, without any interval, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Great Hell to undergo various intense sufferings.
Therefore, it is called the practice of extremely grave, heavy, and evil karma that leaves one without refuge.

A *pudgala* who commits this extremely grave, heavy, and evil karma of the practice without refuge will certainly be unable to exhaust all afflictions within their current body, nor even achieve any *samādhis*, let alone enter the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
"When that person’s life ends, they will certainly be reborn in hell and undergo various heavy sufferings.

Furthermore, Mahābrahmā, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with pure faith, takes refuge in my Dharma— whether proceeding toward the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or the Mahāyāna— and within my Dharma, out of pure faith leaves the household life and receives full ordination, then with a profound mind of reverence for the training rules (śikṣāpada), they firmly, courageously, and diligently guard the four fundamental root downfalls."

Such a person is constantly followed and protected by all humans and non-humans alike; they are said to receive the offerings of devas and humans not in vain, and according to their own inclination among the three vehicles, they are able to swiftly enter and accomplish the ultimate goal.
Therefore, one who truly seeks nirvāṇa would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever transgress these four dharmas. Why is this?
Because all sentient beings must rely on three causes to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa:
First, taking the Tathāgata as the basis for the cause;
second, taking my holy teaching as the basis for the cause;
third, taking my disciples as the basis for the cause.
All classes of sentient beings, relying on these three causes, practice with diligent effort and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
If a person violates these four dharmas, I am not their teacher, and they are not my disciples.

If a person violates these four dharmas, they transgress the profound and vast teachings I have proclaimed concerning impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—the instructions for the individual liberation that bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

If one transgresses such teachings on individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), one will become blind and dark regarding all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and concentrations (*samādhi*), unable to enter them; bound by various afflictions (*kleśa*) and evil karma, one becomes an unfit vessel for the Three Vehicles and shall fall into the miserable realms (*apāya*) to undergo manifold heavy sufferings.

“If a son of good family or a daughter of good family remains pure and unoffending regarding the four root heavy offenses prescribed in the Prātimokṣa teachings I have spoken, I am their teacher and they are my disciples; following my words and dwelling well in my Dharma, all that they undertake shall be brought to fulfillment.”

Because this person abides well in the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha), they are said to "abide well in all wholesome dharmas," or "fully abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas," or "fully abide in the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas," or "fully abide in the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna)."

Why is this? If one is able to guard and uphold these four fundamental precepts of natural transgression, it should be known that this establishes the supreme cause for all conditioned and unconditioned wholesome dharmas.
Therefore, upholding these four dharmas is called the root of all wholesome dharmas.
Just as all medicinal herbs, grains, plants, trees, and forests grow by depending upon the great earth,
so too do all wholesome dharmas grow by relying upon the excellent preservation of these four fundamental precepts.
Just as all mountains—the Lesser Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains, and Sumeru, the King of Mountains—rest securely upon the great earth;
so too, by relying upon and perfectly upholding the four fundamental precepts, all those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and the Unsurpassed Mahāyāna rest securely.
Just as one obtains all the exquisite flavors of the world by relying upon the great earth,

so too, by relying upon and perfectly upholding the four fundamental precepts, one obtains all mindfulness, concentration, dhāraṇīs, patience, and the noble path, up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, just as the great earth impartially supports both the pure and the impure, so too do these good sons and good daughters who perfectly uphold the four fundamental precepts;

they maintain an even mind toward those who are vessels for the Dharma and those who are not, neither mocking nor deriding them, nor being conceited, nor hastily censuring them, and thus they serve as the source from which all wholesome dharmas arise.

Furthermore, just as all sentient beings together rely upon and utilize the great earth to survive, so too it is with those sons and daughters of good family who perfectly uphold the four root precepts;

they give rise to the foremost joy and pure faith toward the sublime Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas, maintain an undifferentiated attitude toward all sentient beings, and impartially embrace them through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). All sentient beings together rely upon them, partaking in the joy of the Dharma to sustain their own lives.

At that time, the Venerable Upāli, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As the Buddha has taught, those sons and daughters of good family who most excellently guard and uphold the four fundamental precepts maintain an even mind toward both those who are vessels of the Dharma and those who are not; they do not mock, nor do they deride, nor do they become conceited, nor do they hastily rebuke or expose others' faults.

If this is so, in future ages there will be certain bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct; though they are not truly śramaṇas, they call themselves śramaṇas, and though they are not truly practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya), they call themselves practitioners of the holy life. By what skillful means should the community of bhikṣus reprove, censure, and expel such persons?
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Upāli, saying:

"I never permit non-Buddhists or laypeople to raise charges against a bhikṣu. I do not even permit the community of bhikṣus to hastily rebuke or charge a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts without relying on the Dharma, much less to expel him."
If one hastily censures or expels a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts without acting in accordance with the Dharma, one incurs a great offense. Upāli!
You should now know that there are ten unrighteous ways of hastily censuring a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, which result in a great offense.
All those who possess wisdom should not accept [these]. What are the ten?
First, without the consent of the Saṃgha, one rashly rebukes and denounces a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts before the king.
Second, without the consent of the Saṃgha, one rashly censures and exposes a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts before an assembly of brahmins.
Third, without the consent of the Saṃgha, one rashly censures and exposes a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts before an assembly of government officials.
Fourth, to cause discord within the Saṃgha by rashly censuring and exposing a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts in the presence of a multitude of elders and lay devotees.
Fifth, to rashly censure and expose a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts in the presence of a multitude of women.
Sixth, to rashly censure and expose a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts before a group of laymen.
Seventh, to rashly censure and expose a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts before a group of attendants (karmadāna).
Eighth, to impulsively reprove and expose a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts in the presence of a large assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Ninth, to impulsively reprove and expose a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts in the presence of someone with whom one harbors a long-standing grudge or resentment.
Tenth, harboring internal resentment, one impulsively rebukes and accuses a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts.
These ten types are called "unlawful impulsive rebukes and accusations against bhikṣus who have broken the precepts," for which one incurs great sin.

Even if one were to rebuke and accuse based on actual facts, one should still not accept [such an accusation]; how much more so when it is not based on fact? All those who accept [such an accusation] likewise incur great sin.
"Furthermore, there are ten kinds of improper rebukes for a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, which result in great transgression.
Wise persons should likewise not accept them.
What are these ten?
First, various other non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) rebuke and censure bhikṣus.
Second, laypeople who do not observe the prohibitive precepts rebuke and censure bhikṣus.
Third, those who have committed an immediate transgression (ānantarya) and yet rebuke a bhikṣu;
fourth, those who slander the True Dharma and yet rebuke a bhikṣu;
fifth, those who revile the noble ones (ārya) and yet rebuke a bhikṣu.
Sixth, one who is deluded, insane, or mentally deranged censures and accuses a bhikṣu.
Seventh, one who is afflicted by intense pain and suffering censures and accuses a bhikṣu.
Eighth, a lay attendant (upāsaka) of the Saṃgha from the four directions censures and accuses a bhikṣu.
Ninth, a park keeper rebukes and censures a bhikṣu.
Tenth, a punished bhikṣu rebukes and censures a bhikṣu.
These ten kinds of unlawful rebukes and censures against a bhikṣu who violates the precepts result in the commission of a great offense.
If one is censured and rebuked based on actual facts, one should still not accept it, let alone if it is not based on facts!
Those who do accept such [reproach] will also incur a grave offense. "Furthermore, Upāli!"
If there is a bhikṣu who has violated the prohibitive precepts yet continues to dwell together with the Saṃgha;
and among that assembly of monks, there is another bhikṣu whose conduct and observances are entirely complete, and in whom all five virtues are fully perfected.

One should rise from one's seat, adjust one's robes, and respectfully prostrate at the feet of the community of bhikṣus. Then, approaching the bhikṣu who has violated the precepts, one should request permission to censure him, speaking as follows:

"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. I now wish to censure the offense committed by the Venerable One; it shall be based on truth and not falsehood, at the proper time and not an improper time, with gentle words and not harsh ones, with a compassionate heart and not with anger, for the benefit of others and not for their detriment, so that the Tathāgata’s Eye of Dharma and Lamp of Dharma may long remain blazing."
‘Venerable sir, if you will listen, I shall formally charge you with your offense according to the Dharma.
If he listens, one should then formally charge him according to the Dharma and in accordance with the facts.
If he does not listen, one should again prostrate at the feet of the elder monks and respectfully say:
"Thus, O Bhikṣus, when one has committed such an offense, I shall raise it up according to reality by means of five methods.

At that time, the senior Bhikṣu among the Saṃgha should carefully examine the accuser and the accused, as well as the reality and gravity of the offense committed. Relying upon the Vinaya and the Sūtras, he should employ skillful means to interrogate, console, and reprove them, eliminating the offense appropriately through seven methods. If a grave offense has been committed, a severe punishment should be administered; if a middling offense, a middling punishment; if a light offense, a light punishment. This shall cause them to feel shame and remorse, leading them to repent for their transgressions.
Then Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is indeed a bhikṣu who commits transgressions and evil deeds, yet relies on the power of laypeople, or the power of wealth and treasures, or the power of extensive learning, or the power of eloquence, or the power of his disciples—and by virtue of such various powers—he treats the Saṃgha with contempt and defiance; and when elder bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās instruct him according to the Dharma, he does not comply with them at all.”
"In this way, Bhikṣu, how should he be punished? The Buddha said, "Upāli!"

The senior bhikṣu who upholds the Tripiṭaka should harmonize with the Saṃgha and dispatch a messenger to inform the king and his ministers, requesting their supportive authority; thereafter, he should punish [the offender] in accordance with the Dharma as the facts warrant.
At that time, Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are bhikṣus who commit transgressions and evil deeds, yet by the power of wealth and treasures, or the power of extensive learning, or the power of eloquence, or through various skillful means, they cause kings and ministers to take pleasure in them; and if these [rulers] all remain within the faction of those who break the precepts and act contrary to the Dharma, permitting such evil bhikṣus to commit offenses and refusing to allow them to be punished according to the law as it truly is.”
"At that time, how should the Saṃgha proceed? The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
If that bhikṣu practices without reliance and the signs of his grave offense have not yet been manifested within the Saṃgha, at that time the Saṃgha should temporarily set him aside.

If that bhikṣu practices without reliance and the signs of a grave offense have become manifest within the Saṃgha, at that time the Saṃgha should act in harmony and, in accordance with the Dharma, expel him from the Buddha-Dharma.
Upāli! It is like wild oats in a field of grain; their sprouts, stalks, branches, and leaves resemble those of the grain, thus defiling the pure grain.
As long as the ears of that weed have not emerged, the farmer should temporarily set it aside.
Once the ears have emerged, the farmers, fearing that they might defile the pure wheat, cut them out by the roots and discard them outside the field.
It is the same for bhikṣus who practice without reliance and violate the precepts.

Relying on various powers such as those of laypeople, one dwells among the Saṃgha with deportment and appearance similar to those of the monks, defiling the pure assembly; as long as the virtuous deities have not yet perceived this, and the signs of grave offenses have not yet been manifested within the community of monks, the Saṃgha should temporarily set such a person aside.

If various benevolent deities have already alerted them and the signs of grave transgressions have become manifest within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should then assemble in harmony and, in accordance with the Dharma, expel them from the Buddha-Dharma.

Upāli! Just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse, so too is it with my community of śrāvaka disciples: we do not dwell together with the corpses of bhikṣus who have broken the precepts and engaged in evil conduct.
Then Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If those bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct have been collectively expelled by the harmonious Saṃgha."

Those evil bhikṣus, by means of the power of wealth and treasures, or the power of extensive learning, or the power of eloquence, or various skillful means, cause kings and ministers to take pleasure in them; they all abide within the faction of those who break the precepts and act contrary to the Dharma, using their coercive power to oppress the Saṃgha and causing such precept-breaking bhikṣus to dwell together with the community.
"At that time, what will the Saṃgha do? The Buddha said, "Upāli!"

At that time, among the Saṃgha, there may be bhikṣus who are capable of remorse and shame and who uphold the precepts. For the sake of protecting the precepts, they should not respond with anger or abuse toward bhikṣus who have broken them; rather, they should inform the king or his ministers. However, if they fear intimidation or oppression and do not inform them, they should abandon their original residence and go elsewhere.

The Third Chapter on Practice Without Reliance, Part Two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!

Are there any Buddha-lands where, during the five turbidities of an evil age when no Buddha is present, the sentient beings therein have flourishing afflictions, habitually practice various evil deeds, and are so foolish and perverse that they are difficult to transform?

These are the candālas among kṣatriyas, the candālas among officials, the candālas among householders, the candālas among elders, the candālas among śramaṇas, and the candālas among brāhmaṇas. Such persons as these have meager roots of goodness and lack faith; they are deceitful, crooked, and foolish, harboring pride in their supposed cleverness. They neither perceive nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives, and being estranged from virtuous friends, they even head toward the Avīci Hell.

Such persons, for the sake of wealth and profit, associate with and assist those bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct, forming unlawful factions; all of them are certain to head toward the Avīci Hell.

If such a place exists, I shall dwell therein; by means of the supreme, subtle, and wondrous nectar-like flavor of the Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma—who benefits and brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings—I shall skillfully transform and guide them so that they may receive and practice it, thereby delivering such *kṣatriya-caṇḍālas* as well as *brāhmaṇa-caṇḍālas*, and causing them not to head toward the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha, saying: "Good son!

In a future age, there will be sentient beings in this buddha-field whose afflictions are blazing, who habitually engage in evil deeds, and who are ignorant, perverse, and difficult to transform and guide—namely, the Cāṇḍālas among kṣatriyas, the Cāṇḍālas among officials, the Cāṇḍālas among householders, the Cāṇḍālas among elders, the Cāṇḍālas among śramaṇas, and the Cāṇḍālas among brāhmaṇas."
Such persons as these have meager roots of goodness and lack faith; they are deceitful, crooked, and foolish, harboring pride in their supposed cleverness;
they distance themselves from virtuous friends, their speech lacks truth, and they cannot comply with the words of virtuous friends;
they constantly engage in slandering, reviling, and abusing all the true Dharmas.
Hesitant and holding perverted views, they neither see nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives;

they constantly delight in associating with those of evil discipline, taking pleasure in committing acts ranging from killing to wrong views, deceiving the world and bringing ruin to both themselves and others.

These are the candālas among kṣatriyas, and even the candālas among brāhmaṇas, who corrupt and disrupt my Dharma; having gone forth within my Dharma, they violate the prohibitions and precepts, delighting instead in worldly occupations.

Those kṣatriyas, up to and including the brahmins, show respect and make offerings [to others] while being greedy for profit and seeking wealth; they speak of one thing but act on another, transmitting letters and sending seals, exchanging communications and correspondence, engaging in trade and commerce, delighting in the study of non-Buddhist scriptures, cultivating crops and farming, hoarding precious objects, guarding gardens and houses, and attending to wives, concubines, sons, and daughters;

they practice the use of talismans and seals, incantations, the summoning of spirits, and the divination of good and bad fortune; they compound medicinal decoctions to treat illnesses and seek wealth to sustain their own lives;
and they are greedily attached to food and drink, clothing, and precious ornaments.
Diligently engaged in worldly affairs, they violate the precepts (śīla) and practice various evil dharmas, possessing the voice of a conch yet the conduct of a dog;
though not truly śramaṇas, they call themselves śramaṇas, and though not truly practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya), they call themselves practitioners of the holy life.
Those who are *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* up to and including *brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas* will delight in, draw near to, revere, make offerings to, and listen to and accept their instructions.

This person of broken precepts also delights in associating with, honoring, making offerings to, and listening to the instructions of those who are *caṇḍālas* among kṣatriyas, up to and including *caṇḍālas* among brahmins.

If one sees someone within my Dharma who, having gone forth, is endowed with the precepts, rich in virtue, diligent in practice, engaged in the conduct of those in training and those beyond training, and even attains the final, ultimate fruit.

Those Cāṇḍālas among Kṣatriyas, up to and including Cāṇḍālas among Brāhmaṇas, will instead give rise to hatred and envy; they will take no pleasure in approaching, honoring, making offerings to, or listening to and receiving their instructions.

“Good son! It is like a person who enters an island of jewels and, having discarded various kinds of great-value true treasures—such as indranīla, mahānīla, gold, silver, pearls, and beryl with the color of a red lotus—takes instead a kāca bead.”

In future ages, within this buddha-field, there will likewise be *kṣatriya*-cāṇḍālas and even *brāhmaṇa*-cāṇḍālas who, having entered the island-continents of my True Dharma Jewel, will abandon those various individuals—whether *śaikṣas* or *aśaikṣas*, or virtuous ordinary beings—who possess the full precepts, are rich in merit, delight in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and are endowed with shame and dread of blame; and who are true noble disciples diligently training in the six *pāramitās* and possessed of all virtues.

Instead, they will take as their field of merit those monks who break the precepts, who delight in committing various evils, who lack shame and dread of blame, whose speech is coarse and harsh, whose bodies and minds are arrogant, who have abandoned all pure dharmas, and who are devoid of loving-kindness and compassion, engaging instead in evil conduct; and they will revere, make offerings to, and listen to the instructions of such persons.
Such evil persons, both teacher and disciple, are certain to proceed together toward the Avīci Hell. "Good son!

There are ten wheels of evil. In a future age, within this Buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya*-cāṇḍālas, official-cāṇḍālas, householder-cāṇḍālas, elder-cāṇḍālas, śramaṇa-cāṇḍālas, and brahmin-cāṇḍālas."

Such persons, regarding the wheel of the ten non-virtuous actions, whether they have accomplished one or all of them, will cause all the roots of goodness previously cultivated and accumulated to be destroyed, scorched, and reduced to ashes. Before long, their limbs shall become impaired and deficient; for many days and nights they shall be tongue-tied and unable to speak, undergoing various bitter poisons and agonizing pains that are difficult to endure. At the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
What are these ten?

"In this way, there may be kṣatriyas, ministers, and others who tolerate the evil views of a bhikṣu of broken precepts and immoral conduct, and they slander a pure forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka) bhikṣu, saying:
'O worthy ones!'"
Such bhikṣus are foolish and vulgar; they falsely manifest extraordinary signs to deceive the world, seeking food, clothing, gain, honor, and reputation, praising themselves and disparaging others.
They are jealous, divisive, and greedily attached to fame and profit, never knowing contentment.
They should be expelled and their words not accepted.
In this way, such bhikṣus practice exclusively in falsehood and depart from the dharma of truth and reality;

among them, none attain the fruits of the path, nor do any transcend desire to bring about the eternal exhaustion of all outflows. They dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇya) solely for the sake of gain, honor, and reputation, while falsely representing themselves as possessing virtue.
"Be careful not to make offerings to, revere, or serve such deceitful and crooked persons who are not true fields of merit and are not practitioners of the Path.

At that time, those Cāṇḍālas among Kṣatriyas, up to and including Cāṇḍālas among Brāhmaṇas, will be unable to give rise to genuine faith or thoughts of rarity toward the pure bhikṣus dwelling in the forest (araṇya). With no reverence in their hearts and minds harboring contempt, they will take no pleasure in approaching, serving, or making offerings to them; they will not listen to or accept anything these [bhikṣus] say, and by thus slighting and disparaging the pure bhikṣus dwelling in the forest, they are slighting and disparaging the Eye of All Dharmas and the lineage of the Triple Gem.

At that time, there were among the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits in that land those who had faith and reverence for the Three Jewels that was unshakable. They felt indignation toward the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya king, and even toward the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and said to one another:

"Virtuous ones, you should observe these *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriyas, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; they all disparage and destroy the Eye of All Dharmas and the lineage of the Three Jewels, and they diminish their roots of goodness. By the power of evil friends, they embrace various sinful karmas and shall surely fall into the evil destinies."
"From this day forward, we shall no longer protect these *kṣatriya*-cāṇḍālas and the lands, cities, and towns where they dwell!

Having spoken these words, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits completely abandoned them, no longer protecting those *kṣatriya*-cāṇḍālas nor the lands, cities, and towns where they resided.
In that land, all who are vessels of the Dharma and true fields of merit shall depart from the country;
even those who remain will give rise to a mind of renunciation and no longer offer protection or mindfulness.

“By the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits, as well as by those who are vessels of the Dharma and true fields of merit, all protection and mindful guardianship have been abandoned toward the kṣatriya caṇḍālas and others, as well as the kingdoms, cities, and towns where they dwell.”

At that time, in that land, the armies of one's own side and those of others rose up in competition to invade and oppress, mutually inflicting harm upon one another; consequently, epidemics and famine broke out once again.

In that realm, from the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings down to the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, all the citizens shall find no joy; those things they previously cherished, they shall now be separated from entirely.

Friends and kinsmen will harbor mutual resentment, plotting in secret, being suspicious and duplicious, lacking compassion and pity, and being envious, stingy, and greedy. All manner of evils will arise, namely:
killing up to and including wrong views, shamelessness, and lack of remorse; they will consume the property of stūpas and the communal property of the Saṅgha without ever feeling regret.

That kṣatriya caṇḍāla king, hating and envying the loyal and virtuous while delighting in flattery and sycophancy, causes his officials and subjects to mutually oppress, resent, and harbor grudges against one another, giving rise to all manner of strife and contention.
When engaging in battle against neighboring states, the soldiers' hearts will turn away and they shall not fail to retreat.

Those Cāṇḍāla-like Kṣatriya kings, as well as their ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—all such Cāṇḍālas—will before long have their limbs mangled and crippled; for many days and nights they will remain tongue-tied and speechless, suffering various agonizing pains that are sharp and unbearable, and at the end of life they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, good son!

There are *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* kings, as well as ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins who are *caṇḍāla* persons; they follow the ways of evil friends, possess meager roots of goodness, are deceitful, crooked, and foolish, harbor pride in their supposed intelligence, and lack a pure and sincere mind toward the Triple Gem. They neither perceive nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives."

There is a certain class of people who have attained only a slight degree of faith in the Śrāvaka-yāna; though they are actually foolish, they consider themselves clever and sagacious. They revile and slander the Pratyekabuddha-yāna and Mahāyāna teachings I have expounded, refusing to allow sentient beings to receive, uphold, read, or recite them, even down to a single verse.

Furthermore, there is another class of people who have gained a slight degree of faith in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; yet being truly foolish while considering themselves clever and discerning, they revile and slander the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna teachings as expounded by me, refusing to allow sentient beings to receive, uphold, read, or recite them, even down to a single verse.

Furthermore, there is another class of people who have gained a slight degree of faith in the Mahāyāna teachings; yet being truly foolish while imagining themselves to be wise, they revile and slander the Śrāvaka vehicle and Pratyekabuddha vehicle taught by me, refusing to allow sentient beings to receive, uphold, read, or recite even a single verse from them.
Such persons as these are called those who slander the Buddha’s true Dharma; they are also those who oppose all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
They destroy the entire treasury of the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods, incinerating and annihilating it until nothing but ashes remains;
they sever and ruin the entire Noble Eightfold Path, and gouge out the Dharma-eye of immeasurable sentient beings.

"If a *caṇḍāla* king of the Kṣatriya caste, or even a *caṇḍāla* among śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, should obstruct, conceal, or cause the disappearance of even a single verse of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna as taught by the Buddha—
know that such a person is called one who does not revere the eye of all dharmas or the lineage of the Triple Gem."

By reason of these causes and conditions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the land and possess unwavering faith and reverence for the Triple Gem will give rise to anger and resentment toward the *caṇḍāla* kṣatriya kings, and even toward the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—these *caṇḍāla* persons—will before long have their limbs withered and impaired; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to bear, and at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.
"Furthermore, noble son!
There are *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* kings, as well as *amātyas*, householders, elders, *śramaṇas*, and *brāhmaṇas* who are *caṇḍālas*, who follow the conduct of immoral and evil *bhikṣus*.

To speak at length, even unto this: within that land, there are those who are vessels of the Dharma and true fields of merit; toward the *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas* and others, they maintain a mind of equanimity and do not harbor resentment.
Although they dwell in that country, they abide according to the Dharma; they never take pleasure in living among the laity, nor do they frequently visit the homes of donors.

Even if they do visit for a time, they guard their speech; though they may speak, they never utter falsehoods. Ultimately, they never, in the presence of householders, revile, disparage, or mock those who have broken the precepts.

Regarding bhikṣus who violate the precepts and engage in evil conduct, he never casually subjects them to interrogation, nor does he manifest signs to expose their faults; he always stays close to those who are fields of merit and keeps his distance from those who break the precepts.
Yet those bhikṣus of broken precepts and evil conduct, in turn, give rise to resentment, contempt, and aggression toward these practitioners of pure and virtuous conduct who uphold the precepts.

Before Kṣatriya Caṇḍāla kings, and even before Caṇḍāla-like śramaṇas, brahmins, and others—whether laymen or laywomen, great or small—they employ various forms of flattery and crookedness, engaging in false discourse to disparage and slander these upholders of the precepts.

They cause the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, and even the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, to give rise to hatred toward my disciples—those bhikṣus who have few desires, are contented, uphold the precepts, are learned, and possess sublime eloquence—and to revile and oppress them with various harsh words, causing their minds to be distressed and their bodies to be ill at ease; or they rob them of their robes, bowls, and other requisites for the body, leaving them in want; or they seize the offerings made to the Saṅgha from the four quarters and prohibit their use; or they cast them into prison, subjecting them to shackles and torture; or they dismember their limbs or decapitate them.

“Good son! You should observe that such kṣatriya caṇḍāla kings, and even those who are caṇḍālas among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, associate with bhikṣus of broken precepts and evil conduct, commit these various kinds of great sins, and shall eventually fall into the Avīci Hell.”

If sentient beings commit the five acts of immediate retribution, or violate the heavy precepts, or approach the nature of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) that border on immediacy, such offenses are still lighter than the obstructive transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

Likewise, those *kṣatriya* outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), up to and including *śramaṇas* and *brāhmaṇas* who are outcasts, who associate with those who break the precepts, commit grave sins that transgress the Dharma.

"Good son! Although such a bhikṣu of broken precepts and evil conduct has committed such grave transgressions against the Dharma, he still relies upon my teaching; having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the kāṣāya robe, his deportment and dignified demeanor are identical to those of the noble sages."

I do not even permit kings, ministers, or householders to rely on worldly secular laws to scourge their bodies with whips or staves, or to imprison them, or to revile them, or to dismember their limbs, or to take their lives.
How much more so for those who rely on what is contrary to the Dharma?
If kings, ministers, or laypeople commit such an act, they will incur a great transgression and will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"One should not even inflict such punishments upon bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct, let alone those who uphold the precepts and practice true goodness!
O son of good family!"

If there is a bhikṣu who, among the fundamental and gravely serious offenses, commits even one such offense, he is indeed called a bhikṣu of broken precepts and evil conduct; yet the restraint he received within the harmonious Saṃgha of his preceptor remains uninterrupted, and even until he abandons the śīla he has studied, the fragrance of the white dharmas still follows him.
Kings, ministers, and laypeople lack the vows of discipline; therefore, they should not be treated with contempt nor subjected to punishment.

Likewise, although a bhikṣu may not be a fit vessel for the Dharma, having fallen away from the noble teachings and defiled the pure assembly, thereby destroying all the monastic activities of a śramaṇa and being forbidden from using the property of the Saṅgha from the four directions—nevertheless, because he has not abandoned the discipline he received within the harmonious Saṅgha under his preceptor, he remains superior to all laypeople clad in white.

If this must be so even for those who have committed natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), how much more so for those who have committed other minor prohibitory offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)!
Therefore, it is not permitted for kings, ministers, or laypeople to treat them with contempt or to punish them.
"Why is this? Good son! In the distant past, there was a king of Kāśī named Brahmadatta, who commanded a caṇḍāla: "
“There is a great elephant king named Blue Lotus Eye, endowed with six tusks, who dwells on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains.
You should go there and pull out his tusks and bring them here.
If you do not succeed, none of you five shall have any hope of survival.”

At that time, the caṇḍāla, in order to protect his own life, took up his bow and arrows, donned a crimson kāṣāya robe, and assuming the deceptive appearance and deportment of a śramaṇa, went to the edge of the Snowy Mountains to where the elephant king was.
At that time, the female elephant saw from afar a man approaching, carrying a bow and arrows; terrified, she fled to the place where the elephant king was and said to him: "Great Lord!
"Now we see someone with bow drawn and arrow nocked, walking slowly while spying on us and approaching.
Could it be that our lives are about to end?
Having heard this, the Elephant King raised his eyes and immediately saw a person with shaven hair and beard wearing a *kāṣāya* robe; he then spoke a verse for the sake of the female elephant:
"Marked by the Dharma-banners of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges,
observe that this one is free from all evils and will certainly not harm sentient beings."
Then, that mother elephant replied in verse:
"Though you wear the Dharma robes, you carry a bow and arrows;
you are a wicked Caṇḍāla, delighting in evil and devoid of compassion."
Then the Great Elephant King spoke again in verse:
"Seeing the single mark of the *kāṣāya*, I know it to be the source of compassion.
This one must be a follower of the Buddha, Out of pity for all sentient beings."
"Do not harbor doubt or anxiety; you should quickly collect your mind.
Those who wear this Dharma robe desire to cross the ocean of birth and death.
At that time, the Caṇḍāla drew his bow and shot a poisoned arrow with precision, striking the elephant king in the heart.
When the female elephant saw him, she raised her voice in a mournful cry, choked with grief, and spoke in verse:
"This man who wears the Dharma robes ought surely to have taken refuge in the Buddha;
though his deportment is tranquil, he harbors a poisonous and evil heart."
"You should quickly trample upon his body, severing his life-force;
destroy this enemy completely, for he has shot at the celestial body.
At that time, the Great Elephant King replied in verse:
"Better to swiftly relinquish body and life than to give rise to an evil mind;
though they harbor a deceitful heart, they still resemble disciples of the Buddha."
"The wise do not destroy their pure mind for the sake of life;
rather, to deliver all sentient beings, they constantly practice the conduct of bodhi.
At that time, the Great Elephant King gave rise to a heart of compassion and slowly asked the man:
"What do you require? The man replied,
"I desire your tusks."
The Elephant King was filled with joy; he immediately pulled out his tusks and gave them to the caṇḍāla, speaking this verse:
“I now give my white tusks to you, Without anger, without resentment, and without stinginess.
May the merit of this gift lead to the attainment of Buddhahood, And extinguish the sickness of afflictions for all sentient beings.”

“Good son! You should observe that although this past elephant king received the body of an animal in a state of no leisure, for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he was able to cast away his life and limb without stinginess, showing reverence and respect to those who wore the kāṣāya robe.”
"Even though they act as enemies, one does not retaliate against them.

However, in future ages there will be *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* kings, as well as *cai-guan*, householders, elders, *śramaṇas*, and *brāhmaṇas* who are *caṇḍālas*. They are truly foolish yet harbor pride in their supposed intelligence; they are sycophantic, crooked, deceitful, and fraudulent, deluding the world while neither seeing nor fearing the bitter fruits of future lives."

Regarding those who have gone forth into my Dharma, whether they be disciples who are vessels for the Dharma or those who are not vessels, one might harass or revile them, strike their bodies with whips and staves, imprison them, or even deprive them of life.

This constitutes a grave offense against all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; one will certainly proceed to the Avīci Hell, severing one's roots of goodness and incinerating the continuum of consciousness, and will be shunned by all those possessed of wisdom.
Having committed such grave offenses, they further harbor arrogance and deceive the world, claiming:
"We too seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; we belong to the Mahāyāna and shall become Buddhas."
"It is like a person who plucks out his own eyes; being blind and seeing nothing, he wishes to lead others up a great mountain—such a thing can never happen.
In future ages, there will likewise be *caṇḍāla* kings of the kṣatriya caste, as well as *caṇḍāla* officials, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins, who are just like this."

Toward those disciples who have gone forth in my Dharma—whether they be vessels of the Dharma or not—one might harass or revile them, lash their bodies with whips and staves, imprison them, or even deprive them of life.

This constitutes a grave offense against all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it severs one's roots of goodness and incinerates the continuum of consciousness. It is shunned by all those possessed of wisdom, and such a person is certain to fall into the Avīci Hell.
Having committed such grave offenses, they further harbor arrogance and delude the world, declaring:
"We too seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; we belong to the Mahāyāna and shall surely attain Buddhahood."

Because he has disturbed those who have left the household life, it will be difficult for him even to obtain a human body of low station, let alone be able to realize the enlightenment of the two vehicles;
as for the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, it is utterly beyond his reach!
"Furthermore, noble son!
In the past, there was a country named Pañcāla, ruled by a king titled Jayasena.
At that time, in that land, there was a great burial mound called Kalandava, which was most terrifying."
Yakṣas and rākṣasas dwell there in great numbers; anyone who enters it finds their heart trembling and their hair standing on end.

At that time, there was a man in the kingdom whose crime merited death. The king commanded the jailer to bind him at five points and send him to the great mountainous wilderness of Khaḷambā, ordering the various malevolent spirits to devour his body.
Having heard this, the sinner, in order to protect his life, immediately shaved off his hair and beard and sought out a *kāṣāya* robe; encountering a single fragment, he tied it around his own neck.
Then, as commanded by the king, the jailer bound him at five points and sent him into the mountain tomb.

When the people had returned and it was the middle of the night, a great rākṣasī mother named Sword-Eye arrived at the cemetery with five thousand attendants; seeing her from afar, the sinners’ bodies and minds were struck with terror.

At that time, the rākṣasī mother saw this man bound at five points, with his hair and beard shaven and a fragment of saffron robe tied around his neck. She immediately circumambulated him to the right, paid him respect, prostrated, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
"May you comfort yourself; I shall never harm you.
Seeing your shorn hair and dyed robes, it causes me to remember the Buddha."
Then the rākṣasī’s son said to his mother:
“Mother, I am tormented by hunger and thirst, which press upon my body and mind with great intensity.
I pray that you will permit me to eat this man, so that my suffering may cease and my body and mind may find peace.”
Then the rākṣasī mother said to her son:
"One who conceives an evil thought toward those clad in the robes of the banner of liberation of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell."
Then the rākṣasa youth, together with his retinue, circumambulated this person to the right, paid him respect, prostrated, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“We repent before you, one clad in dyed robes; We would rather commit evil deeds of body, speech, and mind against our own parents, But we shall never cause you any harm.”
At that time, there was also a great rākṣasī mother named Khara-dantī (Donkey-Mule Tooth), who, surrounded by five thousand attendants, entered the cemetery.

At that time, the rākṣasī mother also saw this man bound at five points, with his hair and beard shaven and a fragment of saffron robe tied beneath his neck. She immediately circumambulated him to the right, paid him respect, prostrated herself, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“O man, do not fear me! The garment tied around your neck Is the banner of the sages; I pay homage and offer it worship.”
Then the rākṣasī’s son said to his mother:
“Human flesh and blood are sweet and delicious; I pray that you, Mother, will allow me to eat them, so that my physical and mental strength may increase and I may be courageous and fearless.”
Then the rākṣasī mother spoke to her son, saying:
“The sublime joys of humans and devas Arise from honoring those who have gone forth;
Therefore, by making offerings to those clad in dyed robes, One shall obtain immeasurable happiness.”
Then the rākṣasī’s son, together with his retinue, circumambulated this person to the right, paid him respect, prostrated, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“I now pay respectful homage To the one who has shaved his hair and donned dyed robes.
May we always, in the future, Behold the Buddha and give rise to deep faith.”
At that time, there was also a great rākṣasī mother named Jaṭāmukhī, who, surrounded by five thousand attendants, came into the cemetery.

At that time, the rākṣasī mother also saw this man bound at five places, with his hair and beard shaven and a fragment of saffron robe tied beneath his neck; she immediately circumambulated him to the right, paid him respect, prostrated, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“The banner-like garment of the Great Sage Should be praised and honored by the wise;
If one can practice such offerings, One will surely sever all bonds of existence.”
Then the rākṣasa youth said to his mother:
“The flesh and blood of this man are what the king relies upon;
I pray you grant me leave to devour him, so that I may gain the strength to serve my mother.”
Then the rākṣasī mother spoke to her son, saying:
"Such a person who wears dyed robes is not fit to be your food;
whoever conceives ill will toward him shall become a vessel for great suffering."
Then the rākṣasa youth, together with his retinue, circumambulated this person to the right, paid him honor, prostrated at his feet, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“You belong to the lineage of the Great Sages, Worthy to be a field of merit;
Therefore I practice offerings to you, Vowing to sever all bonds of existence.”
At that time, there was also a great rākṣasī mother named Sword-Mouth, who, surrounded by five thousand attendants, entered the cemetery.

At that time, the rākṣasī mother also saw this man with his five limbs bound, his hair and beard shaven, and a fragment of saffron robe tied beneath his neck. She immediately circumambulated him to the right, paid him honor, prostrated herself, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
“You now wear the Dharma robes; You will surely proceed to the bliss of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, I shall not harm you, Fearing the reproach of all the Buddhas.”
Then the rākṣasī’s son said to his mother:
“I constantly suckle vital essence and devour human flesh and blood;
I pray you will permit me to eat this man, so that my physical strength and vigor may be fully restored.”
Then the rākṣasī mother spoke to her son, saying:
"If you harm one who wears the kāṣāya robe and has shaved off his hair and beard,
you will surely fall into the Avīci Hell and endure great suffering for a long time."
Then the rākṣasī, together with her retinue, circumambulated this person to the right, paid him respect, prostrated, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these verses:
"We are terrified of the hells; Therefore we do not harm your life.
We shall release your body; May you be freed from the suffering of hell."

At that time, the rākṣasīs, along with their children and retinues, simultaneously gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness and untied this man’s bonds; they apologized, consoled him, and joyfully released him to return home.
This man went quickly to the king’s residence early in the morning and reported the matter in detail to him.

At that time, King Jayasena and his retinue were struck with amazement and leaped for joy, exclaiming that such a thing had never been seen before. They immediately established a regulation and proclaimed it to the people of the kingdom:

"From this day forward, within my realm, if there are disciples of the Buddha—whether they observe the precepts, violate them, or even lack them entirely—provided only that they have shaved their hair and beards and wear the saffron robes, anyone who insults, assails, or harms them shall be punished with the death penalty."

"By virtue of these causes and conditions, the multitude admired his virtue and gradually turned to him for transformation; they all together, with sincere hearts, took refuge in and honored the Triple Gem. Good son!..."

One should contemplate that although these rākṣasas of the past had received the bodies of hungry ghosts in the states of no-leisure— sucking the vital essence of humans, devouring their flesh and blood, possessing blazingly fierce malice, and lacking any compassion—

upon seeing those who were unvirtuous yet had shaved their hair and beards and hung a fragment of a *kāṣāya* around their necks, they immediately circumambulated them to the right, honoring, prostrating to, respecting, praising, and regarding them with a mind free from harm.

Nevertheless, in future ages, there will be *caṇḍāla* kings of the kṣatriya caste, as well as *caṇḍāla* officials, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins, whose hearts harbor poison and evil, who lack compassion, whose commission of transgressions exceeds that of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and who, through folly and arrogance, sever their roots of goodness.

Toward those who have gone forth in my Dharma—whether they be vessels of the Dharma or not—among my disciples who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes, one does not give rise to respect, but instead harasses, disturbs, or reviles them; or one strikes their bodies with whips and staves, or imprisons them, even unto taking their lives.

This constitutes a grave offense against all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it severs the roots of goodness and incinerates one's mental continuum. It is shunned by all those possessed of wisdom, and one will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, noble son!
In the past there was a king named Atiśaya-puṇya.
There was a man who had committed an offense for which he deserved the death penalty; however, the king was by nature compassionate and did not wish to take his life."
A certain high minister, possessed of great wisdom and strategy, came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"Please do not grieve; we shall ensure that Your Majesty incurs no sin of taking life, nor shall we hand this man over to an executioner to be put to death."
Then, by his own intellectual power, the minister handed the criminal over to a fierce, intoxicated elephant.

At that time, the fierce, intoxicated elephant seized the criminal’s two shins with its trunk, lifted him up into the air, and exerted all its strength, intending to dash him to the ground. Suddenly, seeing that the man’s garment was red, it took it for a *kāṣāya* robe and conceived pure faith in its heart.

He then slowly set [the foot] down, prostrated himself before him in repentance and lamentation, and with his nose wiped the person's feet; with a heart of profound reverence, he gazed up at that person.
Having seen this, the minister hurried back and informed the king.

Upon hearing it, the king was both delighted and struck with wonder, exclaiming that such a thing had never occurred before. He then issued a decree to the people of the kingdom to increase their reverence for the Triple Gem; consequently, throughout Jambudvīpa, the king brought an end to the taking of life.
“Good son! You should observe that although this past intoxicated elephant received the body of an animal in the realm of no leisure, he respected the *kāṣāya* and did not commit evil deeds.”

However, in future ages, there will be *caṇḍāla* kings of the kṣatriya caste, as well as ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins who are like *caṇḍālas*. Their hearts harbor poisonous evil and they lack compassion; they commit various sinful deeds like elephants intoxicated by their own wickedness, and through folly and arrogance, they sever their roots of goodness.

Regarding those who have gone forth in my Dharma—whether they be vessels of the Dharma or not—if one fails to show respect toward these disciples who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes, but instead harasses, disturbs, or reviles them; or strikes their bodies with whips and staves; or imprisons them, even unto taking their lives.

This constitutes a grave offense against all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; it severs one's roots of goodness and incinerates the continuum of consciousness. It is shunned by all those possessed of omniscience, and one will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"If a kṣatriya caṇḍāla king, or even a caṇḍāla among śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, accomplishes such a third evil wheel."

By this cause and condition, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the kingdom and possess unwavering faith and reverence for the Triple Gem will give rise to anger and resentment toward the kṣatriya caṇḍāla kings, and even toward the caṇḍāla śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—these *caṇḍāla* persons—will before long have their limbs maimed and crippled; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to bear, and at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

In a future age, within this buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya* outcasts—whether they be kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, or brahmins—who follow the ways of evil friends and possess meager roots of goodness;
as has been explained at length, they do not perceive nor do they fear the bitter fruits of future lives."
One sees that there are objects given as property for the Saṅgha of the four directions, namely:

various monasteries or monastery property; various groves or grove property; various fields or field property; or those male and female attendants (kappiyakāraka) who have been accepted; or those species of livestock that have been accepted; or the clothing, food, and drink that have been accepted; or the beds, seats, and bedding that have been accepted; or the medicines for the occasion of illness that have been accepted; or various kinds of requisites for the body that are fit for use and have been accepted.

Such gifts of property for the Saṅgha of the four directions are to be used by pure bhikṣus who possess the precepts, are rich in virtue, are diligent in practice, and follow the path of learners and non-learners, up to those who have realized the final, ultimate fruit.
That *kṣatriya* outcaste king, and even those outcaste persons such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, by means of their coercive power, seize and usurp [the property];

they do not permit those bhikṣus who possess the precepts and are pure to enjoy it, but instead bestow it upon bhikṣus of broken precepts and evil conduct who manage various worldly secular affairs, so that they may enjoy it either together or individually.
Once those precept-breaking bhikṣus have received [the offerings], they may consume them together with others, consume them alone, or consume them in common with laypeople.

Due to these causes and conditions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the kingdom and possess unwavering faith and reverence for the Triple Gem will give rise to anger and resentment toward the cruel kṣatriya kings, and even toward the cruel śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—these *caṇḍāla* persons—will before long have their limbs withered and impaired; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, undergoing various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to endure, and upon the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, good son!

In a future age within this buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* kings, as well as ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins who are *caṇḍālas*. Following the ways of evil friends, their roots of goodness will be extremely meager;
to speak at length, they will not see nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives."

He sees those who have gone forth in reliance upon his Dharma—those who are wise, learned, and possess perfectly refined speech—who are able to transmit the Śrāvaka vehicle, or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle, causing them to spread widely for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Toward such a Dharma-preacher, they revile, insult, slander, mock, deceive, oppress, and harass them, thereby obstructing the True Dharma.

By reason of these causes and conditions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the land and possess unwavering faith and reverence for the Triple Gem will give rise to anger and resentment toward the *caṇḍāla* kṣatriya kings, and even toward the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—these *caṇḍāla* persons—will before long have their limbs withered and impaired; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to bear, and at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, good son!

In a future age, within this buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya* outcasts—kings, officials, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—who follow the ways of evil friends and possess meager roots of goodness;
as has been explained at length, they do not see and do not fear the bitter fruits of future lives."

He saw that there were various items belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters as offerings, including monasteries, fields and estates, people and livestock, wealth and treasures, flowering trees, fruit trees, dyeing trees, shade trees, fragrant medicinal trees, and other diverse articles for the support of the body.

It is for my disciples who possess the precepts, are rich in virtue, practice with diligence, and follow the path of those in training and those beyond training—even up to the pure bhikṣus who have realized the final, ultimate fruit—that these things are intended for their use.

That *kṣatriya* outcaste king, or even those outcaste persons such as śramaṇas and brahmins, by means of their forceful power, either personally seize and take away, or instruct others to seize and take away, whether for their own use or for the use of others.

By reason of these causes and conditions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the land and whose faith and reverence for the Triple Gem is unshakable will give rise to anger and resentment toward the *caṇḍāla* kṣatriya kings, and even toward the *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the *caṇḍāla* Kṣatriya kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins—these *caṇḍāla* persons—will before long have their limbs withered and impaired; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, undergoing various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to endure, and at the end of life they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, good son!

In a future age within this buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya* outcasts—whether they be kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, or brahmins—who possess meager roots of goodness and lack faith. Deceitful, ignorant, and harboring pride in their own cleverness, their words will lack truth. They will distance themselves from virtuous friends and follow the conduct of evil associates; their minds will harbor doubt regarding the noble teachings, and they will neither perceive nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives.

Constantly delighting in associating with those of evil discipline, they take pleasure in committing acts ranging from killing to holding wrong views. Yet, filled with arrogance, they deceive the world by claiming for themselves: 'I am one who abides in the discipline.'"
Those *kṣatriya* caṇḍāla kings, and even those *caṇḍāla* persons among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, will destroy my Dharma through various means.

Toward those who have gone forth into homelessness having taken refuge in my Dharma, they will repeatedly harbor anger and resentment, reviling, insulting, humiliating, torturing, imprisoning, mutilating their limbs, and even depriving them of life. They will refuse to believe or accept the Dharma I have taught;

they will destroy stūpas and monasteries, compel bhikṣus to disrobe and return to lay life, obstruct the shaving of hair and the wearing of the kāṣāya robe, and employ them in various menial tasks like common servants.

By reason of these causes and conditions, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and other spirits who protect the land and possess unwavering faith and reverence for the Triple Gem will give rise to anger and resentment toward the caṇḍāla-like kṣatriya kings, and even toward the caṇḍāla-like śramaṇas, brahmins, and others.

To speak at length, even those such as the kṣatriya caṇḍāla kings, ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins who are like caṇḍālas will, before long, have their limbs withered and impaired; for many days and nights they will be tongue-tied and unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to bear, and at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.

“Good son! If a *kṣatriya* outcaste king, a minister, a householder, a merchant leader, a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa—any such outcaste person—should, regarding the ten kinds of evil wheels described above, either partially or fully accomplish them, then all the roots of goodness previously cultivated and accumulated will be destroyed, burned away, and reduced to ashes. Before long, their limbs shall become impaired and deficient; for many days and nights they shall be tongue-tied and unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains that are difficult to bear. At the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.”

These *caṇḍāla* kings of the kṣatriya caste, as well as *caṇḍāla* officials, householders, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins, will find it difficult even to obtain a human body of low birth in future ages, let alone be able to realize the enlightenment of the two vehicles.
They are utterly devoid of the capacity for the unsurpassed Mahāyāna!
For such evil persons, even the mere name of the Mahāyāna is difficult to hear, let alone being able to realize the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood!
Such a person ultimately brings harm to themselves and others, and cannot be saved by any of the Buddhas. "Good son!
It is like a person whose livelihood is pressing oil; within every single sesame seed there are insects born, and as they press them with the wheel, the oil flows out."
"You should observe this oil-presser: how many living beings does he kill during the course of a single day and night?

Suppose such an oil-presser were to press continuously with ten sets of wheels; in one day and night, the amount of oil pressed by each wheel would fill a thousand *hu* measures. If this were continued in succession for a full thousand years,"
"Observe this person: how many lives has he killed?
Is the karmic retribution for his offenses not great indeed?
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
"Venerable Sir!

The number of beings this person has killed is immeasurable and boundless; the karmic offenses he has incurred are beyond calculation and cannot be reached by any analogy or mathematical reckoning. Only a Buddha can know them; no one else can."
The Buddha said, "Good son!

Suppose there were a person who, for the sake of profit, established ten brothels; in each brothel he placed a thousand courtesans, each of whom was adorned in various ways to deceive and entice many people, constantly engaging them in sexual acts."
If such a succession continues for a full thousand years, the offenses incurred by this person will be beyond measure, exceeding what can be reached through calculation, number, or analogy.
This is equivalent to the karmic offenses incurred by ten oil-pressers using stone wheels, which equals the karmic offenses incurred by a single brothel.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose there were a person who, for the sake of profit, established ten wine shops, each adorned with various ornaments, and through skillful means enticed a thousand wine-addicts to drink and enjoy themselves, without ceasing day or night.
If such a succession continues for a full thousand years, the offenses incurred by this person will be beyond measure, exceeding what can be reached through calculation, enumeration, or analogy.
As previously stated, the sin of ten brothels is equal to the karmic retribution obtained from a single tavern.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose there were a person who, for the sake of profit, established ten slaughterhouses, and in each slaughterhouse, throughout a single day and night, slaughtered the lives of a thousand beings—cattle, sheep, camels, deer, chickens, pigs, and so forth."
If one continues in this manner for a full thousand years, the offenses this person incurs will be beyond measure, beyond the reach of calculation, number, or analogy.
As previously stated, the sin of ten wine shops is equal to the karmic offense incurred by a single slaughterhouse.

"The sins of the ten slaughterhouses mentioned previously are equal to the karma obtained by a *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* king, or even by *caṇḍāla* persons such as śramaṇas and brahmins, for a single day and night, in having committed even one of the ten unwholesome paths."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The sin of ten oil-pressing wheels is equal to one brothel;
placing ten brothels together is equal to the sin of one tavern."
The sin of establishing ten wine shops is equal to that of one slaughterhouse;
the sin of establishing ten slaughterhouses is equal to that of one [royal] palace.
*Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra*, Volume Four.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Daśacakra Kṣitigarbha Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: On the Practice of Non-Reliance, Part Three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Virtuous World-Honored One!

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriyas, true and virtuous officials, true and virtuous laypeople, true and virtuous elders, true and virtuous śramaṇas, or true and virtuous brāhmaṇas—such persons as these are able to well protect themselves, well protect others, well protect future generations, and well protect the Buddha-dharma."

Whether they are vessels for the Dharma or not vessels for the Dharma—even down to those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya robes despite lacking the precepts—one should universally and skillfully protect, revere, and make offerings to them.

Furthermore, one should skillfully protect the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna, listening to them with reverence, accepting them with faith, and making offerings to them.

Regarding those who abide in the Mahāyāna, who are endowed with ethical discipline, rich in virtue, and diligent in practice—even up to those individuals who abide in the fruits—one should skillfully protect them, assist their strength, consult with them, listen to them, receive their teachings, and delight in conversation with them, while remaining far removed from bhikṣus who violate the precepts and engage in evil conduct.

Regarding all items given as offerings to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, he never allows others to expend them in an unrighteous manner; he diligently guards and protects them to provide for the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
As for stūpas and the property of the Saṃgha, he never seizes them himself nor instructs others to seize them, nor does he use them himself nor instruct others to use them.

Toward those who can eloquently expound the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, one should show reverence and provide offerings, granting them protection and strength so that others may not slander or humiliate them;
