one should honor and comfort all renunciants, faithfully accept and uphold the Dharma taught by the Buddha, never destroy stūpas, and always protect and maintain monasteries.
Toward those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the *kāṣāya* as renunciants, he never disparages or abandons them.
Regarding the wheel of the ten non-virtues, he does not personally defile himself with them;

furthermore, he constantly exhorts others to abandon the wheel of the ten non-virtues. He fully studies the true Dharma for governing a state according to former kings, succeeds to the lineage of the Triple Gem, and always causes it to flourish. He constantly delights in drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), nurturing all the people of the nation with a compassionate heart, and using skillful means (*upāya*) appropriate to their needs to guide them, causing them to renounce false teachings and practice the true Dharma.
"How much merit do such truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, and even truly virtuous Brahmins and others, obtain?
And how much sin do they extinguish?
The Buddha said:

“Good son! Suppose there were someone appearing in the world who possessed great power; in the first part of the day, he gathered the seven treasures to fill the continent of Jambudvīpa and offered them to the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples;
in the middle part of the day, he likewise gathered the seven treasures to fill the continent of Jambudvīpa and offered them to the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples.”
Furthermore, during the latter part of the day, one were to gather the seven treasures to fill Jambudvīpa and offer them to the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples.
If one were to continue giving in this manner every day for a full hundred thousand years, would the mass of merit of such a person not be great?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha said: "Very many,
World-Honored One!"
"Very much so, Venerable Sir!
The mass of merit of this person is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy."
"Only the Buddha can know this; no one else knows it!
The Buddha said, "Good son!..."
It is so, it is so, just as you have said.

If there are true and virtuous Kṣatriya kings, or even true and virtuous Brāhmaṇas, who do not themselves become defiled by or habituated to the ten wheels of evil, and who also constantly exhort others to leave the ten wheels of evil behind, the mass of merit they obtain exceeds the previous mass of merit; it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable.
Furthermore, noble son!

Suppose there were someone appearing in the world endowed with great power, who would construct monasteries for the Saṃgha of the four directions, as vast in scale as the four great continents, fully equipped with excellent dwellings, bedding, clothing, food, drink, medicine, and all necessary requisites, so that the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of disciples might reside therein and diligently cultivate various categories of wholesome qualities, without weariness by day or night;
and suppose they were to provide such offerings and support continuously for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years.
“Is the mass of merit of this person not great?
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva replied,
“It is exceedingly great.”
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so,
O Virtuous One!”
The mass of merit of this person is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy;
only a Buddha can know it, and no one else!
The Buddha said, “Good son, it is so,
it is so; it is just as you have said.”
Furthermore, noble son!

Suppose there were someone appearing in the world endowed with great power, who would construct monasteries for the Sangha of the four quarters, as vast in measurement as the fourteen great continents, fully equipped with excellent dwellings, bedding, clothing, food and drink, and medicinal requisites, so that the Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and the assembly of great disciples might reside therein and diligently cultivate various categories of wholesome qualities, without weariness or rest by day or night;
and for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years, they would provide for and make offerings to them in an uninterrupted succession.
"Is the mass of merit of this person great or not?
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva replied,
"It is exceedingly great."
"World-Honored One!
It is very much so,
O Virtuous One!"
The mass of merit of this person is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable; it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy;
only a Buddha can know it, and no one else!
The Buddha said, “Good son! It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said.”
Furthermore, son of good family!

Suppose there were someone appearing in the world who possessed great power and majesty, and for the sake of the Buddha’s relics, erected a stūpa that was magnificent, lofty, and vast, equal in measure to a trichiliocosm;
and suppose they performed the accumulation of merit from building monasteries for the Saṃgha of the four quarters as previously described.

The mass of merit obtained from erecting a stūpa for the relics of the Buddha as described above does not approach even a hundredth part of this; it does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a koṭi-th part, nor a nayuta-th part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fractionally estimated part, nor even a part comparable by analogy, up to an *upaniṣad* part.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Suppose there were great Arhats who had attained the pāramitās and were endowed with the eight liberations, dhyānas, and samāpattis, filling the trichiliocosm like rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, sugarcane, or thickets; and suppose they were all firmly bound at the five locations for hundreds of thousands of years."

At that time, a person appeared in the world who possessed great power; out of a desire for merit and virtue, he liberated all the Arhats from their bonds, bathed them with fragrant water, and offered them robes and alms bowls. For hundreds and thousands of years, he provided them with superior dwellings, bedding, clothing, food and drink, medicine, and all manner of necessary requisites in accordance with the Dharma.

After the various Arhats have entered parinirvāṇa, they shall be honored with offerings, cremated, and their relics collected; stupas made of the seven exquisite jewels shall be erected, and [the relics] placed therein.
Furthermore, they made offerings with various jeweled banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and music.

As previously stated regarding the mass of merit obtained from erecting a stūpa for the Buddha’s relics, the mass of merit from making such offerings to an Arhat as described here does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal even one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one koṭi-th part; it does not equal even one nayuta-th part, nor a numerical part, nor a calculable part, nor a fraction, nor a comparable part, nor even an upaniṣad part.

“Good son! If there is a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, or even a truly virtuous Brāhmaṇa, who does not personally become defiled by the ten wheels of unwholesome action and also constantly exhorts others to abandon them, the merit they obtain exceeds the previous accumulation of merit, being immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable. Just as the number of merits produced is so great, the destruction of their sins is likewise.”

“Good son! If there are true and virtuous kṣatriya kings, as well as true and virtuous ministers, householders, elders, śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, who, in the future age during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, are able to skillfully protect and uphold my eye of the Dharma—protecting themselves well, protecting others well, protecting future generations well, and protecting my Dharma well.”

Whether they be disciples who have left the household life and are vessels of the Dharma or not, even down to those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya but lack the precepts, you should universally and skillfully protect them, honoring and making offerings to them so that they suffer no harm or affliction, and furthermore, you should skillfully protect the true Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

When listening to and receiving the teachings for śrāvakas, they do not give rise to disparagement toward the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the Mahāyāna, nor do they harbor hatred or envy toward those who follow the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the Mahāyāna.

When listening to, receiving, and making offerings to the teachings of the Pratyekabuddhas, one does not give rise to slander toward the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna, nor does one harbor hatred or envy toward those who follow the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Mahāyāna.

When listening to, receiving, and making offerings to the Mahāyāna Dharma, one does not give rise to disparagement toward the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna teachings, nor does one harbor hatred or envy toward those who follow the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna;
one does not seek to realize the fruits of the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna, but seeks only to realize the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

They frequently associate with, serve, and make offerings to those who abide in the Mahāyāna, who are endowed with ethical discipline, rich in virtue, and diligent in practice, even up to those individuals who abide in the fruits [of the path]; they hold them in deep respect with a sincere heart, inquire of them, listen to their teachings, and receive them, while remaining far removed from bhikṣus of broken precepts and evil conduct.

Regarding all items given as offerings to the Saṃgha of the four directions, he never allows others to expend them in an unrighteous manner; he diligently guards and protects them to provide for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
As for stūpas and the property of the Saṃgha, he never seizes them himself nor instructs others to seize them, nor does he use them himself nor instruct others to use them.

One should respectfully serve and make offerings to those who can eloquently expound the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, providing them with protection and empowerment so that others may not slander or humiliate them; one should honor and comfort all renunciants, faithfully accept and uphold the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, never destroy any stūpas, and always protect and maintain the monasteries of the Saṃgha in the four directions.
Regarding my ordained disciples, he shall never disparage or dismiss them, nor shall he force them to return to lay life or employ them for his own service.

He shall not personally defile himself with the wheel of the ten non-virtuous actions, but shall also constantly exhort others to abandon them. Fully training in the true Dharma of statecraft as practiced by former kings, he shall utilize the path of the ten virtuous actions to gather and transform the world. He shall always draw near to spiritual friends, succeed to the lineage of the Triple Gem and ensure it remains ever-flourishing, and skillfully protect the Eye of the Dharma so that it does not perish or disappear.

"In this way, a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, and even a truly virtuous Brāhmaṇa and others, because they possess such meritorious qualities, are said to receive the stipends and emoluments of the people not in vain."
All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and spirits, down to the kaṭapūtanas and others, shall all give rise to joy and protect them with compassion.
All who are vessels of the Dharma and true fields of merit shall likewise give rise to joy and guard them with compassionate mindfulness.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the lands he inhabits and all sentient beings therein flourish and multiply, remaining secure, peaceful, and prosperous;
the military forces of neighboring countries cannot inflict harm upon them, and all, admiring his virtue, come of their own accord to submit and seek refuge.
By means of this, they successively exhort one another to cultivate wholesome karma, thereby exhausting the miserable realms and increasing the ranks of devas and humans.
They protect their own bodies and lives so that they may endure for a long time, extinguishing their own afflictions and causing others to extinguish theirs as well.
Abiding in the six *pāramitās* of the path to enlightenment, they shall destroy all evil and heterodox paths and will not sink for long into the ocean of birth and death.

Always avoiding evil friends and always drawing near to virtuous friends, they shall constantly encounter all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in every lifetime, revering and serving them without ever ceasing for a moment; before long, they shall all dwell peacefully in their respective Buddha-lands according to their hearts' desires and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

At that time, all the celestial kings within the assembly and their retinues, up to and including all the piśāca kings and their retinues, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Virtuous World-Honored One!

In the future age, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish in this buddha-field, if there should be a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, or even a truly virtuous Brāhmaṇa and so forth, who can personally distance themselves from the ten wheels of evil and also exhort others to distance themselves from them; who skillfully protects both themselves and others, skillfully protects future generations, and upholds the True Dharma—thereby ensuring that the lineage of the Triple Gem flourishes and is never severed—in short, as the Buddha has taught.

Such persons as these will reverently listen to and receive the teachings of the Three Vehicles without ever concealing them; they will protect, support, and make offerings to those of the Three Vehicles so as not to cause them disturbance or distress; and they will diligently guard the property of the Triple Gem so as not to allow it to be encroached upon or damaged.

We, along with our retinues, shall diligently protect these truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, and even these truly virtuous Brahmins and others, so that their ten qualities may all flourish and increase.
What are the ten? First, the increase of lifespan;
second, the increase of freedom from calamities.
Third, the increase of freedom from illness;
fourth, the increase of retinues;
fifth, the increase of wealth and treasures.
Sixth, the increase of requisites;
seventh, the increase of mastery;
eighth, the increase of renown.
Ninth, the increase of virtuous friends;
tenth, the increase of wisdom.
O Virtuous World-Honored One!

If those truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, up to and including truly virtuous Brahmins and others, are able to distance themselves from the ten wheels of unwholesome action and can also exhort others to distance themselves from them—possessing all the aforementioned merits—we shall protect them, and they will certainly attain the increase of these ten dharmas.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there should be a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king, or even a truly virtuous Brāhmaṇa, who accomplishes the merits previously described, we and our retinues will diligently provide protection, causing them to remain far removed from ten things."
What are the ten? First, being far removed from all enemies and adversaries;
second, being far removed from all unlovely objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Third, they are far removed from all obstructive pestilences and diseases;
fourth, they are far removed from all perverse attachments and evil views;
fifth, they are far removed from all false and deluded refuges.
Sixth, they remain far removed from all evil calamities and portents;
seventh, they remain far removed from all evil undertakings;
eighth, they remain far removed from all evil associates.
Ninth, they remain far removed from the mire of all household life;
tenth, they remain far removed from all untimely deaths.
Venerable One!
World-Honored One!

If those truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, up to and including truly virtuous Brāhmaṇas, should accomplish the various merits previously described, we shall protect them, and they will certainly attain this distancing from the ten dharmas.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

If there should be a truly virtuous Kṣatriya king who fully cultivates the merits as previously described, we and our retinues will diligently provide protection, so that this monarch, along with his retinue and all the people of his realm, shall be able to remain far removed from ten things."
What are the ten? First, being far removed from all enemies and adversaries of other nations;
second, being far removed from all enemies and adversaries within one's own nation.
Third, they will be far removed from all malevolent spirits and demons;
fourth, they will be far removed from all instances of excessive heat and drought;
fifth, they will be far removed from all instances of suppressed cold and stagnant rain.
Sixth, they are far removed from all untimely cold and heat, fierce winds, torrential rains, frost and hail, and calamities;
seventh, they are far removed from all malignant stars and portents;
eighth, they are far removed from all famine and scarcity.
Ninth, they are far removed from all untimely death and illness;
tenth, they are far removed from all false attachments and evil views.
O Virtuous World-Honored One!

If that truly virtuous Kṣatriya king fully cultivates and perfects the merits previously described, we and our retinues will diligently provide protection, ensuring that this monarch, along with his attendants, his kingdom, and all its people, shall certainly attain these ten dharmas of remoteness.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the various celestial emperors and their retinues, as well as all the emperors of the piśācas and their retinues, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
That you are able to make such vows is precisely what you ought to do.
By reason of these causes and conditions, it shall bring you peace and happiness for a long night.
At that time, the Great Brahmā Devagarbha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray only that you will grant me leave to speak, for the sake of all truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings in this buddha-field in future ages, a great dhāraṇī mantra of clear phrases capable of protecting the nation through the mind of the Non-Retrogression Wheel.”

By the power and majesty of these words and phrases of the Great Dhāraṇī Mantra of the Non-retrogressive Wheel for Protecting the Nation, all truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings in this Buddha-field during future ages shall not be overcome by any enemies or evil associates, and they shall be able to cause all enemies and evil associates to naturally retreat and disperse.

They are able to skillfully guard and maintain the actions of body, speech, and mind, and are constantly praised by all the wise. They remain free from all unwholesome dharmas and always practice wholesome dharmas; they are forever free from all wrong views and false refuges.
They constantly and diligently cultivate the Mahāyāna with courageous and firm resolve;

they are always able to bring to maturity immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to be converted. Their wisdom does not rely on others, being naturally skillful; they possess the ability to practice the precious treasury of the six *pāramitās*, remaining far removed from all afflictions and stains such as anger, stinginess, and envy.

They are always revered and protected by all humans and non-humans; in whatever they do, their minds are never forgetful; they do not abandon sentient beings and delight in the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*);
and they are never separated from those who are vessels of the Dharma and fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
The Buddha said, “Devendra-garbha!

I now grant you leave to expound for future generations, within this buddha-field, for all truly virtuous kṣatriya kings, the great dhāraṇī mantra-verse of the ‘Indestructible Wheel of Mind that Protects the Nation. By the majestic spiritual power of these great dhāraṇī mantra-verses of the Indestructible Wheel of Mind that Protects the Nation, may all truly virtuous kṣatriya kings in this buddha-field of future ages not be overcome by any enemies or evil associates; and so forth, until they are never separated from all Buddhas and their disciples.”
At that time, the Great Brahmā Devakūṭa spoke these words of the Great Dhāraṇī-Mantra of the Heart of the Non-Retrogressive Wheel for Protecting the Nation:
"Tadyathā: mune 1, munaye 2. (In the language of Tang [Chinese], this means: *muni*, 1; *munaye*, 2.)
1. Munir hiri-dāye | 2. Muniro ha-vi-che-li | 3. Muna-har-ṣṭe | 4.
Muna-har-ṣṭe | 5. Muna-har-ṣṭe ||
7. Muniguptaṣaṭkṛtvarabhojī 8.
Prathamaśatabhojī (with the initial *ś* pronounced as *ch*)
Mila-pakṣa (蜜羅博差), Saurabha-gṛddhite (騷剌婆紇栗帝), Dharana-gṛddhile (妬剌拏紇栗折隸).
12. *Bhadrakṣa-ṛddhe* | 13. *Kukkuṇa-male* | 14. *Avakṣasale* (with the initial *ava-* having the *u* sound as in *u-ha*) | 14.
*Phakṣasale* (with the initial *pha-* having the *a* sound as in *a-ha*).
E-na-wo-ho-chi-li-fa (15) Mo-ni-po-ta-fa (16) Sva-hā.
In the language of Tang, this means "Well-spoken. After the Great Brahmā Tianzang had spoken this mantra, he again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will all give their approval to this Great Dhāraṇī which I have spoken.
The World-Honored One replied,
"Excellent, excellent!"
The entire great assembly also spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Sons of good family!

You should all receive, uphold, and transmit these words and phrases of the Great Dharani Mantra of the Heart of the Non-retrogressive Wheel for Protecting the Nation, as spoken by the Great Brahma Deva-garbha. Entrust them to all truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings within this Buddha-field of the future, so that they may personally receive and uphold them, and cause them to be widely disseminated.”
By these causes and conditions, those truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, along with their retinues and the people of the realm, shall all obtain benefit and peace;

they will constantly turn the wheel of Dharma, their fame will reach far and wide, their majestic virtue will blaze forth, they will destroy false views and establish right views, protect the eye of the Dharma, and continue the lineage of the Triple Gem, causing it to flourish and never be severed.
They bring immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to maturity;
possessing firm and pure faith in the Mahāyāna, they abide long and perfectly, are able to fully cultivate the six pāramitās, sever all obstacles, and swiftly reach the ultimate goal.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Then the Great Brahmā Devagarbha Questioned the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings:
'Beings with sharp faculties and the like Delight in cultivating meditative concentration, recitation, and merit;'"
"When a wise king accomplishes the Dharma, does it lead to transcendence or to sinking into the depths?
Among the three things he cultivates, is there only that which removes delusion and prevents regression?
The World-Honored One replied to him:
"If one commits acts that leave no refuge, though their awakening and wisdom be sharp and keen, they will head toward the Avīci Hell;
because it is not true intelligence, they delight in practicing the wheel of the ten non-virtues,
severing all roots of goodness, and swiftly proceeding to hell."
Concentration can truly sever the afflictions; it is not through the merit of listening or reciting.
Therefore, those who seek nirvana should always cultivate meditative absorption.
Possessing wisdom and diligent effort, they shall protect and uphold my True Dharma.
Through reverence for the *kāṣāya*, one can cross the ocean of afflictions;
by delighting in dwelling in secluded forests, one stays far from those who commit the *ānantarya* crimes.
By reverently upholding the precepts and cultivating meditative concentration, one can cross the ocean of all existences.
Universally trusting and revering the Three Vehicles, Causing my True Dharma to flourish,
And making offerings to those clad in dyed robes— One shall surely succeed in becoming an ocean of merit;
Able to subdue the difficult-to-tame mind, One does not expose the faults of the bhikṣus.
Cultivating the noble lineage of contentment, one shall become a Honored One among two-legged beings.
Remaining far from evil bhikṣus and drawing near to the sphere of holy practice,
refraining from consuming the property of the Saṅgha, one will swiftly realize Great Bodhi.
Peace and happiness within the three realms / All arise from the Three Jewels;
therefore, those who seek peace and happiness / Should constantly make offerings to the Three Jewels.
Even the Caṇḍāla kings and others / Who side with wicked bhikṣus,
To commit an offense against the Triple Gem is to fall swiftly into the Avīci Hell.
The sin of ten oil-pressing wheels is equal to that of one brothel;
ten brothels are equal to the sin of one tavern.
The sin of establishing ten taverns is equal to that of one slaughterhouse;
the sin of establishing ten slaughterhouses is equal to that of one king.
A truly virtuous king who promotes my True Dharma [is free from such faults].
Universally making offerings to those of the three vehicles, one shall succeed in becoming an ocean of merit.
Even if one were to fill Jambudvīpa with the seven treasures and offer them to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
the mass of merit obtained thereby would not equal that of protecting the Buddha’s Dharma.
If one were to build a monastery for the Buddha and the Sangha, equal in size to the fourteen continents,
the mass of merit obtained thereby would not equal that of protecting the Buddha-dharma.
Or if one were to construct a stūpa for the Buddha, equal in size to the three-thousandfold world system...
The mass of merit obtained by that person is not equal to protecting the Buddha-dharma.
Though one may untie the bonds of an Arhat and perform various offerings,
if one does not obstruct my True Dharma, their merit shall surpass that of the former.
Throughout thousands of koṭis of kalpas, the superior wisdom born from the diligent cultivation of meditative concentration by the wise is not equal to that gained by protecting my Dharma.
True and virtuous kings and others who remain far removed from the wheel of the ten non-virtues [attain this].
Protecting my true Dharma and those who wear the kāṣāya,
not slandering my teachings, the Triple Vehicle, or its practitioners;
universally hearing and making offerings to them, and protecting those who preach the Dharma.
Not damaging the property of the Triple Gem, not obstructing or clinging to the *kāṣāya*,
and always honoring those who possess the vessel as well as those who do not— their merit is peerless and beyond compare.
It is like five suns appearing simultaneously, by which the great oceans are all dried up.
Thus guarding my Dharma can dry up the afflictions;
just as when the wind-disaster arises and all mountains are scattered and destroyed,
so too guarding my Dharma can eliminate and extinguish the afflictions.
Just as when the calamity of water arises, the great earth is all swept away and destroyed;
so too does the protection of my Dharma destroy undesirable fruits.
Like a wish-fulfilling jewel, it fulfills every aspiration according to one's wishes.
Thus, the Dharma of the Three Vehicles can fulfill the vows of sentient beings;
just as encountering a wise vase eliminates poverty and secures wealth and joy,
so too by encountering the Buddha-Dharma, one extinguishes delusions and realizes Bodhi.
Like the moon on the fifteenth night, Its bright radiance fills the void;
So too does the Dharma-protector’s wisdom Pervade the entire realm of phenomena.
Like space, it is impartial, Without substance and without marks.
Thus, those who protect the Dharma know that all phenomena are of one flavor;
like the sun emitting radiance, they constantly dispel the darkness of the world.
So too do these protectors of the Dharma always shine universally upon the world.

**Chapter Four: On Practice with a Basis, Part One** At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha in verse:
“It was previously said that those who break the precepts lose their pure virtues; they are not vessels for the noble ones nor are they my sons.
Having cast aside all the dharmas of a śramaṇa like discarded ashes, they should not dwell among my pure assembly.”
Defiled by the three impurities and having lost the path to cessation, they are incapable of digesting superior offerings;
even a small portion of the property belonging to the Saṅgha of the four directions, I do not permit them to accept.
If one commits even a single of the four root offenses, one is cast out by the pure assembly like a corpse from the sea;
why then do you now speak of wicked bhikṣus, saying they should be met with patience and compassion rather than punishment,
and further urging that one should diligently make offerings to them, feeling pity and not giving rise to even a slight thought of ill will?
Listen with reverence to the Dharma that is taught; you shall thereby obtain merit, wisdom, and great compassion.
As for those who possess the six supernormal powers and save the world—though these are explained in other sutras—you all should place your faith in the Mahāyāna.
You should abandon the path of liberation of the two vehicles and follow the upright and subtle path to Bodhi.
Why do you now again speak of the three vehicles, universally exhorting [beings] to listen, uphold, and practice offerings?
Are the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and fruits of the śramaṇa found within this sūtra, or are they absent elsewhere?
The Noble Eightfold Path is peerless; those of all three vehicles travel this same path.
Desiring liberation, they apply themselves with diligent effort, each realizing Bodhi according to their own aspirations.

O Honored One among sentient beings, please examine this: may you bring together the teachings of the past and present so that they are not in conflict, enabling the assembly of devas, humans, and bodhisattvas to attain realization with joyful hearts and witness the ultimate truth.
Upon hearing the Mahāyāna being taught, who is benefited?
Upon hearing the Mahāyāna being taught, who is harmed?
Regarding the ten kinds of liberation of the Śrāvaka vehicle, upon hearing them taught, who is harmed and who is benefited?
Who, upon hearing the Dharma, advances further?
Who, upon hearing the Dharma, regresses and sinks?
How does one grow weary of all conditioned phenomena and swiftly dry up old age and death?
Those who diligently cultivate all virtues day and night— by what sublime principle and by which vehicle can they cross the four deep and vast torrents?
O Savior of the World, please explain this for us all.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent,
excellent, noble son!"

You now, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and to perform a great service for the sake of gods, humans, asuras, and others, have questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning.
"You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said, "Good son!"
There are ten types of individuals who wander through birth and death and find it difficult to obtain a human body.
What are these ten types of individuals?
First, those who do not plant roots of goodness.
Second, not having cultivated meritorious deeds;
third, the continuity of defiled states;
fourth, following the conduct of evil associates.
Fifth, not seeing and not fearing the bitter fruits of future lives;
sixth, intense and fierce greed;
seventh, intense and fierce anger.
Eighth, intense ignorance;
ninth, a mind that is deluded and distracted;
tenth, adhering to evil and false views.
These ten kinds of causes for conduct without reliance cause sentient beings to commit root offenses, violate the śīla, and fall into the various evil destinies.
What are the ten forms of conduct without reliance?
That is to say, among those who have gone forth within my Dharma, there are those whose application is impaired but whose intention is not;
those whose intention is impaired but whose application is not;
and those whose both application and intention are impaired.
There are those whose morality is impaired but whose view is not;
there are those whose view is impaired but whose morality is not;
and there are those whose both morality and view are impaired.
There are those who, although their application, intention, ethical discipline, and view remain entirely unimpaired, nevertheless act without reliance due solely to the influence of evil friends.

There are those who, although they rely on spiritual friends and exert effort, are nevertheless dull-witted like sheep that are mute; they do not discern any of their undertakings at all. When they hear spiritual friends speak of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, they are unable to receive them, unable to retain them, and unable to understand the meaning of what is wholesome and unwholesome. Due to these causes and conditions, they engage in conduct that lacks a foundation.

There are those who are never satiated with various kinds of wealth and possessions; driven by the causes and conditions of their pursuit, their minds become deluded and they engage in practices that lack a refuge.
There are those who, being oppressed and afflicted by various illnesses, seek out various sacrifices and incantations; for these reasons, they engage in practices that lack a refuge.

These ten kinds of causes for conduct lacking reliance cause sentient beings to commit root offenses; in this present life, they become unfit vessels for the noble ones, violate the precepts, and fall into the various evil destinies.

“Good son! If there is a person whose application is impaired but whose intention is not impaired, and who encounters any one of the causes for conduct without support and commits a root offense, they become deeply terrified and feel shame and remorse, thereby abandoning it and no longer repeatedly committing various evil deeds.
For the sake of benefiting them, the Tathāgata speaks of śramaṇas who defile the path.
Why is this? Because after they have committed such grave and evil karma, they immediately disclose it and do not dare to conceal it, feeling shame and remorse, and performing repentance.
Through such shame, remorse, and confession, his offenses are eliminated and their continuity is forever severed, so that he does not commit them again.

Although he should be expelled from all monastic affairs and forbidden from using any of the requisites belonging to the śramaṇas, because that person has become a vessel for the Dharma within the Three Vehicles, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, may teach him the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

There is such a possibility that, during their second or third rebirth, by exerting the power of right aspirations and encountering the power of virtuous friends, all the karmic obstructions of the evil deeds they have committed will be entirely extinguished.

Some have realized the fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle; some have realized the fruits of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and entered parinirvāṇa; and some have awakened to and entered the vast and profound principle of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
In the same way, it should be understood that for one whose ethical discipline is impaired but whose view is not impaired, the case is likewise.

"If there is a person whose intention is impaired but whose application is not impaired, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting them, teaches the method for seeking the four Brahma-vihāras; such a person is a vessel for the Śrāvaka-yāna, or perhaps a vessel for the Pratyekabuddha-yāna."
"If there is a person whose application and intention are both corrupted, they are not a fit vessel for any of the vehicles.
For the sake of benefiting such a person, the Tathāgata praises and teaches generosity."

"If there is a person whose views are corrupted but whose precepts are not, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting them, teaches the Dharma of dependent origination so that they may abandon their evil views and enter either the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle in this very life, or be able to awaken and enter it in a future body."
"If there is a person whose ethical discipline and views are both ruined, they are not a fit vessel for the noble Dharma.
For their benefit, the Tathāgata praises and speaks of generosity."

"If there is a person whose application, intention, ethical discipline, and view are unimpaired, yet who relies solely on the power of an evil friend, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting such a person, praises and speaks of the ten paths of wholesome action."
"If there is a person who, although relying upon a spiritual friend and exerting effort, is nevertheless dull-witted like a mute sheep and unable to comprehend wholesome or unwholesome dharmas."
For their benefit, the Tathāgata praises and teaches the practice of recitation.

If they are oppressed by various diseases of craving or deluded by various speculative views, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefiting such as these who seek liberation, reveals to them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, which can bring about transcendence from birth and death;
and to those who hold nihilistic views, he praises and teaches the Dharma of dependent origination.

For those who hold the view of eternalism, he explains that all existences and destinies within the three realms involve death here and birth there, like a potter’s wheel whose rotation continues without interruption, characterized by such phenomena as impermanence.
“Good son! There is not a single name, expression, or sound spoken by the Tathāgata that is empty or fruitless; there is nothing that does not serve to bring sentient beings to maturity.”

Therefore, the sin of slandering the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata and destroying the eye of the True Dharma for all sentient beings exceeds all immeasurable heavy sins, such as the ānantarya and the anantaryakalpa-like offenses.

If there are those who, regarding the true Dharma spoken by me for the sake of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings—namely, the true Dharma spoken in reliance upon the Śrāvaka vehicle, or the true Dharma spoken in reliance upon the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the true Dharma spoken in reliance upon the Mahāyāna—should slander, obstruct, conceal, or cause it to disappear, even down to a single verse, you should know that such persons are called slanderers of the true Dharma, destroyers of the Eightfold Noble Path, and those who ruin the eye of the true Dharma for all sentient beings.

Such a person, having themselves practiced great unbeneficial conduct, also causes all sentient beings to practice great unbeneficial conduct; relying upon the shameless and immodest monastic community, this person thus slanders the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, good son, there are four kinds of Saṃgha. What are the four?
First, the Sangha of ultimate meaning;
second, the conventional Sangha;
third, the sheep-like mute Sangha.
The fourth is the monastic community lacking shame and remorse.
What is called the "ultimate monastic community"?
It refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Whether they be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas whose virtue is most exalted and who have attained mastery over all phenomena;
or pratyekabuddhas; or arhats;
Whether they are non-returners, once-returners,
or stream-enterers;
These seven types of *pudgalas* are subsumed within the ultimate Saṃgha.

If there are sentient beings who, while bearing the appearance of householders—neither shaving their hair and beards nor wearing the saffron robes—do not receive any of the *prātimokṣa* vows of renunciation and are excluded from all *karmavācanā*, *poṣadha*, and *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, yet possess the noble Dharma and have attained the fruits of the noble ones, they are subsumed within the ultimate Saṃgha; this is called the ultimate Saṃgha.
"What is called the conventional Saṃgha?
It refers to those who have shaved their hair and beards, donned the saffron robes, and accomplished the prātimokṣa precepts of renunciation; this is called the conventional Saṃgha."
"What is meant by 'dumb sheep monks'?

It refers to those who do not understand whether fundamental and other offenses have been committed or not; who do not know the gravity of their transgressions; who violate various minor and secondary precepts; and who do not know how to confess and repent for the offenses they have committed."

Dull-witted and obtuse, they do not perceive or fear even minor transgressions; they do not dwell in reliance upon wise and virtuous persons, nor do they go from time to time to those who are learned and wise to attend upon them and serve them.
Nor did he repeatedly and respectfully inquire: "What is wholesome?
What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy?"
What is blameless?
What practice is sublime?
What action is evil?
All such individuals are subsumed within the category of the "dumb sheep" *saṃgha*; this is what is called the "dumb sheep *saṃgha*.
What is meant by the "shameless and unashamed *saṃgha*"?
It refers to those sentient beings who, for the sake of making a living, take refuge in my Dharma and seek to go forth as renunciants.
Having gone forth, they violate all the Pratimokṣa precepts they have undertaken; lacking shame and a sense of propriety, they neither perceive nor fear the bitter fruits of future lives.
Internally harboring corruption like a filthy snail or a conch, they have the voice of a conch but the conduct of a dog; they constantly delight in empty words and possess not a single truth.
Greedy and stingy, envious, ignorant, and arrogant, they abandon the three superior karmas and are greedily attached to gain, offerings, respect, and reputation.
They are addicted to the six sense objects, delighting in lustful dissipation, and craving the sensory realms of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
All such individuals are included within the Saṃgha of the shameless; they slander the True Dharma, and are thus called the Saṃgha of those lacking shame and remorse. "Good son!
Regarding the Sangha of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-saṃgha*), some among them are also included within the category of śramaṇas of the supreme path (*uttara-mārga*).

As for those of the supreme path, it refers to those who, by relying on the Noble Eightfold Path, are able to cross the violent torrent of all afflictions themselves and cause others to cross as well.
What, then, is this? It refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One; the Pratyekabuddhas; and the Arhats.
These three types of individuals (pudgala) have already abandoned all the branches and attendants of existence; therefore, they are called those who have attained the Supreme Path.

Furthermore, there is the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, without depending on external conditions, possess unobstructed knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena and embrace the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; they are also included among those known as śramaṇas of the supreme path.
"Regarding those who are the ultimate Saṅgha and the conventional Saṅgha, among them there may be some who are also included within the category of 'shamans who point out the path.

If there is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is truly virtuous and has attained the prātimokṣa vows, up to and including being endowed with mundane right view, and who—by the power of their prophetic declarations and miraculous manifestations—is able to extensively proclaim and reveal the dharmas of the noble paths to others, it should be known that such a *pudgala* is called the most inferior 'shaman who points out the path.'"
The person who has realized the fruit of stream-entry is called the second.
The person who has realized the fruit of once-returning is called the third.
The person who has realized the fruit of non-returning is called the fourth.

Furthermore, there is a group of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas called the fifth, namely those dwelling from the first stage through the tenth stage, up to those abiding in their final existence; all of these are included among the śramaṇas who demonstrate the path.
"If one accomplishes the ritual of the Prātimokṣa precepts, then one's conduct will be pure and complete; all such individuals are subsumed under the 'Śramaṇas who live by the Path.
Because they sustain their lives by means of the Path, they are called 'those who live by the Path' (mārgajīvika)."

Furthermore, there is the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, desiring to gather in and benefit all sentient beings and to bring them peace and happiness, fully practice the six pāramitās; this is also called the Path of Life.
"These three kinds of śramaṇas—the one who possesses the supreme path, the one who shows the path, and the one who lives by the path—are called the true fields of merit in the world.
All other śramaṇas are called 'corrupters of the path'; though they are not real [fields of merit], they may nonetheless be included among the category of fields of merit."

"If there is an individual who relies upon a monastic community lacking shame and dread of blame, they are called a corpse within my True Dharma and Vinaya; they should be expelled from the ocean-like assembly of pure monks, for they are not a fit vessel for the Dharma."
I do not call that person my Great Teacher, nor is that person my disciple.
There are shameless monks who do not constitute vessels for the Dharma; yet they claim me as their teacher and develop deep faith and reverence for my relics and my images;
they also develop deep faith and reverence for my Dharma, Sangha, and the precepts beloved by the noble ones.
They do not themselves cling to various evil and false views, nor do they cause others to cling to evil and false views;
they are able to extensively proclaim my Dharma for others, praising and extolling it without giving rise to slander;
they constantly make right vows, and whenever they commit an offense, they repeatedly feel weary of it and abandon it.
By confessing and repenting, numerous karmic obstructions can all be eliminated.

You should know that such a person, by virtue of their faith, reverence for the Triple Gem, and the power of the noble precepts, surpasses the ninety-five types of non-Buddhist practitioners by many hundreds of thousands of times.
"One cannot enter the city of Parinirvāṇa quickly; even a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King cannot equal them, let alone other miscellaneous classes of all sentient beings!
For this reason, after the Tathāgata has observed the various distinctions in the karmic retributions of all sentient beings, he declares:
'Within my Dharma, regarding those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāṣāya robes, I shall never permit Kṣatriyas or others to insult, humiliate, or punish them.'"
"If there are those who insult, humiliate, or punish any person who has left the household life, the retribution for their sins shall be as extensively described before.

Furthermore, those who renounce the world and leave the household life in accordance with my Dharma—shaving off their hair and beards and donning the saffron robe—are immediately protected by the compassion of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
and their dignified demeanor, physical appearance, and the robes they wear are likewise guarded by the compassion of all the World-Honored Buddhas of the past, future, and present."

Therefore, to disparage and revile those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes as renunciants is to disparage and revile all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present.

For this reason, those who possess wisdom, who loathe and fear all forms of suffering, and who aspire to the happiness of humans, devas, or nirvāṇa, should not disparage, revile, or reject those who have left the household life, shaved their hair and beards, and donned the saffron robes.

"There are monks who lack a sense of shame and modesty, who violate the prohibitive precepts, and who fail to become worthy vessels for the noble ones of the Three Vehicles; having themselves stubbornly clung to various evil and false views, they are also able to cause others to cling to evil and false views."

That is to say, for the sake of true and virtuous kṣatriyas, true and virtuous brāhmaṇas, true and virtuous officials, true and virtuous householders, true and virtuous śramaṇas, true and virtuous elders, true and virtuous vaiśyas, and true and virtuous śūdras—whether men or women—he teaches that in all the worlds there is no father and no mother, and so forth, up to: there is no retribution obtained from wholesome or unwholesome karma; there is no one who can attain the fruits of the noble path; and all phenomena do not arise from causes.
Some maintain that the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is eternal and not subject to transformation or decay;
others maintain that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is eternal and not subject to transformation or decay.
Some hold the view that the various ascetic practices devised by non-Buddhists lead to ultimate purity.
Others hold the view that only the Śrāvaka Vehicle leads to ultimate purity, neither the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle nor the Mahāyāna;

they place their faith in, revere, praise, proclaim, and reveal the Śrāvaka Vehicle, while slandering, despising, obstructing, and concealing the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle and the Mahāyāna, so as not to allow them to circulate.
There are some who hold the view that only the Pratyekabuddhayāna attains ultimate purity, neither the Śrāvakayāna nor the Mahāyāna.
They place their faith, respect, and praise upon the Pratyekabuddhayāna, proclaiming and elucidating it.
Regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Mahāyāna, they slander, despise, obstruct, and conceal them, not allowing them to circulate.
Or there are those who hold the view that only the Mahāyāna attains ultimate purity, while the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle do not.

Regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, having already developed faith in it oneself, they teach others to develop faith; having already shown reverence themselves, they teach others to show reverence; having already offered praise themselves, they teach others to offer praise; having already transcribed it themselves, they teach others to transcribe it; having already recited and chanted it themselves, they teach others to recite and chant it; having already heard and received it themselves, they teach others to hear and receive it; and having already contemplated it themselves, they teach others to contemplate it. Whether other sentient beings are vessels for the Dharma or not vessels for the Dharma, they extensively expound, reveal, and explain for them the subtle and profound meanings of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, they slander, despise, obstruct, and conceal them, not allowing them to circulate.

They themselves do not give rise to faith and obstruct others from giving rise to faith; they themselves do not show reverence and obstruct others from showing reverence; they themselves do not praise them and obstruct others from praising them; they themselves do not copy them and obstruct others from copying them; they themselves do not read, recite, listen to, receive, or contemplate them and obstruct others from reading, reciting, listening to, receiving, or contemplating them; and they take no pleasure in extensively explaining, revealing, or interpreting the meanings of the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
"Some may hold the view that only by practicing generosity does one attain ultimate purity, and not through morality, patience, or even wisdom.
Others may hold the view that only by practicing the precepts does one attain ultimate purity, and not through generosity, patience, or even wisdom."
Some hold the view that only by cultivating patience does one attain ultimate purity, and not through generosity, ethical discipline, or even wisdom.
Others hold the view that only by cultivating diligence does one attain ultimate purity, and not through generosity, ethical discipline, or even wisdom.
Some maintain that only the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) leads to ultimate purity, and not giving, nor ethical discipline, nor even wisdom.
Others maintain that only the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*) leads to ultimate purity, and not giving, nor ethical discipline, nor even meditative concentration.
Some maintain that by practicing only the various worldly arts and skills, one attains ultimate purity.
Others maintain that by practicing only such acts as leaping from cliffs, entering fire, or self-starvation, one attains ultimate purity.

“Good son! In this way, bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct—those who are not vessels for the Dharma—deceive and delude various sentient beings who are true vessels for the Dharma, causing them to cling to wrong views.”

Due to their perverted and evil views, they destroy the pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom of true and virtuous kṣatriya kings, and even true and virtuous śūdras, whether male or female.
They transform Kṣatriyas into Caṇḍālas, and even Vaiśyas and Śūdras into Caṇḍālas.

These bhikṣus who are not vessels for the Dharma and have broken their precepts, along with these Kṣatriya-Caṇḍālas and others—both teachers and disciples—shall sever all roots of goodness and eventually fall into the Avīci Hell.

“Good son! It is like a human corpse that has become bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling; all who come to see it are熏 (xūn) by its stench. As they approach and touch the putrid corpse, or as they interact with it, they are all subsequently熏染 (xūnrǎn) by its filth and stench.”

In this way, whether they be true and virtuous kṣatriya kings, or even true and virtuous śūdras, and so forth—whether male or female—if they associate with, socialize with, dwell together with, or engage in common activities alongside monks who have broken their precepts, act wickedly, and are unworthy vessels of the Dharma, they will be tainted by the foul stench of those evil views.

In this way, in this manner, they cause those truly virtuous Kṣatriya kings, and even those truly virtuous Śūdras and others—whether male or female—to lose their pure faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom; they become Caṇḍāla masters and disciples, severing all roots of goodness, and shall eventually fall into the Avīci Hell.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Five.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: On Reliance on Practice, Part Two. "Good son!

Observe these immeasurable sentient beings, such as kṣatriyas and others, who associate with such monks who violate the precepts, engage in evil conduct, and are not vessels for the Dharma; they fall away from all wholesome dharmas and shall eventually fall into the Avīci Hell."

Therefore, those who wish to attain the bliss of rebirth in the heavens or the supreme, wondrous state of nirvana should all draw near to, serve, and make offerings to śramaṇas of the superior path, seeking to consult them and hear the essential teachings of the Three Vehicles;
or they should seek out śramaṇas who demonstrate the Way and guide others along it.
If such śramaṇas of the three paths do not exist, one should seek them among those who are defilers of the path.

Even if their precepts have degenerated, if they possess right view and are complete in their intention and application, one should go to them, attend upon them, serve and make offerings to them, and consult them to hear the essential teachings of the Three Vehicles.
One should not associate with, serve, or make offerings to those whose application, intention, and view are impaired.
Although such persons may have impaired ethical discipline, they lack wrong views because their intention, application, and view are fully complete.
One should go to where they are to consult them and listen to the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna; one should not disparage them.

Among these three vehicles, according to one’s own inclination and preference, one should make a vow and apply oneself with diligence to study one vehicle, while not disparaging the remaining vehicles.
If one should disparage even a single verse of any of the three vehicles, one should not associate with them, nor socialize with them, nor dwell together with them, nor engage in joint activities.
"If anyone associates with them, or befriends them, or dwells together with them, or engages in the same activities as them, they will all certainly fall into the Avīci Hell. Good son!..."

Therefore, if one wishes to rely upon any one of the three vehicles in order to seek escape from birth and death, to delight in peace and happiness, and to weary of danger and suffering, one should have deep faith and reverence for the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata—whether it be the True Dharma taught according to the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the True Dharma taught according to the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the True Dharma taught according to the Mahāyāna—and never slander, obstruct, or suppress it, even so much as a single verse.
One should always respectfully recite, read, and listen to it, and should give rise to firm and correct vows seeking its realization.
Those who slander or disparage any one of the three vehicles should not dwell with them even for a single night; they should not draw near to them, nor consult them, nor listen to their teachings.

If sentient beings, in accordance with the three vehicles, disparage even one vehicle, or if they draw near to those who disparage the three vehicles to consult them and receive their teachings, by reason of these causes and conditions, they will all certainly fall into the Avīci Hell, where they will undergo great suffering and torment from which it is difficult to find release.
Why is this? Son of good family!

In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path and diligently seeking to realize unsurpassed wisdom, I would—whether for the sake of requesting even a single verse of the true Dharma as taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, or otherwise—even abandon my own hands, feet, blood, flesh, skin, bones, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.

Or, for the sake of requesting even a single verse of the sublime Dharma as taught in the Pratyekabuddhayāna, they may go so far as to sacrifice their own hands, feet, flesh, blood, skin, bones, head, eyes, marrow, and brain.

Or, for the sake of requesting the sublime Dharma as taught in the Mahāyāna, they may even go so far as to abandon their own hands, feet, blood, flesh, skin, bones, head, eyes, marrow, and brain, down to a single verse.

Exerting themselves with such diligence and hardship, even those who seek to attain but a single verse of the Dharma from among the three vehicles give rise to profound joy and respectfully uphold it; they practice according to the teachings without ceasing for even a moment.
Having practiced all difficult and arduous austerities for immeasurable kalpas, he realized the fruit of ultimate, unsurpassed wisdom.
Furthermore, for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, he proclaimed and revealed the true Dharma of the three vehicles.
For this reason, one should not slander, disparage, obstruct, or conceal [this teaching], even down to a single verse;
rather, one should always respectfully read, recite, and listen to it, and should form firm and correct vows to seek its realization. "Good man! [he said].

Thus, this sublime Dharma of the essential path for the three vehicles has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—and is collectively sustained by their great majestic spiritual power. It is intended to deliver all sentient beings from the great suffering of birth and death, and to cause the lineage of the Three Jewels to flourish and remain unbroken.
Therefore, one should universally have faith and reverence for this True Dharma of the Three Vehicles; do not slander, disparage, obstruct, or cause it to be hidden.
If anyone slanders, disparages, obstructs, or causes the True Dharma of the Three Vehicles to be hidden—even down to a single verse—they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Furthermore, good son!

In a future age, within this Buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya-cāṇḍālas*, *brāhmaṇa-cāṇḍālas*, *amātya-cāṇḍālas*, *gṛhapati-cāṇḍālas*, *śramaṇa-cāṇḍālas*, *śreṣṭhin-cāṇḍālas*, *vaiśya-cāṇḍālas*, and *śūdra-cāṇḍālas*—whether male or female—who are crooked and deceitful, foolish, and conceited in their supposed intelligence;
whose nature is fierce, rebellious, violent, and coarse."
They do not perceive or fear the bitter fruits of future lives;

they take pleasure in killing, up to and including holding wrong views, being envious, stingy, greedy, hating and turning their backs on virtuous friends, and associating with evil friends; such persons are not vessels for the noble ones of the Three Vehicles.

Or, having heard and studied only a small portion of the Śrāvaka vehicle, they slander, revile, obstruct, and conceal the Pratyekabuddha vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle—which are protected and sustained by all Buddhas—and do not allow them to circulate.

Or, having heard or studied only the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, they slander, revile, obstruct, and conceal the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Unsurpassed Vehicle—which are collectively upheld by all Buddhas—and do not allow them to circulate.

Or, having heard and studied the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle for only a little, they then slander, revile, obstruct, and conceal the Śrāvaka Vehicle and Pratyekabuddha Vehicle—which are collectively upheld by all Buddhas—so as not to allow them to circulate.
For the sake of seeking fame and profit, they utter these words:
"I am a follower of the Mahāyāna; I belong to the faction of the Mahāyāna.

I delight only in hearing, studying, and upholding the Mahāyāna, and I do not delight in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor do I delight in associating with those who study the two vehicles."

"In this way, those who falsely claim to belong to the Mahāyāna, by the power of their own ignorance and arrogance, slander, obstruct, and conceal the true Dharma of the Three Vehicles so that it does not circulate;
they harbor hatred and jealousy toward those who study and practice the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, slandering and insulting them to deprive them of their dignity and influence."

“Good son! All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, as well as all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, uphold two matters through the power of great compassion:
first, in order to perpetuate the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it never ceases, they renounce worldly life to leave the home, shave their hair and beards, and don the kashaya robes;”
Second, the true Dharma associated with the Four Noble Truths and other essentials for the deliverance of the three vehicles.

These two matters can be properly upheld only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the great Bodhisattvas; they cannot be upheld by the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others, nor by hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Great Brahmā Kings, Śakras, or Universal Monarchs who rule over the four continents.

In future ages, within this Buddha-field, there will be *kṣatriya* outcaste kings who, upon seeing those who have gone forth from home by relying on my Dharma—having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the *kāṣāya*—will seek out their transgressions through various means. They will revile, insult, or humiliate them; they may lash them with whips and staves, imprison them, confiscate their requisites, or strip them of their *kāṣāyas*, forcing them to return to lay life. They will compel them to perform various domestic tasks, or subject them to arbitrary corvée labor, or unjustly exile them, or deprive them of food and drink, or even take their lives.

That *kṣatriya-caṇḍāla* king, by means of his own folly, arrogance, and power, will insult and punish my disciples who are protected together by the great compassionate power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he will slander and destroy my profound Dharma, which is protected together by the great compassionate power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and regarding the True Dharma of the Three Vehicles protected together by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time, he will obstruct, obscure, and cause it not to circulate.
"There may be a *kṣatriya* *caṇḍāla* king, or even a *vaiśya* or *śūdra* *caṇḍāla*, whether male or female, who is foolish and arrogant, yet claims for himself the title of 'Mahāyāna. "
Such a person is not even a vessel for the teachings of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, let alone a vessel for the unsurpassed Mahāyāna!

For the sake of gain, honor, and reputation, they deceive the ignorant masses of the world, claiming, "We are followers of the Mahāyāna," while slandering and disparaging the true Dharma of the Tathāgata’s two vehicles.
Such persons as these, due to the causes and conditions of ignorance, deceit, arrogance, jealousy, and stingy greed, will destroy my Dharma-eye and cause it to quickly vanish and perish.
They commit a grave transgression against all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
they also commit a grave transgression against all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time;
and furthermore, they commit a grave transgression against all Śrāvakas of the three periods of time.
Before long, their limbs will become impaired and deficient, and they will encounter various kinds of grave and evil diseases.

Those *kṣatriya* caṇḍāla kings, and even those *vaiśya* and *śūdra* caṇḍālas—whether male or female—because they have committed evil karma and given rise to inverted views, destroy and sever all their roots of goodness.

Even if at times they cultivate much merit through giving, they will in future lives be born among the hungry ghosts or the animals to experience the fruits of wealth and pleasure; yet within those bodies, they cannot even give rise to the inferior roots of goodness belonging to the form or formless realms, let alone be able to plant the seeds of the roots of goodness for the wisdom of omniscience—which arises effortlessly—belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle!

Furthermore, their tongues will be afflicted by disease, remaining locked and unable to speak for many days and nights; they will experience various bitter poisons and agonizing pains so intense as to be unbearable, and at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Great Hell.

"Therefore, out of compassion and pity for all true and virtuous Kṣatriya kings, and even down to true and virtuous Śūdras—whether male or female—the Tathāgata, so that they may obtain benefit and peace for a long night, earnestly and sincerely speaks these words:

'You should, with great care, refrain from harassing, reviling, or punishing those who have gone forth from home, having shaved their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes, who have taken refuge in my Dharma.'"
Regarding the true teachings of the three vehicles that I have expounded, you must carefully refrain from slandering, obstructing, or concealing them.
If you should contravene my words and intentionally commit such acts, the retribution for the resulting offenses shall be as extensively described previously.

Why is this so? This appearance of one who has gone forth from home—having taken refuge in my Dharma by shaving off hair and beard and donning the saffron robe—is protected by the great compassionate spiritual power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.
This appearance of one who has shaved off hair and beard and donned the saffron robe as a renunciant is the banner of liberation for all noble ones;
it is also the banner of the flavor of the Dharma of liberation enjoyed by all followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
and it is likewise the banner of the flavor of the Dharma of liberation enjoyed by all followers of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
It is also the banner and sign for all followers of the Mahāyāna to partake in the flavor of the Dharma of liberation.
The true Dharma of the three vehicles taught by the Tathāgata is likewise sustained by the great compassionate spiritual power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time;
it is the refuge for the liberation of all noble ones (ārya), and it is also the basis upon which all followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna rely to partake in the flavor of the Dharma of liberation.
It is also the basis for all those of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle to enjoy the flavor of the Dharma of liberation;
it is also the basis for all those of the Mahāyāna to enjoy the flavor of the Dharma of liberation.

“Good son! For this reason, those who seek liberation should draw near to, revere, and make offerings to those who have gone forth from home under my Dharma—those who have shaved their hair and beards and donned the saffron robes—and they should first believe in and respect the Śrāvaka vehicle.”

Whether one personally listens and receives [the teachings] or instructs others to listen and receive them; whether one personally recites and chants or instructs others to recite and chant; whether one personally writes or instructs others to write; whether one personally gives or instructs others to give; or whether one personally proclaims or instructs others to proclaim them—one should contemplate and practice them, causing them to spread widely.

In this way, one who has faith and reverence for the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas—whether listening to it oneself or causing others to listen, reciting it oneself or causing others to recite, writing it down oneself or causing others to write it down, giving it away oneself or causing others to give it away, or explaining it oneself or causing others to explain it—should contemplate and practice it, causing it to spread widely.

In this way, one has faith and reverence for the Mahāyāna Dharma; whether by personally hearing and receiving it or teaching others to hear and receive it, by personally reading and reciting it or teaching others to read and recite it, by personally copying it or teaching others to copy it, by personally giving it away or teaching others to give it away, or by personally proclaiming it or teaching others to proclaim it.
Contemplate and practice this so that it may be widely disseminated.

If one is not a suitable vessel, one should not listen to it oneself, nor should one teach others to listen, and so forth, as explained at length. Furthermore, one should distance oneself from all unwholesome dharmas; one should abandon evil friends and associate with virtuous friends; one should diligently cultivate the six pāramitās; one should frequently repent of all evil karma; and one should earnestly make correct vows according to what is appropriate.

If one can act in this way, it is possible that they will, in this very life, become a vessel for the Śrāvaka vehicle, or attain non-retrogression regarding the seeds of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or likewise attain non-retrogression regarding the seeds of the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, those of all three vehicles should practice and study; they should not be arrogant, falsely claiming to belong to the Mahāyāna, while slandering and disparaging the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Previously, I spoke these words—“Only by practicing the Mahāyāna can one attain the ultimate”—solely for those who were firm practitioners and vessels for the Mahāyāna.
"Therefore, what was said in the past and what is said now do not contradict one another.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Before the great assembly, Vajragarbha questioned me:"
"Why do you encourage the offering of support to evil bhikṣus who break the precepts,
who have lost the virtues of *dhūta* practice, who are possessed by delusion and wrong views,
and who— being unfit vessels for the Dharma— pollute the Path, yet you do not permit their punishment?"
Furthermore, it is said that from him one hears the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles—
the excellent medicine of true liberation— that leads to the tranquility of Nirvāṇa.
For what reason do other sūtras speak of liberation through the Single Great Vehicle?
Having previously refuted the teachings of the two vehicles, why do you now speak of three?
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, so that they may abandon evil karma and attain benefit and peace,
we pray that you will explain this to dispel our doubts.
For the benefit of kṣatriyas, and even for śūdras,
it is not permitted to harass bhikṣus, lest they incur great sin.
Shaved heads and the wearing of the kāṣāya are the signs of the Dharma-banner of all Buddhas.
The Buddhas all protect and uphold the eye of the path to liberation.
Even if one violates the various codes of discipline, it does not permanently obstruct liberation;
if one can abandon all wrong views, one shall swiftly proceed toward nirvana.
Just as a potent medicine, though decayed, can still cure many ailments,
so too one who has violated the disciplinary code can still extinguish the suffering of others.
One must not allow such a bhikṣu to participate in the poṣadha or the formal ritual proceedings (karmavācanā).
If you permit me to preach the Dharma for others, we shall both undoubtedly obtain merit.
If you take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem, and acknowledge me as your Great Teacher,
you will be able to abandon all evils and surpass all the hosts of non-Buddhists.
Just as when merchants fall upon a rākṣasa island, they are all struck with terror;
yet by each grasping a single hair of a beast, they cross the sea and escape the peril.
So too is it for one who has broken the precepts: by abandoning all evil and wrong views, [they may likewise find deliverance].
With faith as the single cause, one is liberated from the rākṣasas of affliction.
By guarding the characteristics of liberation, one is protected by all the Buddhas;
by not troubling monks who have broken the precepts, one can distance oneself from all grave evils.
Those who possess much merit and delight in seeking true liberation,
protecting equally those who are vessels and those who are not, will realize liberation without difficulty.
Those who are deluded and arrogant claim to follow the Mahāyāna, yet they lack the power of wisdom.
If one is still deluded regarding the Dharma of the Two Vehicles, how much less could one understand the Mahāyāna!
Just as one whose eyes are impaired cannot see various forms,
so too one whose faith is impaired cannot understand the Mahāyāna.
If one lacks the strength to drink from a pond or a river, how could one swallow the great ocean?
Without practicing the teachings of the Two Vehicles, how can one study the Mahāyāna?
Only after first gaining faith in the teachings of the Two Vehicles can one then gain faith in the Mahāyāna.
Those who recite the Mahāyāna without faith have empty words that yield no benefit.
Internally harboring nihilistic views while falsely claiming to follow the Mahāyāna,
they fail to guard the sins of the three karmas and thus destroy and disorder my True Dharma.
After that person’s life has ended, they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell;
therefore, one should preach according to the capacity of the listener, and not for those who are unfit vessels.
Those who are arrogant and lack compassion, who are violent, evil, and of inferior intent— [for such as these, one should not speak].
The wise should know that such a person harbors the view of nihilism;
they are neither a Śrāvaka nor a Pratyekabuddha, nor are they a vessel for the Mahāyāna.
Deceitful and slandering the Buddhas, they will surely fall into the Avīci Hell.
Those who uphold the precepts yet delight in clamor, who are stingy with the Dharma and fear suffering and evil—
the wise should understand that this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Those who delight in giving, contemplate arising and ceasing, and always rejoice in solitary, quiet places;
The wise should understand that this is called the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
To be fully endowed with all roots of goodness, to guard the foundation of compassion,
and to always delight in gathering and benefiting sentient beings— this is called the Mahāyāna.
Sacrificing body and life to protect the precepts, not harassing or harming sentient beings,
and diligently seeking the dharma of emptiness— know that this is the Mahāyāna.
With a mind capable of enduring all phenomena, one speaks virtuous words without secrecy or stinginess.
Always delighting in the Dharma— know this to be the Mahāyāna.
Regarding those who are vessels for the Dharma and those who are not, maintaining an impartial mind toward their benefit and happiness,
and remaining unstained by worldly dharmas— know this to be the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, those who possess wisdom universally revere the teaching of the three vehicles;
by not causing distress to my monastic community, they shall swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriyas, true and virtuous brāhmaṇas, true and virtuous officials, true and virtuous householders, true and virtuous elders, true and virtuous śramaṇas, true and virtuous vaiśyas, or true and virtuous śūdras—whether male or female—who accomplish the ten types of dependent wheels of conduct, they will be able to swiftly plant the seeds of the Śrāvaka-yāna within their current bodies so that they do not fall away, or they will become noble vessels for the Śrāvaka-yāna in this very life;
however, they are not yet vessels for the Pratyekabuddha-yāna or the Mahāyāna.
What are the ten? First, being fully endowed with pure faith, believing in the existence of the fruits of all wholesome and unwholesome karmas;
second, being fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, remaining far removed from all evil friends and wrong views.
Third, they abide securely in ethical discipline, remaining far removed from killing up to and including the consumption of intoxicants;
