fourth, they abide securely in a mind of loving-kindness, remaining far removed from all forms of malice, anger, and resentment;
fifth, they abide securely in a mind of compassion, rescuing and uplifting all weak and vulnerable sentient beings.
Sixth, abiding in a mind of joy, one distances oneself from all four types of verbal non-virtuous karma;
seventh, abiding in a mind of equanimity, one distances oneself from all stinginess, greed, and envy;
eighth, possessing correct refuge, one distances oneself from all false attachments to good fortune and misfortune, and never takes refuge in heterodox deities or non-Buddhist paths.
Ninth, they are endowed with diligence, cultivating all wholesome dharmas with firm resolve and heroic vigor;
tenth, they always delight in tranquility, seeking the meaning of the Dharma with joyful tirelessness.

“Good son! If there are truly virtuous kṣatriya kings, or even truly virtuous śūdras and so forth—whether male or female—who accomplish these ten kinds of wheels of conduct based on support, they will be able to swiftly plant the seeds of the Śrāvaka Vehicle within their present bodies so that they do not fall away; or they may, in their present bodies, realize all the noble dharmas of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and become noble vessels for the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
However, they do not realize the noble dharmas of the Pratyekabuddha or Mahāyāna, nor do they become noble vessels for the Pratyekabuddha or Mahāyāna.”
It should be understood that here, both the Pratyekabuddhas and the Mahāyāna speak in this same way.
"O son of good family!
These ten kinds of wheels of practice based on support are shared in common by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas."
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten kinds of wheels of practice based on support that are not shared with śrāvakas, but are common to pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas alike.

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriya kings, or even true and virtuous śūdras and so forth—whether male or female—who accomplish these ten kinds of wheels of conduct based on support, they will be able to swiftly plant the seeds of the pratyekabuddhayāna within their current bodies so that they do not fall away, or they may realize all the noble dharmas of the pratyekabuddhayāna in this very life, becoming vessels for the noble dharma of the pratyekabuddhayāna.
What are the ten? First, practicing pure actions of body, speech, and mind;
second, being endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, and feeling weary of one's own self.
Third, they conceive a profound fear toward the five aggregates of clinging;
fourth, they perceive the river of birth and death as being extremely difficult to cross;
fifth, they constantly delight in tranquility and remain aloof from all clamor and distraction.
Sixth, they delight in forest hermitages (āraṇya) and do not criticize the failings of others;
seventh, they guard their sense faculties, and their minds are always tranquil and concentrated;
eighth, they skillfully contemplate dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and carefully examine cause and effect.
Ninth, they always delight in diligently cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dhyāna;
tenth, they are able to thoroughly eliminate and extinguish all phenomena that arise through accumulation. "Good son!..."

If there are true and virtuous kṣatriya kings, or even true and virtuous śūdras, whether male or female, who accomplish these ten kinds of wheels of practice based on support, they will be able to swiftly plant the seeds of the pratyekabuddhayāna within their current bodies so as not to lose them, or they will realize all the noble dharmas of the pratyekabuddhayāna in this very life, becoming noble vessels for the pratyekabuddhayāna.
"Good son! This is called the wheel of dependent practice of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
By relying on this wheel, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can swiftly cross over the great ocean of the three realms of existence and swiftly enter the city of parinirvāṇa."
“Good son! There is the wheel of practice based on dependence. What is the meaning of this phrase?
To say ‘based on dependence’ means there is grasping, there is that which is relied upon as ‘mine,’ there is that which is appropriated, and there is that to which one is bound.”
"Practice" refers to:
the practice of the aggregates, the practice of the elements, the practice of the sense bases, and the practice of that which is bound by existence.
"Wheel" refers to:
The wheel of instruction and admonition;
like the chariot wheel or the vanguard wheel of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas rely upon these wheels to seek the path to nirvāṇa; therefore, these two types are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because they rely upon inferior practices, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.

Because they grasp at their own aggregates and practice out of fear, aversion, and a desire for their own liberation from all suffering and grief—rather than seeking the liberation of all sentient beings—they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.

Because they rely upon the movements of their own respective elements, they experience alarm and revulsion, seeking liberation for themselves from all sorrow and suffering; since they do not seek the liberation of all sentient beings while practicing, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.

Because they embrace their own engagement with the sense bases, they are struck with fear and revulsion toward them, seeking only their own liberation from all sorrow and suffering; since they do not seek the liberation of all sentient beings while practicing, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.

Because they are bound by attachments and act out of such attachment, they take no delight in gathering in sentient beings; lacking compassion and being bound by attachment, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Because they observe others undergoing manifold sufferings yet abandon them without seeking to rescue them, seeking liberation for themselves alone, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Because they sever the heads of their own afflictions while taking no pleasure in severing the heads of the afflictions of all sentient beings, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Because they are unable to control the Mahāyāna wheel and proceed toward enlightenment, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Because they are unable to follow the great circle of light and proceed toward enlightenment, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
Because they take delight in entering the city of nirvāṇa alone and without a companion to practice therein, they are not vessels for the Mahāyāna. "Good son!

There are sentient beings who have not yet applied themselves with diligent effort to study the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; such beings have faculties that are not yet matured, faculties that are inferior, and little vigor."
If one preaches the subtle, profound, and sublime Mahāyāna True Dharma to others, both the speaker and the listener shall incur great transgressions and will likewise be in opposition to all Buddhas.

Why is this so? If sentient beings have not yet applied diligent effort to study the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and their faculties are not yet mature, being inferior and their diligence meager, yet they listen to and receive the subtle and profound True Dharma of the Mahāyāna—such beings are truly deluded while claiming to be wise; they fall into the extreme of nihilism, descend into deranged conceptions, cling to the doctrine of causelessness, harbor notions of annihilation regarding all karmic fruits, and repudiate all that is well-done and ill-done.

They falsely proclaim the Mahāyāna to subvert and disorder my Dharma; they speak what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma; those who are truly not śramaṇas claim to be śramaṇas, while those who are truly śramaṇas claim not to be śramaṇas; they speak what is truly not the Vinaya as the Vinaya, and what is truly the Vinaya as not the Vinaya.

Possessing ignorance, perversion, arrogance, jealousy, and a partisan mind, they praise and protect the Mahāyāna teachings, causing them to spread widely, while slandering and obstructing the teachings of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, preventing them from spreading.

They are unable to truly rely upon the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Unsurpassed Vehicle to renounce worldly life for the homeless state, receive full ordination, and become bhikṣus; nor are they able to truly cultivate and accumulate the causes and conditions for all wholesome dharmas.

Toward my disciples—whether they be vessels of the Dharma or not—namely those who diligently practice, whether they be learners (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), even up to those who have realized the ultimate and supreme reality, as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), and whether they observe the precepts, violate them, or have no precepts at all—one might subject them to various forms of reviling, scolding, and harassment; seize their robes and alms bowls; deprive them of the use of all requisites for life; or bind and imprison them.

Thus, those who repudiate all cause and effect and advocate for nihilism, though they dwell among humans, are in truth rākṣasas; in future worlds, throughout incalculable great kalpas, it will be difficult for them to obtain a human body.
It would be better to undergo immeasurable suffering in the hells than to dwell among humans while giving rise to the view of annihilationism.

"Such a deluded person shall, before long, have his limbs rendered crippled and incomplete; for many days and nights he will remain tongue-tied and speechless, undergoing various bitter poisons and agonizing pains that are difficult to endure, and at the end of life, he will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell."

They wander and transmigrate through the various evil realms, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction, from which they are difficult to rescue; for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it is difficult to regain a human body.

Even after passing through immeasurable and incalculable kalpas and finally obtaining a human body again, they are born into a world of the five turbidities where no Buddha dwells; they are born blind, deaf, mute, or tongueless; they are constantly afflicted by various grave illnesses; or their bodies are stunted and ugly such that people do not wish to see them; their speech is clumsy and dull, and their words are loathsome to hear; their minds are perpetually deluded and confused, lacking any understanding; they are born into impoverished families where all necessities are lacking; they do not encounter virtuous friends but follow the ways of evil associates, delighting in committing evil deeds; they take pleasure in clinging to wrong views and creating crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*); they fall back once more into the Avīci Hell, transmigrating through the evil realms with no foreseeable end to their departure.

“Thus, these deluded proponents of annihilationism disrupt, confound, and destroy my True Dharma; they harass and punish my disciples—whether they observe the precepts, violate them, or possess no precepts at all—causing them all to dwell in unease and fail to cultivate various wholesome qualities.”
Due to these causes and conditions, for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas they will sink into the various evil realms, passing from darkness into darkness with no foreseeable time of escape.

Such is the retribution for the sins of those sentient beings who, instead of first seeking to hear and study the subtle, profound, and sublime Mahāyāna True Dharma, sought to hear and study the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
For such proponents of the nihilistic view of ignorance, even a human body of inferior quality is difficult to obtain, let alone being able to become a vessel for the noble ones!
They cannot even attain the nirvāṇa realized by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, much less attain the vast, profound, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment!

"Such faults as these possessed by sentient beings all arise because they have not first studied the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, but have instead entered the Mahāyāna. Good son!..."
For example, if a clay jar has many cracks and fissures, when it contains oil, milk, or other liquids, they all leak away; both the container and the contents are ruined and lost. Why is this so?
Because there is a deficiency in their vessels.

Such sentient beings have not yet applied themselves with diligent effort to study the Dharma of the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; their faculties are not yet matured, their faculties are inferior, and their diligence is slight.

If one preaches the subtle, profound, and sublime Mahāyāna True Dharma to others, both the speaker and the listener shall incur great transgressions; they will also be in opposition to all Buddhas, and their faults shall be as extensively described previously.
For example, it is like a worldly storehouse with collapsing walls and holes; when various treasures and goods are placed therein, much is lost.

In the same way, sentient beings slander and do not believe in the teachings of the Two Vehicles, refusing to practice or study them; they explain the Mahāyāna to others without understanding it as it truly is, and because of this, they commit offenses and transmigrate without end.
For example, a ship that is full of leaks is unfit for carrying passengers across the great ocean.

Likewise, sentient beings who harbor much stinginess and envy, who have never trained in the teachings of the Two Vehicles, who falsely claim to belong to the Mahāyāna while actually harboring nihilistic views, and whose bodies are "leaky" due to arrogance, flattery, and crookedness, are incapable of relying upon them to enter the ocean of omniscience.
For example, suppose there is a person whose eyes are blind; one cannot present various precious jewels to them.

In the same way, sentient beings who are arrogant and heedless, who cling to the view of emptiness, and who do not study the two vehicles, are blind and lack the eye of wisdom; they are incapable of displaying the precious jewels of the merits of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.

For example, suppose there is a person whose body is foul and filthy; even if they were to smear it with various kinds of exquisite and sublime perfumes, they would ultimately be unable to make the body fragrant and clean.

In the same way, sentient beings who are foolish and arrogant do not delight in diligently practicing the teachings of the Two Vehicles, nor do they abandon killing up to and including wrong views. Although they may diligently listen to and receive the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, they ultimately cannot understand the profound Dharma.
“Suppose there is a stony field where, although one plants excellent seeds and exerts great effort in cultivation, no fruit is ever produced.

Likewise, these sentient beings, regarding the teachings of the Two Vehicles, are arrogant and indolent, taking no pleasure in diligent practice; they greedily pursue the five desires without ever feeling weary of them. Thus, even if they plant the seeds of the Mahāyāna within those very bodies, despite their vigor and arduous toil, nothing will ever be accomplished.”
For example, if a vessel that previously held poisonous medicine is later filled with a small amount of rock honey, it is unfit for consumption.

Likewise, if sentient beings are unwilling to study and practice the teachings of the Two Vehicles and instead cling to the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), even if one preaches the Mahāyāna to them, they will ultimately be unable to achieve the benefit of themselves or others.
For example, it is like a jar that first contained rock honey but into which a small amount of poison was later cast; it is no longer fit for consumption.

In the same way, if one teaches the Mahāyāna to sentient beings who have not yet perfected their diligent cultivation and study of the true Dharma of the Two Vehicles, both [the original practice and the new teaching] will be ruined and lost.
For example, suppose there is a person who is foolish, deranged, and mentally disturbed; when music is played for him, he is unable to understand it.

In the same way, sentient beings who have never studied the teachings of the Two Vehicles, whose minds are agitated by the fierce afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, who cling to theories of causelessness and nihilism, and whose faculties are not yet mature—if one were to preach the Mahāyāna to them, they would not understand it even after a long period of time.

For example, suppose there is a person who enters the midst of a battle array without donning armor and without carrying weapons; they will inevitably suffer injury and endure all manner of afflictions.

In the same way, if sentient beings have never studied or practiced the teachings of the Two Vehicles, their wisdom is narrow and inferior and their faculties are not yet matured; if one were to preach the Mahāyāna to them, they would certainly give rise to false attachments, and by means of this, they would successively create endless evil.

Such a deluded person shall, before long, have his limbs impaired and crippled; for many days and nights he will remain tongue-tied and unable to speak, undergoing various bitter poisons and agonizing pains that are difficult to endure, and at the end of life, he will certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Regarding the wandering and coming and going through the various evil realms, it should be understood as previously explained in detail in sequence.
"Good son! Therefore, a wise person should first observe the minds of all sentient beings before preaching the Dharma."

First, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, altruism, non-laziness, patience, freedom from arrogance, freedom from envy, freedom from stinginess, and a mind of meditative equipoise; only then should one proclaim the True Dharma for others.
He never causes other sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma he preaches, to wander through birth and death or fall into great peril.
Therefore, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands the mental characteristics of all sentient beings and, with a wheel of practice free from defilement and grasping, preaches the True Dharma for them.

It is likewise for all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are equipped with the great armor: when they teach the Dharma to others, it is out of compassion, in order to cause the cessation of all afflictions, in order to enable them to cross over the ocean of the three realms of existence, and so that all sentient beings may, according to their inclinations among the three vehicles, swiftly fulfill one vehicle; thus they preach the true Dharma, never causing them to wander in birth and death or fall into great peril.
"What is called the wheel of practice free from dust and defilement?

To be 'free from dust and defilement' means that when preaching the Dharma, one does not do so for the sake of the existence of the aggregates (*skandha*), nor for the sake of the existence of the bases (*āyatana*), nor for the sake of the existence of the elements (*dhātu*). One does not do so for the sake of the existence of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nor for the existence of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), nor for the existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). One does not do so for the sake of the existence of this world, nor for the existence of other worlds; nor for the existence of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), nor for the existence of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), or attention (*manasikāra*); nor for the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*), up to and including for the sake of the existence of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), nor for the sake of the existence of [the cessation of] formations or their non-existence. It is for these reasons that one proclaims the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."

It is solely for the sake of all aggregates, bases, and elements—extensively explained up to their functioning and non-functioning—that they are all utterly quiescent; it is for the sake of proclaiming the True Dharma to all sentient beings that, by this meaning, it is called "free from dust and defilement."

"Practice" refers to that which is able to permanently sever the cycle of death here and birth there, proclaiming the True Dharma for all sentient beings; it is that which is able to permanently sever the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth, up to permanently severing both conditioned activity and non-activity, proclaiming the True Dharma for all sentient beings—this is called practice.
As for the "wheel," it is like the full moon’s light—cool, unobstructed, pervading all of space, and illuminating and touching all unimpeded realms.

In this same way, the three supreme wheels of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas—their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), their prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*), and their instructions (*anuśāsana*)—function without obstruction throughout all worlds, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings who are to be transformed.

It causes all sentient beings to have no divergent destinations, to be distinct from all worldly beings, and to be distinct from all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it enables sentient beings to sever and extinguish the dharmas of the various sufferings and afflictions of birth and death, and to realize the bliss of bodhi and nirvāṇa—this is called a wheel.
This is called the wheel of stainless conduct of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is called the wheel of non-clinging conduct?

It means being without obstruction regarding all phenomena; like sunlight that shines universally upon all things, they proclaim the True Dharma according to what is appropriate for the faculties of the three vehicles, remaining without any attachment.

That is to say, the Tathāgatas teach such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; it is like space, possessing no marks of differentiation. Through the mastery and adornment of sporting in immeasurable samādhis, they dwell in the maintenance [of the Dharma] and teach the subtle and wondrous Dharma to all sentient beings without any attachment.
It is likewise for all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are equipped with the great armor when they teach the Dharma to others:
namely, that all phenomena are neither existent nor empty;
that emptiness is neither identical to form nor separate from form, and so on, up to emptiness being neither identical to consciousness nor separate from consciousness.
It is not that the eye itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the eye; this extends up to: it is not that the mind itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the mind.
It is not that forms themselves are empty, nor are they empty apart from forms; this extends up to: it is not that phenomena themselves are empty, nor are they empty apart from phenomena.

It is not that eye-consciousness itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from eye-consciousness; this extends up to: it is not that mind-consciousness itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from mind-consciousness.

It is not that the desire realm itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the desire realm; this extends up to: it is not that the sphere of infinite space itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the sphere of infinite space; it is not that the sphere of infinite consciousness itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the sphere of infinite consciousness; it is not that the sphere of nothingness itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the sphere of nothingness; it is not that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception itself is empty, nor is it empty apart from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

It is not that emptiness is identical to the four foundations of mindfulness, nor is it separate from the four foundations of mindfulness; this extends up to: it is not that emptiness is identical to the noble eightfold path, nor is it separate from the noble eightfold path; it is not that emptiness is identical to the law of dependent origination, nor is it separate from the law of dependent origination; it is not that emptiness is identical to the three ways in which the Buddha is self-guarded, nor is it separate from the three ways in which the Buddha is self-guarded; it is not that emptiness is identical to the four fearlessnesses, nor is it separate from the four fearlessnesses; it is not that emptiness is identical to the ten powers, nor is it separate from the ten powers; it is not that emptiness is identical to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor is it separate from the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it is not that emptiness is identical to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, nor is it separate from great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity; it is not that emptiness is identical to nirvāṇa, nor is it separate from nirvāṇa.
This is called the Tathāgata and the various bodhisattvas proclaiming the subtle, sublime, and Middle Way Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Good son! In this way, the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, preaches the Dharma by means of the wheel of practice free from dust and defilement."
Like the full moon, it is cool, refreshing, and unimpeded, pervading all of space and illuminating every unobstructed realm.
To speak further in detail: moreover, by means of the wheel of non-grasping conduct, he teaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma;

being without any hindrance regarding all phenomena, he is like the sunlight that shines universally upon all things, proclaiming the True Dharma according to the suitability of the faculties of the three vehicles, without any attachment.

This means that the Tathāgatas, for the sake of all sentient beings, preach such a Dharma as being like space, devoid of any marks of differentiation. By means of infinite meditative concentrations, they sport with mastery and abide in majestic adornment; for the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma without attachment, causing them to enter the three vehicles according to their suitability.

It is likewise for the assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are equipped with the great armor: when they preach the Dharma to others, they cause sentient beings, upon hearing this most supreme and profound Dharma, to mature their various roots of goodness according to what they delight in and whichever vehicle they aspire to among the three vehicles.

They cause them to dwell securely within a single vehicle, never allowing them to increase various evil and unwholesome dharmas within saṃsāra, but ensuring they remain firm and non-regressive in nirvāṇa.
“Good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others in order to sever the measureless and incalculable cycle of birth and death for sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only in order to sever their own cycle of birth and death.”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others in order to enable immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to cross over the four torrents;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only in order to enable themselves to cross over the four torrents.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others in order to eliminate the diseases of affliction of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only in order to eliminate their own diseases of affliction.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma to others in order to sever the afflictions of the aggregates, the habitual tendencies, and their continuities for sentient beings, so that they may be exhausted without remainder;

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma to others only for the sake of severing the afflictions of their own aggregates, habitual tendencies, and continuities, leaving a remainder that is not yet exhausted.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others because they have great compassion as their cause in order to achieve the fruit that flows from great compassion;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, do not preach the Dharma for others because they lack the cause of great compassion and do not seek the fruit that flows from great compassion.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for all sentient beings out of a sense of concern and regard for them;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for all sentient beings without such concern or regard.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others in order to pacify all the suffering of other sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only in order to pacify their own suffering.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others in order to fulfill the flavor of the Dharma for all sentient beings;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only in order to fulfill the flavor of the Dharma within their own persons.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach the Dharma for others so that all sentient beings may attain the supreme illumination of the Dharma;
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, however, preach the Dharma for others only so that they themselves may attain the supreme illumination of the Dharma.

“Good son! To state it briefly, the immeasurable vows of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas universally serve to eliminate the great darkness of ignorance, all matters of great fear, and all forms of decline for all sentient beings; they attain great radiance and great renown, realize the wisdom of all-knowledge as it truly is, and preach the Dharma for others.”

The limited restraint of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas serves only to eliminate the darkness of their own ignorance, to attain slight radiance and minor renown, and to realize a small portion of the knowledge of phenomena as they truly are, so that they may teach the Dharma to others.

“Good son! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not truly cherish others; they do not truly feel compassion for others; they do not truly refrain from mocking others; they do not truly act for the benefit of others; they do not truly provide rescue for others; they do not truly offer recommendations for others; they do not truly desire to praise others; they do not truly praise others without guile or crookedness; they do not truly disregard their own bodies to bring peace and happiness to others; and they do not truly avoid committing errors in the actions of body, speech, and mind toward others.”

"Good son! One who abides in the Great Vehicle does not harbor any real concern for themselves, and so on, up to: they do not give rise to any mistaken actions of body, speech, or mind toward others."
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Sūtra on the Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha, Volume Six;
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Sūtra on the Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha, Volume Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: On the Practice of Reliance, Part Three.
"Furthermore, good son, there are sentient beings whose nature is violent and evil, and whose speech is coarse and harsh;
Truly they are deluded, harboring pride in their supposed intelligence; they do not desist from killing, up to and including holding wrong views.
They give rise to deep envy toward the gains, honors, and worldly praise received by others;
they constantly pursue gains, honors, and worldly praise for themselves, never feeling weary or satiated.
They constantly praise themselves and disparage others;
they fail to guard their actions of body, speech, and mind, and always delight in practicing all manner of evil deeds.

Internally, they act with cruelty and lack compassion; being without shame or remorse, they take pleasure in provoking and distressing others, and they habitually discriminate between the superior and inferior among those worthy of offerings.

Regarding those who have gone forth as renunciants within my Dharma, they constantly delight in seeking out any flaws or vulnerabilities; having perceived even a slight sign, without yet discerning whether it is true or false, they immediately disparage, revile, and punish them.

Their minds are stubborn, perverse, and deluded; they always take pleasure in provoking and harassing renunciants, failing to reflect upon their own faults while fixating on the deficiencies of others.
Although they hear praise of the merits of the Mahāyāna and resolve to seek it, their minds delight in committing various grave evils and have never been tranquil.

For the sake of deceiving and deluding others, regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, they pretend to listen to it themselves and teach others to listen; they pretend to recite it themselves and teach others to recite it.

In order to recommend themselves and to suppress others, they respectfully praise and extol the Mahāyāna Dharma; yet, while they have never studied nor attained realization regarding the spheres of practice within the Mahāyāna themselves, they claim for themselves, "I am a follower of the Mahāyāna," and entice and urge others to join them in study, seeking fame and profit to sustain their own livelihoods.

For example, it is like a precept-breaking and evil upholder of the Vinaya who, while personally violating the śīla and delighting in unwholesome conduct, entices and exhorts others for the sake of fame and profit, urging them to diligently study the Piṭaka of Vinaya.

For such sentient beings who are sycophantic, crooked, and deceitful, even a lowly human body will be difficult to obtain; they fall away from the happy realms and the nirvana of the two vehicles, let alone attaining the Mahāyāna, which is utterly impossible. They shall fall into the evil destinies with no foreseeable time of escape; therefore, wise people should not associate with them.

Yet, lacking a sense of shame or remorse, they proclaim themselves to be Mahāyāna practitioners amidst the great assembly like the roar of a lion; for the sake of fame and profit, they entice and deceive the ignorant, causing them to draw near to them and form partisan factions.
It is like a donkey that dons a lion’s skin and then claims for itself to be a lion.
Someone seeing it from afar might think it is a true lion, but once it brays, everyone recognizes it as a donkey and spits upon it, saying:
"This is no lion; it is a consumer of impurities, a truly wretched and evil donkey."
Having rebuked him in various ways, they all departed together.

"I say that such a person, who constantly delights in practicing the ten paths of unwholesome action, burns away the seeds of all humans and devas; he has already fallen back from the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, let alone being able to become a vessel for the Mahāyāna!"
Foolish and arrogant, they claim for themselves the title of Mahāyāna practitioners, deceiving others to attract gain and offerings.
They are like a foolish and arrogant man without hands or feet who wishes to wage war and enter a great battle array; though he may laboriously exert effort, he will ultimately achieve nothing.

It is likewise with those who falsely claim to follow the Mahāyāna: their faith is their hand and their precepts are their feet, yet neither is complete; they do not examine for themselves what level of practice they can sustain, yet they wish to launch a battle against the great army of afflictions. Their efforts are in vain, and in the end, they achieve nothing.

I say that such a person does not guard the three karmas and exclusively practices evil deeds; though they falsely claim to be of the Mahāyāna, they are in reality unfit vessels for any of the Three Vehicles. To claim they wish to destroy the brave, firm, and solid great army of afflictions of all sentient beings, and wish to manifest the Noble Eightfold Path to all sentient beings so as to lead them into the city of fearless Nirvāṇa—such a thing is ultimately impossible.

"Why is this so? Good son! As for the Great Vehicle, it upholds the foremost pure discipline, practices the foremost subtle and wondrous wholesome conduct, and is fully endowed with the foremost firm sense of shame and dread of blame."
Profoundly perceiving and deeply fearing the bitter fruits of future lives, they remain far removed from all unwholesome dharmas and constantly delight in practicing all wholesome dharmas.

With compassion that pervades all sentient beings, they perpetually and universally work for their benefit and happiness, rescuing and liberating all sentient beings from the manifold sufferings of birth, death, and all calamities. Disregarding their own personal peace and happiness, they seek only the peace and happiness of all sentient beings.
This is what is called one who dwells in the Mahāyāna.
"Good son, what characteristics define the Śrāvaka-yāna?"

It refers to those sentient beings who are constantly diligent and energetic, abide securely in right mindfulness, delight in meditative equipoise, and are free from all guile and deception; who have faith in and understand the results of karma, do not cling to the five desires, and cannot be defiled by the eight worldly concerns; who cultivate the wholesome with such vigor as if their hair were on fire, and constantly and carefully contemplate the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, always delighting in abiding in the noble lineages.
One who possesses these characteristics is called a follower of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
Such a sentient being is not yet even capable of becoming a vessel for the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, let alone a vessel for the Mahāyāna!
“Good son! What are the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle?

It refers to those sentient beings who possess all the merits of the aforementioned Śrāvakas, and who are further able to repeatedly abide in the contemplation of impermanence and repeatedly abide in the contemplation of arising and ceasing with respect to those five aggregates of clinging.”
Throughout all dependently originated phenomena, they are able to discern and contemplate that these are all phenomena subject to cessation.
One who possesses such characteristics is called a follower of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
Such sentient beings are not vessels for the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning,
spoke in verse: "If a truly virtuous kṣatriya, Or even a truly virtuous śūdra,
Cultivates the ten wheels based on faith and the rest, They will swiftly become a vessel for the Śrāvaka Vehicle."
Seeking the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, they purify the three karmas; Possessing shame and remorse, they fear the aggregates (*skandha*).
Knowing their faults, they delight in tranquility and dwell in seclusion; Mindfully guarding the sense faculties, their minds are serene and concentrated.
Skillfully observing dependent origination, they cultivate meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); They are adept at discerning the aggregates, elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*).
Possessing these ten practices, one has the wheel with support, Becoming a vessel for the supreme vehicle to cross the ocean of existence.
If one cultivates only the common wheels of the three vehicles or two vehicles, Seeking liberation for oneself alone from the suffering of afflictions,
Failing to deliver sentient beings and not abandoning habitual tendencies— Such a person is in neither case a vessel for the Mahāyāna.
Foolish, indolent, and of inferior faculties, they do not diligently cultivate the teachings of the Two Vehicles;
certainly unable to fulfill the wheel of the Mahāyāna, they are therefore not vessels for the vastness of the Mahāyāna.
Foolish and solitary, seeking liberation alone, with inferior intent and base conduct, devoid of compassion;
delighting in nihilism, they head toward evil realms; abandoning the True Dharma, they preach what is not the Dharma;
slandering the Two Vehicles, they cast aside the Vinaya and its practice, yet claim to have received the full ordination under the Mahāyāna.
Those who disrupt and corrupt my Dharma and delude sentient beings, thereby making it difficult to regain a human body;
those who harass and disturb the noble ones of my Dharma, or who inflict punishment upon those clad in the saffron robe,
reviling, scolding, or seizing their robes and bowls— such people shall long remain deprived of the realms of humans and devas.
Therefore, if you wish to regain a human body, if you do not fear losing your life through a stroke of the tongue,
and if you always delight in encountering the Buddhas, you should universally propagate and protect the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
If you wish to attain the Supreme Vehicle among the three vehicles, you should skillfully observe the teachings of the three vehicles;
by joyfully revealing them to others everywhere, you shall certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt.
Those who break the precepts, are stingy and jealous, harbor arrogance, praise themselves and disparage others while claiming to follow the Mahāyāna—abandon such people and rely on the wise;
you shall certainly attain Buddhahood and deliver all beings from the three realms.
According to the suitability of those who are vessels for the Three Vehicles, you preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles out of compassion;
fulfilling their aspirations without stinginess or envy, there is no doubt that you shall attain Buddhahood.
Knowing that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all empty and quiescent, with nothing upon which to rely or dwell, like space;
and teaching the Dharma to gather in all sentient beings—such a one shall attain the wondrous enlightenment of boundless wisdom.

With a corrupt intent and a malevolent mind, they hear of the supreme merits of the Mahāyāna and falsely claim to be Mahāyānists for the sake of fame and profit— like a wretched donkey draped in a lion’s skin.

I now address all the assembly: if you wish to swiftly attain supreme enlightenment, you should skillfully cultivate the ten wholesome actions and uphold my Dharma without allowing it to be destroyed.
In other sūtras of the past, I have taught that one should seek great awakening and practice the Mahāyāna,
abandoning the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; for those who are pure, I have preached this Dharma,
having made offerings to immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas, severing evil and diligently cultivating a pure mind.
To encourage those sentient beings, I have taught that there is but a single vehicle and no second.
Yet this present assembly possesses the capacities for three vehicles;
some are fit only to abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle, their minds filled with extreme anxiety and preoccupied with many worldly affairs—they are not vessels for the supreme, wondrous Bodhi.
There are deluded ones who delight in dwelling in solitude as pratyekabuddhas; they are not vessels for the supreme, sublime bodhi.
There are those capable of abiding in the supreme, sublime wisdom; therefore, according to their inclinations, the three vehicles are taught.

Those who possess pure merit and delight in liberation, yet fall into evil realms upon hearing the Mahāyāna preached, are like those suffering from phlegm and mucus who are instructed to drink milk; this only increases their toxic harm rather than curing their illness.
In this way, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle who are not fit vessels, upon hearing the teaching of the Mahāyāna, have their minds become confused;
they then give rise to the view of nihilism and fall into the evil destinies. Therefore, when preaching the Dharma, one should carefully examine the capacities of the audience.

**Chapter Five: Repentance** *The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra of Kṣitigarbha’s Ten Wheels*, Chapter Five: Repentance. At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, there were among the assembled multitude immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who, having previously heard the Dharma erroneously and mistakenly produced a nihilistic understanding, had denied cause and effect, severed their roots of goodness, and were bound for the evil realms; yet, upon hearing this sūtra being preached, they regained right view. They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and before the World-Honored One, gave rise to deep shame and remorse, performing a sincere repentance. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Virtuous World-Honored One!...”
Originally, we were within the Śrāvaka Vehicle and had planted roots of goodness, yet we were unable to mature the vessel for the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Later, we again encountered and heard the teachings of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; being confused and failing to understand them, we gave rise to the view of emptiness and denied the existence of cause and effect.
By reason of these causes and conditions, we have committed immeasurable karmic offenses of body, speech, and mind, and have gone to the various evil realms.

Now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, having heard this sutra being preached, we have regained right view; with deep shame and remorse, we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that all [these offenses] may be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we shall guard ourselves against all future karmic obstacles.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept us, so that our transgressions may be entirely extinguished and we shall never create them again in future lives.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and deliver us from the suffering retribution of the evil destinies in the future.
We now wish to return to practicing the Śrāvaka-yāna path as previously cultivated and accumulated; we only pray, World-Honored One!
“Out of compassion, please instruct me.
The World-Honored One replied,
“Excellent, excellent!”
That you are able to feel such shame and remorse, and to reveal and repent in this way, is commendable.
Within my Dharma, there are two kinds of people who are said to have committed no offense:
first, those whose nature is single-minded and diligent, who from the beginning have never transgressed; [and second, those who, having transgressed, sincerely repent].
Second, having committed an offense, they feel shame and remorse, and openly confess and repent.
These two kinds of people within my Dharma are called the courageous ones who attain purity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, according to their inclinations, skillfully taught them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

Within that assembly, some attained the lower grade of patience (*kṣānti*), some attained the middle grade of patience, and some attained the upper grade of patience; some attained the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), some attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), some attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), and some attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*).
Among them, there were also eighty-four thousand bhikṣus whose outflows were forever exhausted and whose minds attained liberation; with their intentions thoroughly purified, they became arhats.
They joyfully prostrated before the Buddha and returned to their original seats.

At that time, within the assembly, there were furthermore five million seven hundred thousand nayutas of sentient beings who had previously heard the Dharma erroneously and mistakenly conceived an understanding of emptiness; they had repudiated cause and effect, severed their roots of goodness, and were bound for the evil realms. Upon hearing this sutra being preached, they regained right view. They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and before the World-Honored One, gave rise to deep shame and remorse, sincerely repenting. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “Great Virtue, World-Honored One!
We originally belonged to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas and had planted roots of goodness therein, yet we were not yet mature enough to become vessels for the pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Later, we again encountered and heard the teaching of the Mahāyāna; although we conceived a sense of love and joy toward it, we were unable to understand it.
Being foolish, ignorant, and full of doubt, they give rise to the view of nihilism, repudiating cause and effect.
Due to these causes and conditions, they commit immeasurable karmic offenses of body, speech, and mind.
Driven by these karmic conditions, for immeasurable kalpas we have fallen into the various evil realms, undergoing all manner of unbearable and agonizing sufferings.

Now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, having heard this sutra being preached, we have regained right view; with deep remorse and shame, we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that all [karma] may be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we vow to guard against all future karmic obstructions.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us, so that our transgressions may be entirely extinguished and never committed again in future lives.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and deliver us from the suffering retribution of the evil destinies in the future.
We now vow to return to practicing the path of the Pratyekabuddhayāna as previously cultivated and accumulated; we only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant this].
"Out of compassion, please instruct me.
The Blessed One replied, "Excellent, excellent!"
That you are able to feel such shame and remorse, and to openly confess and repent, is truly commendable.
Within my Dharma, there are two kinds of people who are said to be "without offense":
the first are those whose nature is single-mindedly diligent, who have never committed an offense from the very beginning.
Second, having committed an offense, they feel shame and remorse, and openly confess and repent.
These two kinds of persons within my Dharma are called the courageous ones who attain purity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, according to their inclinations, skillfully taught them the Dharma of dependent origination.

He caused all those who practiced the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas to gradually reach fulfillment, so that they all realized the *dhvaja-lakṣaṇa-samādhi* (the concentration of the banner-mark) and attained non-retrogression in the vehicle of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
Rejoicing, they paid homage to the Buddha and returned to their original seats.

At that time, there were further eighty hundred thousand nayutas of sentient beings within the assembly who, in the past, under the teachings of various Buddhas, had slandered the Buddha’s Dharma even down to a single verse; by reason of this, they had fallen into the various evil realms and were undergoing the retribution of manifold sufferings.

Having first regained human form, they were born mute from birth; they constantly suffered from tongue-tiedness and were unable to speak. Upon hearing this sutra preached, they recovered right view—immediately rising from their seats, prostrating at the Buddha's feet, and before the World-Honored One, they felt deep shame and remorse. With utmost sincerity, they repented of their evil karma from past lives. Joining their palms in reverence and gazing up at the World-Honored One, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they were all able to speak once more.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, said:
"What evil karma did you commit in previous lives such that, now being among this assembly, you are unable to speak?
Those people all addressed the Buddha at once, and among them, one group spoke as follows:
“O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!

In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, we either slandered the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, or slandered the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, or slandered the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, even down to a single verse.”

Because of these karmic obstructions, we have transmigrated through birth and death for ninety-one kalpas, constantly dwelling in the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; mute and tongueless, we were utterly unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains that were difficult to bear.
Having now regained a human body in this present life, he remained mute and constantly suffered from a stiff tongue;
only through the Buddha’s spiritual power was he finally able to speak, and he was further able to recollect all the causal conditions and various karmic obstacles from his own past lives.
Furthermore, there was another group who spoke as follows:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Śikhin, some of us slandered the Mahāyāna True Dharma; each [account] follows its own original conditions as explained extensively before."
Furthermore, another group spoke thus:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, we either slandered the Mahāyāna True Dharma, each according to our respective original conditions, as previously explained in detail."
Furthermore, there was another group who spoke as follows:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, some of us slandered the Mahāyāna True Dharma; each according to their original conditions, as explained at length previously."
Furthermore, there was another group who spoke as follows:
"O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!
In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Kanakamuni, some of us slandered the Mahāyāna True Dharma; each according to their own original conditions, as previously explained at length."
Furthermore, another group spoke thus:
"Venerable World-Honored One!

In the past, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, some of us slandered the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, or slandered the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, or slandered the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, even down to a single verse."

Due to these karmic obstructions, from that time until now we have wandered through birth and death, constantly dwelling in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; mute and tongueless, we were utterly unable to speak, enduring various bitter poisons and agonizing pains difficult to bear.
Having now begun by regaining a human body in this life, he still suffered from being mute and constantly afflicted with a stiff tongue;

only through the Buddha’s supernatural power was he finally able to speak, and he was further able to recollect all the causes and conditions of his own past lives, including his various karmic obstacles.

We who are now before the World-Honored One have heard this sutra being preached and attained right view; with deep shame and remorse in our hearts, we confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that all [our transgressions] may be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we shall guard ourselves against all future karmic obstructions.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us, so that our transgressions may be entirely extinguished and we shall never create them again in future lives.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and rescue us from the suffering retribution of the evil realms in the future!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will!
"Out of compassion for us, please teach us the True Dharma.
The World-Honored One replied, "Excellent!"
Excellent! That you are able to feel such shame and remorse, and to reveal and repent in this way, is truly commendable.
Within my Dharma, there are two kinds of people who are said to be "without transgression":
The first are those whose innate nature is focused and diligent, such that they have never committed an offense from the beginning;
the second are those who, having committed an offense, feel shame and remorse, and openly confess and repent.
These two kinds of people within my Dharma are called the courageous ones who attain purity.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, according to their inclinations, skillfully taught them various aspects of the True Dharma.
Each, according to what was appropriate for them, attained benefit.
Rejoicing, they paid homage to the Buddha and returned to their original seats.

At that time, within the assembly, there were further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, recalled the various karmic obstacles of evil deeds they had committed in the past.

They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and before the World-Honored One, gave rise to deep shame and remorse, sincerely repenting. With palms joined in reverence, they all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Virtuous World-Honored One!”

"We recall that in the past, within the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas, we may have spoken of those disciples of those Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not—as having committed many acts of anger, resentment, reviling, abuse, humiliation, sarcasm, derision, and various forms of slander, concealing their virtues and proclaiming their faults."
Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into various evil realms for immeasurable kalpas, undergoing various heavy sufferings and unbearable poisons and torments.
Later, we encountered immeasurable Buddhas, all of whom we personally approached, served, and made offerings to.
Furthermore, they encountered immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whom they all approached, served, and made offerings to.
Before each Buddha and each bodhisattva-mahāsattva, they felt deep shame and remorse, openly confessing and repenting for all their karmic obstructions of evil.

Before each and every Buddha and each and every Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, they heard and received immeasurable Dharma-gates, diligently protected and upheld them, and practiced and studied immeasurable difficult practices and ascetic austerities.
Because those karmic obstructions remain partially unexhausted, we have been unable to realize the bliss of nirvana, nor have we been able to realize the sublime merits of the gateways of samādhi.

Now that we have heard this sutra preached before the World-Honored One, we feel even deeper shame and remorse; we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that all [our transgressions] may be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we vow to guard against all future karmic obstructions.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us, so that all our transgressions may be utterly extinguished and never committed again in future lives.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and deliver us from the suffering retributions of the evil realms in the future.
Now, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, we wish that according to our inclinations, we may swiftly realize the blissful state of nirvāṇa, or attain the sublime merits of the gates of samādhi.
Furthermore, some said:
"Regarding those disciples of the various Buddhas—whether they were vessels for the Dharma or not—we addressed them with coarse and evil words, threatening and intimidating them."
"Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into the various evil destinies for immeasurable kalpas; this should be understood as previously explained in detail in succession.
Furthermore, some said:
"Regarding those disciples of the Buddhas, whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not vessels of the Dharma, we struck and harmed them with clubs."
"Because of these karmic obstructions, we have fallen into the various evil destinies for immeasurable eons; this should be understood as previously explained in detail in sequence.
Furthermore, some said:
"Regarding those disciples of the Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not—we plundered their robes and bowls."
"Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into the various evil destinies for immeasurable eons; this should be understood as previously explained in detail in succession.
Furthermore, some said:
"Regarding those disciples of the Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not—we plundered their various means of livelihood and cut off their food and drink."
"Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into the various miserable realms for immeasurable eons; this should be understood as previously explained in detail and in sequence.
Furthermore, some said:

"Regarding those disciples of the immeasurable Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not—we caused them to return to secular life, stripped them of their *kāṣāya* robes, and subjected them to taxation and forced labor."
"By virtue of these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into the various miserable realms for immeasurable kalpas; this should be understood as previously explained in detail in sequence.
Furthermore, some said:

"Regarding the disciples of those immeasurable Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not, or whether they had committed offenses or not—we bound them with shackles and fetters and imprisoned them in dungeons."
"Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have fallen into the various miserable realms for immeasurable eons; this should be understood as previously explained in detail in succession.
Furthermore, some said:

"Regarding the disciples of those immeasurable Buddhas—whether they were vessels of the Dharma or not—we gave rise to thoughts of contempt and arrogance, harassing them in various ways and causing them to dwell in discomfort."
Due to these obstacles of evil karma, we have undergone various forms of heavy suffering for immeasurable kalpas—agonies so bitter that they were difficult to endure.
Later, we encountered immeasurable Buddhas, all of whom we personally approached, served, and made offerings to.
Furthermore, they encountered immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whom they all drew near to, served, and made offerings to.
Before each and every Buddha and each and every bodhisattva-mahāsattva, they felt profound shame and remorse, openly confessing and repenting for all their karmic obstacles of evil.

Before each and every Buddha and each and every Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, they heard and received immeasurable Dharma gates, diligently upheld them, and practiced immeasurable difficult and arduous austerities.
Because those karmic obstructions remain partially unexhausted, we have been unable to realize the blissful nirvana, nor have we been able to realize the sublime merits of the doors of samādhi.

Now, having heard this sutra preached before the World-Honored One, we feel even deeper shame and remorse; we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that all [our transgressions] may be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we shall guard against all future karmic obstructions.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and accept us, so that all our transgressions may be completely extinguished and never committed again in future lives.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and deliver us from the suffering retributions of the evil realms in the future.
Now, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, we wish to quickly realize the bliss of *nirvāṇa* according to our inclinations, or to realize the sublime merits of the gates of *samādhi*.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! It is well that you are able to thus feel shame and remorse, and to openly confess and repent."
There are two kinds of people who are said to be without transgression:
first, those whose innate nature is focused and diligent, such that they have never committed a transgression from the beginning;
second, those who, having committed a transgression, feel shame and remorse, and openly confess and repent.
These two kinds of persons within my Dharma are called the courageous ones who have attained purity.
Furthermore, noble son!

Compared to the aforementioned offenses that nearly equal the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), the sin of thus harassing and disturbing the disciples of the Buddha is merely a name; it does not yet suffice to be called a grave offense.
However, the offense of causing such affliction and disturbance to a disciple of the Buddha exceeds the aforementioned five crimes of immediate retribution by immeasurable multiples. Why is this?

Even if bhikṣus should violate their prohibitive precepts and commit various evil deeds, they are still able to guide immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings onto the path of the happy realms and nirvāṇa, free from inversion.
They perform great merit for all sentient beings, serving as a treasury of precious jewels, as extensively explained before.
How much more so for those who uphold the prohibitive precepts and cultivate wholesome dharmas!

For this reason, you should know that if anyone harasses or disturbs the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, those who have left the household life, they are severing the seeds of the Triple Gem; they are also said to be gouging out and destroying the Dharma-eye of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, this destroys the True Dharma that I have attained through long and arduous effort, causing great ruin and loss for all sentient beings.
Therefore, the offense of harassing and disturbing a disciple of the Buddha is immeasurably many times greater than the five previously mentioned *ānantarya* crimes.

Therefore, you should now, before me, give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity and increased shame and remorse, and with earnest and sincere devotion, confess and repent for all the karmic obstacles of evil deeds committed in the past.
I now gather you in with compassion, so that your obstacles of evil karma may gradually be extinguished.

Within this Great Bhadrakalpa in this Buddha-field, there shall appear one thousand Tathāgatas in the world; before each of those Tathāgatas, you should likewise with utmost sincerity confess and repent of all obstacles of evil karma, and guard against all future transgressions.

Among the thousand Tathāgatas of this Bhadrakalpa, the final Tathāgata is named Ruci, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān—endowed with these ten titles.
Before that Buddha Ruci, you all should likewise with utmost sincerity disclose and repent for all obstacles of evil karma; only then will they be extinguished without remainder.
Then, the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha simultaneously:
“So be it, World-Honored One!

We truly shall, in the presence of that final Luṣi Buddha, attain right view and abandon all false views; our various karmic obstacles shall be extinguished without remainder, and we shall be liberated from all suffering and affliction.”

If it were to cause us to dwell perpetually within the Great Avīci Hell throughout this Mahābhadrakalpa, constantly undergoing all manner of most grievous suffering and affliction, we would still be able to endure it.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent! It is well that you are thus courageous."

By means of this firm diligence and the power of your own vow, you will certainly be able to completely eliminate all karmic obstructions accumulated in past lives before that Buddha Ruci; you will certainly be able to give rise to superior faith and reverence, and personally attend upon and make offerings to the Tathāgata Ruci;
you will certainly be able to forever sever all afflictions and become an Arhat;
or you will certainly be able to realize the sublime merits of the gateways of samādhi.
At that time, the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas rejoiced, paid homage to the Buddha, and returned to their original seats.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O son of good family!

With my Buddha-eye, I survey the worlds and see that in future ages within this buddha-field, there will be immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kṣatriya caṇḍālas, brahmin caṇḍālas, official caṇḍālas, householder caṇḍālas, elder caṇḍālas, śramaṇa caṇḍālas, vaiśya caṇḍālas, and śūdra caṇḍālas—whether men or women—who have planted few roots of goodness. Although they have obtained human bodies, they follow evil friends and give rise to various false views, committing all manner of evil deeds. They destroy my profound and unsurpassed True Dharma; they lack fervor for what I have taught, and they do not produce faith or joy toward the Dharma of the extinguished flame.
Or they may slander, despise, obstruct, and conceal the true Dharma associated with the Śrāvaka-yāna that I have taught, preventing it from being spread.
Or they may slander, despise, obstruct, and conceal the true Dharma associated with the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas that I have taught, not allowing it to circulate.
Or they may slander, despise, obstruct, and conceal the true Dharma that accords with the Unsurpassed Vehicle as I have taught it, so as not to allow it to circulate.

Or, toward those renunciants who have taken refuge in me—whether they be vessels of the Dharma or not—they frequently act with anger and resentment, reviling, insulting, humiliating, mocking, deriding, and slandering them in various ways; they conceal their virtues and publicize their faults, and so forth, even up to giving rise to a mind of contempt and causing them various forms of affliction.

Such people are not vessels for the noble Dharma; being inherently foolish yet harboring pride in their supposed cleverness, they will, at the end of this life, fall into the three evil realms. There they will undergo immeasurable varieties of supreme, fierce, and unbearable agonies, and after passing through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, it will be difficult for them to regain a human body, as previously explained in detail.

Good son! Such sentient beings would rather dwell within the Avīci Great Hell and undergo all manner of heavy sufferings than receive such a base and evil human body, becoming arrogant and conceited, following evil friends, and committing such evil and unwholesome karma. Thus they wander through birth and death, being difficult to deliver, constantly remaining in saṃsāra and undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction.

At that time, there were immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings of great wisdom in the assembly who rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, wept with tears falling as they addressed the Buddha:

“Great Virtuous World-Honored One, please observe these sentient beings of the world: although they have all obtained this human body so difficult to find, they are far removed from right faith, far removed from right aspiration, far removed from right intention, far removed from right view, far removed from spiritual friends, far removed from favorable times, far removed from favorable places, far removed from pure precepts, far removed from right concentration, and far removed from right wisdom.”

Thus, although these sentient beings have all obtained a human body so difficult to find, due to the power of ignorance and arrogance, they commit grave offenses as previously described, slandering the True Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One and provoking the ordained disciples of the World-Honored One.
We now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, with a sincere heart, make this true vow:

"From this day forth, throughout our wanderings in birth and death until we have attained liberation, we constantly pray never to encounter such evil conditions and resolutely refrain from committing such grave offenses;
we shall never slander the True Dharma of the Buddhas, nor shall we provoke or disturb those who have left the household life."
"We shall certainly not impair the Dharma-eye of sentient beings, nor shall we sever the lineage of the Triple Gem.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will,
out of compassion, accept and sustain these vows we have made."

At that time, there were again immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of intelligent sentient beings within the assembly who rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined their palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Virtuous World-Honored One!
We now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, with a sincere mind, make this true vow: "From this day forth,
throughout our wanderings in birth and death until we have attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti), during that interval,
we constantly vow never to occupy the positions of various kings or emperors, and we constantly vow never to occupy the positions of various ministers or officials."
I constantly vow not to occupy the position of a national preceptor; I constantly vow not to occupy the positions of a city magistrate, a village head, or a commander of a watch-station;
I constantly vow not to occupy the position of a military general; I constantly vow not to occupy the position of a merchant leader;
I constantly vow not to occupy the position of a presiding master of any sacrificial altar, temple, or monastery; I constantly vow not—
While occupying the position of a head of a guild, a householder, or a leader among śramaṇas, he always aspires not to occupy the position of a teacher or elder,
always aspires not to occupy the position of a family patriarch, always aspires not to occupy the position of a judge,
and always aspires not to occupy any position of wealth, nobility, or high status whatsoever.

Until we have attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), if we remain in such positions, they will constitute adverse conditions for the Buddha-dharma; we shall commit grave offenses, slander the True Dharma taught by the Buddhas, and provoke the ordained disciples of the Buddhas. We will surely destroy the Dharma-eye of sentient beings, sever the lineage of the Triple Gem, and cause harm to immeasurable sentient beings.
Consequently, we will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell, where we will cycle through the evil realms with no foreseeable end to our suffering.
“May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, graciously accept these vows we have thus made!

At that time, the entire great assembly who had gathered— the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, humans, non-humans, and others— all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with piteous cries of deep emotion and tears flowing profusely, they joined their palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Great Virtuous World-Honored One!

Since beginningless birth and death, we have, out of ignorance and arrogance, committed various evil karmas—whether through bodily evil karma, verbal evil karma, or mental evil karma—either performing them ourselves, inciting others to do so, or rejoicing upon seeing or hearing them being done.”

Regarding all such transgressions, I now, before the Buddha, feel deep shame and remorse; I openly confess and repent them, not daring to conceal anything, and pray that they may all be completely extinguished.
From this day forward, we shall never again commit such acts; we shall guard ourselves against all future transgressions.
A second and a third time, they spoke thus.
With utmost sincerity, we make this true vow:

"From now until the end of the cycle of birth and death, throughout this interval, we constantly pray that we may never encounter evil associates, nor meet with adverse conditions; should we happen to encounter them, we pray that we shall not follow them, and that we will resolutely refrain from committing the various evil and sinful karmas previously described, so as not to cause us to suffer through the long night."
"May the World-Honored One,
out of compassion, graciously accept these vows we have thus made!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly that had gathered:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are indeed able, out of deep dread of the sufferings of future lives, to confess and repent.
Now that you wish to cross the deep and vast torrent of birth and death and enter the city of fearless Nirvana, you have made such a vow.”
"Good sons! There are ten dharmas that enable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and others to attain the dharma-patience of the faultless, correct path.
What are these ten?"
"O sons of good family!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to the internal body, do not cling to the external body, and do not cling to the internal and external body; if they do not cling to the past body, do not cling to the future body, and do not cling to the present body—this is called the foremost dharma, which enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain the patient acceptance of the faultless path of Dharma."
"Furthermore, noble son!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to internal sensation, do not cling to external sensation, and do not cling to internal and external sensation; if they do not cling to past sensation, do not cling to future sensation, and do not cling to present sensation—this is called the second dharma, which enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain the patient acceptance of the faultless path of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to internal perceptions, do not cling to external perceptions, do not cling to internal-external perceptions; do not cling to perceptions of the past, do not cling to perceptions of the future, and do not cling to perceptions of the present—this is called the third dharma, which enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of the faultless path of Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to internal practice, do not cling to external practice, do not cling to both internal and external practice; do not cling to past practice, do not cling to future practice, and do not cling to present practice—this is called the fourth dharma, which enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain the patient acceptance of the faultless path of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, noble son!

If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to internal consciousness, do not cling to external consciousness, and do not cling to both internal and external consciousness; if they do not cling to past consciousness, do not cling to future consciousness, and do not cling to present consciousness—this is called the fifth dharma, which enables bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to attain the patient acceptance of the faultless path of Dharma."
