Chapter Seven: Characteristics of the Field of Merit The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra on the Ten Wheels of Kṣitigarbha, Part One of Chapter Seven: Characteristics of the Field of Merit "Furthermore, son of good family!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten great armor-wheels of the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes these wheels, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), they are able to sever all five desires (*pañcakāmaguṇa*) and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, becoming a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise offer worship, serve, and protect [this person].
What are these ten? They are:

giving various kinds of food and drink, clothing, precious ornaments, elephants, horses, and carriages; as well as one’s own body, hands, feet, ears, nose, head, eyes, marrow, brain, skin, bones, blood, flesh, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, servants, and fields and houses.
In this way, when practicing each act of giving, they disregard their own body and life.
They do not give with the sole intention of seeking worldly or supramundane happiness for themselves; rather, they resolve their minds to practice giving.
They give with the resolve to universally cause the sprouts of great loving-kindness and great compassion to grow for all sentient beings;
they give with the resolve to bring forth the superior wisdom of skillful means.
They give rise to the mind of generosity for the sake of bringing about the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings;
they give rise to the mind of generosity for the sake of eliminating the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings.
They practice giving without a mind of seeking victory over others, without a mind of coarseness or rudeness, without a mind of envy, and without a mind of stinginess.
Regarding the objects given, whether they be many or few—even down to a single meal—they never harbor a hope for receiving the karmic fruit for themselves as they resolve their minds to give.
They never give rise to the thought of giving with the hope of attaining the fruit of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
They never give rise to the thought of giving with the hope of attaining the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
Whether the objects given be many or few—even down to a single meal—they give rise to the thought of giving solely for the sake of seeking all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

“Good son! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these ten great armor-wheels of the gift of material wealth, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise provide offerings, serve, and protect [this person]. Why is this?
Because while Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas give rise to the mind of giving, they lack great compassion; they do so merely for their own sake, in order to abandon poverty.
It is solely for the sake of liberating one's own body from all suffering;
solely for the sake of attaining peace and happiness for one's own body;
solely for the sake of realizing nirvana for one's own body.
They are unable to practice giving universally for the sake of all sentient beings.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas resolve their minds to practice giving, they do so with great compassion; it is for the sake of universally relieving sentient beings from poverty and for the sake of universally liberating sentient beings from all sufferings.
It is for the sake of all sentient beings attaining peace and happiness;
it is for the sake of all sentient beings realizing nirvana;
one does not practice giving for one's own sake.
For this reason, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer them worship, serve them, and protect them.

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadānapāramitā*), their mind is free from attachment to the five exquisite sensual desires. They are able to universally bestow all the articles of pleasure they have acquired upon all sentient beings. They practice this giving by relying on a mind that universally embraces all sentient beings, by relying on a mind that endures all personal suffering, by relying on a mind that seeks to extinguish the suffering of all sentient beings, by relying on a mind that grants happiness to all sentient beings, and by relying on a mind that leads sentient beings to great *nirvāṇa*."
For this reason, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer them worship, serve them, and protect them.

“Good son! If one’s mind is free from attachment to the five desires and practices giving endowed with great compassion, such a person is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and is also called the true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

If one does not eliminate the five worldly desires and practices giving without great compassion, then even though one may relinquish immeasurable and boundless objects of charity, one still cannot be called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; nor is one a true field of merit for any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for such giving is not sealed with the seal of the Noble Ones.
Therefore, one should sever the five worldly desires and practice giving endowed with great compassion.
If one does not sever the five worldly desires and practices giving without great compassion, such a person is not called a bodhisattva and is not a true field of merit.

Good son! If one practices the wheel of giving while being stained by and attached to the five desires, it cannot even extinguish a small portion of the suffering and affliction within oneself, let alone eliminate the immeasurable suffering and affliction of all sentient beings!
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Accomplishing the wheel of material giving, The wise one with pure intention,
Completely detached from the five desires, Brings peace and happiness to all sentient beings."
For the sake of bringing happiness to all sentient beings, one does not seek personal retribution;
though one practices only a small measure of giving, such a person is called a true field of merit.
Conversely, though one may give to many, if it is based on the five desires, [it is not true giving].
Not sealed by the seal of the noble ones, they dwell within the group of the indeterminate;
though they practice even a small measure of giving, they do not rely on the five desires.
They are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the truly excellent fields of merit.
Therefore, one should renounce the five desires, constantly practice pure giving,
bring peace and happiness to the multitude of sentient beings, and become a true field of merit. "Furthermore, good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten great armor-wheels of the gift of Dharma.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes these wheels, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and swiftly attain the Sunlight Lamp Samādhi.
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
What are these ten? They are: the True Dharma taught by all Tathāgatas;

or the True Dharma associated with the Śrāvaka Vehicle; or the True Dharma associated with the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; or the True Dharma associated with the Mahāyāna; or mundane dharmas; or supramundane dharmas; or contaminated dharmas; or uncontaminated dharmas; or conditioned dharmas; or unconditioned dharmas; or non-dual dharmas. Regarding these ten dharmas, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva deeply believes in and reveres them, listens to them all, and according to his capacity, carefully receives, contemplates, examines, and thoroughly masters them, subsequently expounding them for others as appropriate.

When preaching the Dharma, one should be free from a mind of jealousy, a mind of stinginess, a mind of arrogance, a mind seeking profit, a mind of disparaging others, and a mind of self-exaltation; instead, one should possess a mind of reverence, a mind of benefiting others, a mind of great loving-kindness, and a mind of great compassion.
For individuals belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, he teaches the Śrāvaka Dharma, but does not teach them the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Mahāyāna Dharma.
For individuals belonging to the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he teaches the Pratyekabuddha Dharma, but does not teach them the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Mahāyāna Dharma.
For those individuals belonging to the Mahāyāna, he teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma; he does not teach them the Śrāvaka-yāna or Pratyekabuddha-yāna Dharmas.
He teaches the True Dharma according to the capacity of the faculties of sentient beings, and never teaches it to those who lack such faculties.
Toward those sentient beings who belong to the Mahāyāna, they never encourage the practice of the Pratyekabuddhayāna or the Śrāvakayāna.
Toward those sentient beings who belong to the Pratyekabuddhayāna, they may at times encourage them to practice the Mahāyāna.
Toward those sentient beings who follow the Śrāvaka vehicle, they may at times encourage them to practice the path of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle or the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the sublime Dharma spoken by the Tathāgatas, even down to a single verse or half a line, they believe with deep faith and reverence, never slandering, obstructing, or concealing it.

One should conceive of the Dharma-preacher as the World-Honored One, conceive of the assembly listening to the Dharma as those who are ill, and conceive of the Dharma being taught as excellent medicine.
Having severed the five desires and harboring no expectations, one proclaims the True Dharma.
“Good son! These are called the ten great armor-wheels of the Dharma-giving of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes these wheels, they can sever the five desires and swiftly attain the *sūryaprabhāsa-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Sunlight).”
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles should offer worship, serve, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The wise practice the gift of Dharma, Teaching the Three Vehicles according to the capacity of the recipient;
They do not preach other vehicles, Fearing that upon hearing them, one might slander the Dharma."
They preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, not for those who lack the capacity;
each is exhorted according to their own inclinations, leading them to joy.
They never urge [others] toward the Mahāyāna to practice the ways of the two vehicles.
At times, they may encourage those two to advance in the Middle and Supreme Vehicles;
always listening to the Dharma with reverence, possessing deep faith and never slandering it,
they should honor the Dharma-preacher as they would the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"Exhorting them to hear the medicine of the sublime Dharma, he causes them to eliminate the disease of afflictions;
renouncing gain, offerings, and fame, he proclaims the True Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess the great armor-wheel of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they are able to sever all five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise offer worship, serve, and protect [this].
What is the great armor-wheel of pure ethical discipline? Noble son!
The pure precepts of a bodhisattva have two characteristics:
first, those that are common;
second, those that are uncommon.
What is the bodhisattva’s wheel of shared ethical discipline?

It refers to the vows received by lay followers (upāsaka) and those who dwell nearby (upavāsa), as well as the prātimokṣa precepts received by those who have gone forth and received full ordination (upasampadā).
Such restraint, the prātimokṣa precepts, is called the bodhisattva’s wheel of pure ethical discipline shared with the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles.

By means of this wheel of pure ethical discipline alone, a bodhisattva cannot eliminate the afflictions and all evil views of sentient beings, nor can they liberate them from the karmic obstructions of birth and death; therefore, this is not called the great armor-wheel, nor is one thereby designated a bodhisattva mahāsattva, nor is one called a true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is the bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of uncommon pure ethical discipline?
It is said:

all bodhisattvas universally give rise toward all sentient beings in the ten directions to a mind of equanimity, an unagitated mind, and a mind free from resentment, thereby upholding pure ethical discipline.

They maintain pure ethical discipline with a mind free of discrimination and a perception free of differentiation toward all sentient beings—whether they observe the precepts or violate them, whether they are generous or stingy, compassionate or wrathful, diligent or indolent—and regardless of whether they are of inferior, middling, or superior capacity;
they maintain pure ethical discipline by being free from malice, anger, and all evil conduct toward all sentient beings throughout the three realms;
and they maintain pure ethical discipline by remaining without conceptual discrimination regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases within the three spheres of existence.
They do not rely on the desire realm to uphold pure precepts;
they do not rely on the form realm to uphold pure precepts;
they do not rely on the formless realm to uphold pure precepts.
One upholds pure precepts without regarding any karmic retribution within the realms of existence;
one upholds pure precepts without relying on anything gained or not gained;
one upholds pure precepts without relying on any conditioned formations.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s uncommon great armor-wheel of pure precepts.
Son of good family!

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of pure precepts, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they are able to eliminate and sever all five desires, and thus receives the name "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who abide in the discipline of householders, Or in the liberation precepts of those who have left home,
And share these with the followers of the Two Vehicles, Are not called Mahāsattvas."
The wise one cultivates the dharma of emptiness,
Neither relying on the various worlds nor on any states of existence; They uphold the pure precepts,
Free from the grasping of signs, untainted and without outflows.
"Maintaining such precepts as these is called the true field of merit.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses another great armor-wheel of patience."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should likewise be honored, served, and protected.
What is the great armor-wheel of patience?
O son of good family!
The patience of a bodhisattva has two aspects:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
What is the mundane patience of a bodhisattva?
It refers to impure patience.

Based on sentient beings, there is acceptance arising from grasping and signs, based on various karmic retributions and based on various meritorious deeds; there is acceptance arising from one's own forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

There is patience that merely initiates the path, patience lacking capability, patience of weak and inferior strength, patience that abandons sentient beings, patience characterized by deception and fraud, patience that feigns pleasure for others, and patience that does not act for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
This is called the worldly patience of a bodhisattva.

Such patience is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; it is not called the great armor-wheel, nor does one become a bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of it, nor is one called a true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
What is the bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane patience?
It is said to be untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*).
The great Dharma-light of all worthy and noble ones universally brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings through the patience of non-attachment.
It forever severs all activities, speech, causal signs, written characters, and sounds, abiding in the patient endurance that relies upon practice.

By cultivating this patience, one is able to sever all three fetters, the three feelings, the three marks, the three times, the three realms of existence, the three types of formations, the three unwholesome roots, the four floods, the four yokes, the four graspings, and the four kinds of bodily ties.
When practicing this patience, the mind and mental factors are tranquil.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane patience.
Son of good family!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of patience, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and is thus named a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Patience is said to be of two kinds: That which has signs and that which is signless.
Patience with signs involves attachment; The wise do not praise it."
Cultivating patience based on the three types of conduct, And relying upon the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, etc., Is called tainted patience; it is not the mark of a Mahāsattva.
To extinguish the four inversions, One cultivates the patience of non-attachment.
The tranquility of the three modes of conduct and so forth— this patience is worthy of praise;
The ability to pacify all conditioned activities, to be free from all conceptual constructions,
and for the mind to be as equanimous as space— this patience is worthy of praise.
All phenomena share a single destination: they are empty, signless, and quiescent.
When the mind dwells nowhere and clings to nothing, this patience achieves great benefit.
Furthermore, son of good family:
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess the great armor-wheel of diligence.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise offer worship, serve, and protect [this].
What is the wheel of the great armor of diligence?
Son of good family!
The diligence of a bodhisattva has two characteristics:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
What is the worldly diligence of a bodhisattva? It refers to the fact that bodhisattvas,
with courageous and fierce diligence, assiduously cultivate the three kinds of worldly meritorious activities.
What are the three? First, the meritorious action of giving; second, the meritorious action of ethical discipline;
[and third, the meritorious action of cultivation].
Third, the cultivation of meritorious deeds.
Cultivating these is precisely what is called the three kinds of diligence.
Such diligence takes all sentient beings as its object; it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), with grasping (*sopādāna*), and relies upon various karmic retributions and various meritorious deeds.
This is called the worldly diligence of a bodhisattva.

Such diligence is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; it is not called the Great Armor Wheel, nor does one become a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva by means of this, nor is one called a true field of merit for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is the bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane diligence?
It is this: the courageous diligence of bodhisattvas, who maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings and eliminate all afflictions, karma, and suffering.
Such diligence is praised by all the worthy and noble ones; it is untainted, without grasping, and without dependence.

Toward all beings—whether diligent or indolent, generous or stingy, observant of precepts or breaking them, compassionate or wrathful, and whether of inferior, middling, or superior grade—one applies courageous diligence with a mind free of discrimination and perceptions free of distinction.

Universally toward all sentient beings within the three realms, they are equal and non-dual; they act with courageous diligence, being without attachment to any basis for their activities, speech, thoughts, or various practices.
They are universally without discrimination regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases within the three realms of existence, and they apply themselves with courageous diligence.
They do not rely on courageous diligence in the desire realm, they do not rely on courageous diligence in the form realm, and they do not rely on courageous diligence in the formless realm.
He practices with courageous diligence, not observing any fruits or retributions within the realms of existence.
He practices with courageous diligence, not relying on anything gained or not gained.
He practices with courageous diligence, not relying on any conditioned formations.
Not relying on the three types of worldly meritorious deeds, he exerts courageous diligence;
fully possessing the three types of supramundane meritorious deeds, he exerts courageous diligence.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane diligence.

"Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of diligence, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and is thus named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Attached to the six sense faculties, Fools are swept away by the five torrents;
Though they may be courageous and diligent, The wise all despise and reject them."
Conditioned by the diligence of sentient beings, it is tainted and grasping;
it is not a true field of merit and is not called a Mahāsattva.
When the wise apply themselves with diligent effort, they remain far removed from all attachments.
With a mind that has no point of reliance, one is called a true field of merit.
Unstained by name-and-form and detached from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, such a one acts as a refuge for all beings; this is called a Mahāsattva.
Moving through the world like the moon in water, practicing diligence to the ultimate,
this wheel can forever sever the bonds of affliction for sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas further possess the great armor-wheel of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they are able to sever all five sensual desires, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise make offerings to, serve, and protect it.
What is the great armor-wheel of meditative concentration? Noble son!
The meditative concentration of a bodhisattva has two aspects:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
What is the mundane meditative concentration of bodhisattvas?
It refers to the practice of meditative concentration by bodhisattvas based upon and attached to the aggregates.
One practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to the various elements (*dhātu*).
One practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to the various sense bases (*āyatana*).
One practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
One cultivates meditative concentration based on attachment to the form realm;
one cultivates meditative concentration based on attachment to the formless realm;
one cultivates meditative concentration based on attachment to the three types of restraint.
One cultivates meditative concentration by relying on and adhering to the three doors of liberation;
one cultivates meditative concentration by relying on and adhering to the four foundations of mindfulness;
one cultivates meditative concentration by relying on and adhering to the four right efforts.
Relying upon the four bases of psychic power, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Relying upon the five faculties, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Relying upon the five powers, one cultivates meditative concentration.
One cultivates meditative concentration by relying on the seven factors of enlightenment.
One cultivates meditative concentration by relying on the eightfold noble path.
One cultivates meditative concentration by relying on the earth element.
Relying on and adhering to the water element, one practices meditative concentration.
Relying on and adhering to the fire element, one practices meditative concentration.
Relying on and adhering to the wind element, one practices meditative concentration.
One practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to the element of space;
one practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to the element of consciousness;
one practices meditative concentration by relying on and clinging to pleasant feeling.
One cultivates dhyāna by clinging to painful feeling;
one cultivates dhyāna by clinging to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
one cultivates dhyāna by clinging to the sphere of infinite space.
One practices dhyāna by relying on and clinging to the sphere of infinite consciousness;
one practices dhyāna by relying on and clinging to the sphere of nothingness;
one practices dhyāna by relying on and clinging to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
One practices meditative concentration by relying on attachment to this world;
one practices meditative concentration by relying on attachment to other worlds;
one practices meditative concentration by relying on limited perceptions.
One cultivates meditative concentration by relying on and adhering to the perception of greatness;
one cultivates meditative concentration by relying on and adhering to immeasurable perceptions.
Such meditative concentration is with outflows, with grasping, and with points of attachment; this is called the mundane meditative concentration of a bodhisattva.

Such meditative concentration, when shared with the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is not called the great armor-wheel; nor does one become a bodhisattva mahāsattva by means of it, nor is one designated as a true field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"What is the supramundane meditative concentration of a bodhisattva?
It refers to the bodhisattvas' cultivation of meditative concentration while remaining detached from the aggregates."
One cultivates meditative concentration by remaining detached from the elements.
One cultivates meditative concentration by remaining detached from the sense bases.
One cultivates meditative concentration by remaining detached from the desire realm.
Distant from the realm of form, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the formless realm, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the three types of restraint, one cultivates meditative concentration.
They practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the three gates of liberation;
they practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the four foundations of mindfulness;
they practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the four right efforts.
Distant from the four bases of psychic power, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the five faculties, one cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the five powers, one cultivates meditative concentration.
They practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the seven factors of awakening;
they practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the eightfold noble path;
they practice meditative concentration while remaining detached from the earth element.
Distant from the water element, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from the fire element, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from the wind element, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from the element of space, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from the element of consciousness, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from pleasant feeling, one practices meditative concentration.
Distant from painful feeling, he cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the sphere of infinite space, he cultivates meditative concentration.
Distant from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he cultivates meditative concentration;
distant from the sphere of nothingness, he cultivates meditative concentration;
distant from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he cultivates meditative concentration.
One cultivates meditative concentration by distancing oneself from this world;
one cultivates meditative concentration by distancing oneself from other worlds;
one cultivates meditative concentration by distancing oneself from limited perceptions.
Distant from the perception of greatness, one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Distant from the perception of the immeasurable, one cultivates meditative concentration.

Such meditative concentration can give rise to the vast radiance of the noble ones—untainted (*anāsrava*), without grasping (*anupādāna*), and without dependence or attachment. This is called the Bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane meditative concentration.

"Good son! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), from the first generation of the mind of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*) onward, they are able to sever all five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and is thus named a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
He surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning,
spoke in verse: "To cast off one's own heavy burden, To cultivate a meditative concentration based on attainment,
And to seek the severance of one's own afflictions— This is not the mark of a true wise one."
Relying on the vessel and having something to observe, one cultivates concentration seeking liberation;
yet by grasping at this shore or the other, one does not bring benefit or happiness to sentient beings.
To bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, one cultivates concentration and casts off the heavy burden.
To extinguish all afflictions is the mark of a true wise one.
To cultivate the concentration free from dependence and attachment for the sake of moistening all sentient beings,
and to forever sever craving for existence— this is called one of great wisdom.
To untie the bonds of all existence, And cause others to dwell in the city of fearlessness,
One who practices the samādhi of tranquil cessation Is called a Mahāsattva.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsaṃnipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakra Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
The Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Daśacakra Kṣitigarbha Sūtra, Scroll Thirteen.
Translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.
Chapter Seven: The Characteristics of the Field of Merit, Part Two.
"Furthermore, good son! A bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses another Great Armor Wheel of Prajñā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should likewise offer worship, serve, and protect it.
What is the great armor-wheel of prajñā?
O son of good family!
The prajñāpāramitā of bodhisattvas has two aspects:
first, the mundane; second, the supramundane.
What is the mundane prajñā of bodhisattvas?
It refers to those bodhisattvas who, relying solely upon reading, reciting, copying, and hearing, expound the true Dharma of the three vehicles for others.
They desire to eliminate the darkness of ignorance of all sentient beings;
they desire to give rise to the great light of wisdom for all sentient beings.
That is to say:

Regarding the various sublime dharmas corresponding to the Śrāvaka Vehicle taught by the Tathāgata, they diligently recite, hear, transcribe, and explain them to others, and exhort others to practice them correctly.

Or, regarding the various true dharmas corresponding to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas as taught by the Tathāgata, they diligently read, recite, hear, transcribe, and explain them to others, exhorting them to practice correctly.

Or, regarding the various sublime Dharmas corresponding to the Unsurpassed Vehicle taught by the Tathāgata, they diligently read, recite, hear, transcribe, and explain them to others, exhorting them to practice correctly.

They do not seek the untainted factors of the path of the noble ones, nor do they seek the noble path, nor do they seek the liberation encompassed by the noble path; they do not practice the quiescent, true prajñā, but constantly practice the prajñā characterized by views and signs.
If such prajñā involves grasping and attachment, it is called the mundane prajñā of a bodhisattva.

Such prajñā is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; it is not called the Great Armor Wheel, nor does one become a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva by means of it, though one is called a true field of merit for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
What is the supramundane prajñā of a bodhisattva? It refers to when bodhisattvas,
while diligently practicing the path to enlightenment, study, recite, listen to, transcribe, and expound for others the true Dharma of the three vehicles according to their capacity.
Yet within this, they abide by means of non-apprehension, without movement, without conceptualization, and without foundation.

By means of a mind like space, a universally quiescent mind, wisdom free from increase or decrease, a mind free from grasping, a mind free from arising and ceasing, a non-retrogressive mind, a mind of the equality of phenomena, a mind of suchness, a mind of the limit of reality, a mind of the dharma-realm, a mind of selflessness, a non-discriminative mind, and a mind of quiescent patience that is free from discrimination, they skillfully abide on the ground of neither formation nor destruction, and skillfully abide on the ground of non-abiding, non-attachment, and supreme, wondrous wisdom.
Thus, this prajñā is without grasping and without attachment; it is called the Bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane prajñā.
Son of good family!

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of prajñā, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires and are thus named a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess another great armor-wheel of skillful means.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise offer worship, serve, and protect them.
What is called the Great Armor-Wheel of Skillful Means?
"Good son! There are two kinds of characteristics of a bodhisattva’s skillful means:
first, the worldly; [second, the supramundane]."
Second is the supramundane.
What is called the bodhisattva’s mundane skillful means? It is as follows:
Bodhisattvas, whether for their own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both, constantly maintain these considerations and manifest various crafts and arts.

In order to bring both oneself and others to maturity, one serves and makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; or to various Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas; or to one's mother or father; or to those who are ill, or those who are weak, frail, and without protection.

If they see those who are beset by calamities or facing harm, they diligently employ various skillful means to rescue and relieve them, maturing sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

These bodhisattvas, while abiding themselves in the Great Vehicle, for those belonging to the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles who are not vessels for the Great Vehicle, or for those whose faculties in the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles have not yet matured, they preach the subtle and profound teachings of the Dharma to lead them to practice and study;
or they exhort them to diligently cultivate the various noble meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

In some cases, they reveal the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) to encourage practice, so that beings may transcend the four inversions and awaken to the fourfold nature of phenomena that is free from falling;
or they cause them to enter the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid);

or again, they even encourage them to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, as well as the paths with remainder and without remainder, and the fruits of the path.
They enter into skillful wisdom and bring [beings] to maturity.

If there are sentient beings who crave fame, gain, and wealth, whose faculties are restless, and whose roots of virtue are not yet mature, they encourage them to recite and study the various Āgamas, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
or they encourage them to recite and study treatises conducive to liberation other than those spoken by the Buddha, thereby bringing them to maturity.
If there are sentient beings who do not delight in giving, he exhorts them to generously relinquish various kinds of precious wealth, thereby bringing them to maturity.
If there are sentient beings who are violent, wicked, and unkind, he exhorts them to practice and study the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
If sentient beings have minds characterized by much anger and resentment, they are exhorted to cultivate patience.
If sentient beings have minds characterized by much indolence, they are exhorted to cultivate diligence.
If sentient beings have minds characterized by much distraction, they are exhorted to cultivate meditative concentration.
If there are sentient beings who possess faulty wisdom, one teaches them the True Dharma by means of prophetic declarations and instructions to bring them to maturity.
If there are sentient beings who do not revere the Three Jewels and engage in conduct lacking a refuge, one encourages them to accept the three refuges to cause them to revere the Three Jewels;
or one encourages them to undertake the lay devotee's vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), or encourages them to undertake the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-saṃvara*), thereby bringing them to maturity.
Or they may encourage the cultivation of various crafts, arts, and fields of activity to bring them to maturity.

Such Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through their various worldly skills, expedient means, and wisdom—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—employ all these forms of writing, treatises, crafts, arts, fields of activity, applications, diligence, and skillful wisdom to subdue all non-Buddhist heterodox teachers.
This is called the bodhisattva’s mundane skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

This skillful means is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; it serves as the causal basis for all Buddha-dharmas, it is the locus for skillfully engaging in all practices, and it is the skillful method for spontaneously and effortlessly extinguishing and preventing the dharma of decline and falling back.
"Furthermore, noble son!

If bodhisattvas do not rely on a wise teacher nor rely on virtuous friends, yet practice worldly skillful means, these bodhisattvas are deluded regarding worldly skillful means and head toward the evil realms; they cannot accord with or abide in supramundane wisdom of skillful means, nor are they true fields of merit for all."

Being unable to skillfully discern the differences in the faculties and conduct of sentient beings, and being ignorant of skillful means, they proclaim the Mahāyāna to those who are vessels for the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles rather than the Mahāyāna, as well as to those whose faculties regarding the Mahāyāna are not yet mature, thereby causing them to practice and study it.

Furthermore, for sentient beings who are vessels for the Mahāyāna, he proclaims the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, causing them to cultivate the practices of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
For sentient beings who are vessels for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he teaches the Śrāvaka vehicle, causing them to practice the conduct of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

For sentient beings who are vessels for the Śrāvaka vehicle, they teach the phenomena of birth and death to cause them to become attached to them, rather than proclaiming the phenomena that lead to revulsion toward birth and death.

Furthermore, because they are ignorant of skillful means, if there are sentient beings who delight in killing—extending broadly to even adhering to false views—they preach the profound Mahāyāna to them, rather than teaching about the cycle of birth and death, dying here and being born there, and the retribution of various sufferings, in order to cause them to feel revulsion and fear, and thereby abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, due to ignorance regarding skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they may even cause sentient beings who delight in cultivating ethical discipline (*śīla*) to practice generosity (*dāna*);
those who delight in cultivating patience (*kṣānti*) to abandon patience and cultivate ethical discipline;
or those who delight in cultivating diligence (*vīrya*) to abandon diligence and cultivate patience.
If there are sentient beings who delight in practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he exhorts them to relinquish that concentration and instead practice diligence (*vīrya*);
if there are sentient beings who delight in practicing wisdom (*prajñā*), he exhorts them to relinquish that wisdom and instead practice meditative concentration.
"In this way, a bodhisattva who is deluded regarding skillful means for the world cannot truly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, and acts as an evil friend to them."
This skillful means relies upon apprehension and attachment; such is called the worldly skillful means of a bodhisattva.

This worldly skillful means is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, and it is not called the Great Armor Wheel (*mahā-saṃnāha-cakra*). Nor is one designated a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva on account of this, nor is one called a true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means for transcending the world?
It refers to the various crafts and arts manifested by bodhisattvas solely for the benefit of others, and not for their own benefit."

In order to bring others to maturity, one serves and makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; or to various Bodhisattvas, or Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas; or to one’s mother, or father; or to those who are ill, or to those who are weak, frail, and without protection.

If they see those who are beset by calamity and on the verge of being harmed, they diligently employ various skillful means to rescue and provide relief; they bring sentient beings to maturity through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and according to their inclinations and their faculties, they proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, they can gradually exhort the śrāvakas to cultivate the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and exhort the pratyekabuddhas to practice the Mahāyāna.

For those whose faculties regarding the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha Vehicles have not yet matured, they teach the dharmas for wearying of and renouncing the suffering of saṃsāra, causing them to train therein, so that they may weary of and renounce saṃsāra, and aspire to seek nirvāṇa.

If there are sentient beings who delight in taking life, and so forth, up to those who delight in and are attached to wrong views, [the Buddha], according to their faculties and dispositions, may for them proclaim the cycle of birth and death—how one dies here and is born there—and the retribution of various sufferings, thereby causing them to feel weary of and terrified by these things so that they abandon all unwholesome dharmas;
or he may for them proclaim the true Dharma associated with the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
or he may for them proclaim the true Dharma associated with the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Or he may proclaim for them the shallow and proximate teachings within the Mahāyāna, causing them to practice and study gradually.
If there are sentient beings who already delight in giving, he teaches them the superior and sublime upholding of pure ethical discipline, causing them to practice and study;

and so on in detail, until: if there are sentient beings who already delight in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he teaches them the superior and sublime *prajñā* subsumed under the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*), causing them to practice and study.
This skillful means, which relies on non-apprehension and non-attachment, is called the Bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of supramundane skillful means.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes such a great armor-wheel of skillful means, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and is thus named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer worship, serve, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The wisdom that is cultivated is of two kinds: The mundane and the supramundane.
That which involves grasping and attachment is called mundane; That which is free from grasping and attachment is supramundane."
Cultivating skillful means based on two kinds of distinctions:
that which has attainment is mundane, and that which has no attainment is supramundane.
To speak of only a single vehicle is called the teaching of a poorly expounded Dharma.
Unable to mature themselves, they likewise cannot deliver others.
To preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles to beings who are consistently evil is to be deluded; such a person is not called a Mahāsattva.
For those capable of progressing toward the three vehicles who joyfully seek to hear the true Dharma,
preaching that they should delight in birth and death is not the mark of a wise one;
rather, one should focus the mind on contemplation and teach according to their faculties and inclinations.
This skillful means is praised by the wise;
though sentient beings possess evil, they are capable of entering the three vehicles.
Teaching them according to their faculties, one causes them to be liberated from all evils.
"Furthermore, good son!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses another great armor-wheel of great compassion. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise provide offerings, serve, and protect it.
What is the great armor-wheel of great compassion?
O son of noble family!
There are two kinds of loving-kindness: namely, loving-kindness directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*) and loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).
Loving-kindness directed toward phenomena is called "great loving-kindness" and is named the "great armor."
The loving-kindness that takes sentient beings as its object is not called "great loving-kindness," nor is it the great armor. Why is this?
Because the loving-kindness that takes sentient beings as its object is shared with those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, for the sake of their own benefit and happiness, do not diligently cultivate the compassion directed toward sentient beings.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, for the sake of their own tranquility, for their own nirvāṇa, for the cessation of their own afflictions, and for the cessation of their own fetters, do not diligently cultivate the compassion directed toward sentient beings.
Therefore, this loving-kindness is not called "great loving-kindness," nor is it the great armor.
This dharma of objectless loving-kindness is not shared with those of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles; it can be practiced only by the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of universally benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings, diligently cultivate this dharma-contemplation of loving-kindness (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, for the sake of bringing universal tranquility to all sentient beings and enabling them to attain nirvāṇa and extinguish the fetters of affliction, diligently cultivate this dharma-contemplation of loving-kindness.
Therefore, this loving-kindness is called "Great Loving-Kindness" and is a great armor.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas cultivate the loving-kindness that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), they do not rely upon the aggregates (*skandha*), nor the sense bases (*āyatana*), nor the elements (*dhātu*). They do not rely upon the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), nor even the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*). They do not rely upon the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). They do not rely upon this world, nor the other world; they do not rely upon this shore, nor the further shore; they do not rely upon attainment, nor non-attainment.

In this way, when a bodhisattva cultivates the loving-kindness that takes phenomena as its object, they transcend the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles; this is called the bodhisattva’s great armor-wheel of the great loving-kindness that takes phenomena as its object.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this great armor-wheel of great loving-kindness, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to sever all five desires and is thus named a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
He surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning,
spoke in verse: “Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, Cultivating compassion directed toward sentient beings,
Their minds are accompanied by thirteen faults, Seeking only their own benefit and happiness.”
The Bodhisattva of great renown universally cultivates uncommon great compassion for all sentient beings;
with a mind free from the thirteen faults and a mind cleared of the thirteen stains, he proceeds toward great enlightenment.
Cultivating the great compassion of the object of meditation, the field of merit will be realized before long;
abiding securely in the thirteen powers, one transcends all sentient beings,
just as the lion king surpasses all other beasts.
Having subdued the thirteen enemies, And being free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism,
With a mind untainted by defilement, One swiftly realizes great Bodhi. "Furthermore, good son!

Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the Great Armor-Wheel of Great Compassion. If a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first moment they resolve their mind, they are able to sever all five desires and surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, becoming a great field of merit for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should be honored, served, and protected. Why is this?

It is because all those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas practice compassion solely for the sake of obtaining benefit and happiness for themselves; they do not practice great compassion with the desire to universally obtain benefit and happiness for all sentient beings.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not practice compassion for the sake of obtaining benefit and happiness for their own bodies; rather, they practice great compassion solely because they desire to universally bring about benefit and happiness for all sentient beings.

Therefore, the bodhisattva accomplishes the great armor-wheel of great compassion, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and serves as a vast field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise provide offerings, serve, and protect them.
For the sake of universally benefiting all sentient beings, these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to bring them to maturity.
That is to say:

by means of great compassion, for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, one practices the gathering through generosity, being able to relinquish all precious gems, wealth and goods, birds and beasts, servants and attendants, kingdoms and cities, wives and children, and even one's own body and life, without any sense of stinginess.

Because they take non-apprehension as their skillful means, they do not perceive any sentient beings to be converted; they do not perceive a giver, they do not perceive a recipient, they do not perceive the gift, they do not perceive the act of giving, they do not perceive the fruit of retribution obtained from the act of giving, and they do not even perceive the practice of non-apprehension itself.

Thus, out of great compassion for the sake of universally benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, they practice the gathering through kind speech, the gathering through beneficial conduct, and the gathering through common purpose; as extensively explained above according to what is appropriate, up to the point where they do not perceive even the practice of non-apprehension.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly employs the wheel of great armor of great compassion—which is born from the most supreme mind capable of subduing, the mind capable of pacifying, the immeasurable mind, and the mind that does not engage with any aggregates, sense bases, or elements—to bring all sentient beings to maturity, without ever becoming weary in heart.
This is called the Great Armor-Wheel of the Bodhisattva’s Great Compassion, which is not shared with any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. "Good son!

If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva accomplishes this Great Armor-Wheel of Great Compassion, from the first generation of the mind of awakening, they are able to sever all five desires and is thus named a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
Surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he serves as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should offer him worship, serve him, and protect him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify this meaning,
spoke in verse: "The profound and subtle Dharma, The great compassion it accomplishes,
Is as difficult to fathom as space, Without form and without abiding."
The Bodhisattva of great diligence, Possessing the virtues of the dhūtas,
With supreme wisdom and perfected great compassion, Is courageous and transcends all worlds.
Sentient beings without refuge, Bound by the foul fetters of birth and death’s suffering—
Bathed by the water of great compassion, one is liberated from all sufferings.
When Bodhisattvas practice great compassion, they can dry up the ocean of birth and death;
this is not the practice of the assembly of Śrāvakas, nor that of the Pratyekabuddhas.
Sentient beings, through greed, anger, and delusion, Are deluded and fall into evil realms;
Washed by the water of great compassion, They are freed from suffering and attain serenity. "Furthermore, good son!

Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess the great armor-wheel of firm patience, which can induce the vast and extensive equipment of words and unhindered analytical knowledge that fills space—immeasurable and boundless—as well as all Buddha-dharmas, all samādhis, and all dhāraṇīs.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this wheel, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they are able to completely sever all five desires, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally serving as a great field of merit for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
All those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles should likewise make offerings to, serve, and protect [this wheel].

"How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva bring forth the great armor-wheel of the adamantine great patience, which encompasses all Buddha-dharmas, samādhis, and dhāraṇīs, as well as the unhindered analytical knowledge of vast and boundless speech that fills the entirety of space?"
That is to say:

all bodhisattvas thoroughly and clearly examine all phenomena; like the light of the bright moon pervading space, their minds are equanimous—without dependence, without marks, without dwelling, and without defilement—and their minds remain motionless throughout all samādhi-gates and dhāraṇī-gates.
Regarding all eyes, forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact, he is free from mental defilement and attachment, and his mind is without movement.

Toward the three internal feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arise conditioned by eye-contact, his mind remains constantly tranquil and concentrated, without grasping or attachment.

The same detailed explanation applies to all ear-sounds, ear-consciousness, and ear-contact; to all nose-odors, nose-consciousness, and nose-contact; to all tongue-flavors, tongue-consciousness, and tongue-contact; to all body-tangibles, body-consciousness, and body-contact; and to all mind-phenomena, mind-consciousness, and mind-contact.
Throughout all mind, intellect, and consciousness, the mind is always tranquil and concentrated, without grasping or attachment.

Regarding the three types of sensation arising from mind, intellect, and consciousness—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—the mind is always tranquil and concentrated, without grasping or attachment.
Universally regarding all categories of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases throughout the three periods of time, they are entirely without grasping, and their minds are free from movement.

Universally regarding all categories of the three realms, the three types of conduct, the three contacts, the three feelings, the three faculties, the three vehicles, the three types of restraint, and the three liberations, their minds are tranquil; they abide in equanimity, without dwelling, without signs, and without any grasping.
Universally, with respect to all the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, his mind remains motionless, abiding in tranquility.

"In this way, with respect to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path, his mind is without movement, abiding in tranquility."
Throughout all nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), his mind is free from movement and abides in tranquility.

Furthermore, regarding the functions induced by the path-factors and the essence of the path—the knowledge of unobstructed phenomena within the three modes of conduct—he is entirely without grasping, and his mind is free from movement.

Regarding the ālayavijñāna and that which is not the ālayavijñāna, with grasping and without grasping, with outflows and without outflows, this shore and the other shore, small, great, and immeasurable, performed and unperformed, and among all categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—the mind remains motionless, dwelling in tranquility.

Universally regarding all great loving-kindness, great compassion, skillful means, and the ripening of sentient beings, up to the ten stages, the three forms of non-protection, the four fearlessnesses, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—within all such categories—he remains without grasping or attachment, his mind unmoved, dwelling in tranquility.

“By means of this wheel, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to forever pacify and eliminate the faults of the three types of sensation, forever extinguish all conceptual discrimination, and forever remain detached from the marks of all phenomena; furthermore, he is able to abide securely in the great armor-wheel of skillful means consisting of all the samādhis and dhāraṇīs, such as the *Ākāśanetra* and *Uṣṇīṣa*, which lead to [enlightenment].”

Because the bodhisattva dwells securely within such a wheel, all past drawn-out, yet not-yet-exhausted, evil and unwholesome karma—including rebirths in the states of no leisure, the evil destinies, the various realms of existence, and the karmic actions of birth and death—is entirely extinguished and brought to total cessation without remainder, so that no further retribution is experienced.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like when the world-conflagration is about to arise and five suns appear; all the waters of the small ponds, large ponds, small rivers, great rivers, small seas, and great seas in the entire world will dry up and be utterly extinguished without remainder."

In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the wheel of the great armor of firm patience and the great dhāraṇīs, which brings forth the immeasurable, boundless, and vast equipment of words that pervades all of space, as well as all Buddha-dharmas and samādhis; furthermore, he is able to abide in the wheel of the great armor of skillful means, the various dhāraṇīs, and the samādhis of the "Eye of All Space" and the "Crown of the Head."

All past drawn-out, yet unfinished, evil and unwholesome karma—including the karmas of death and birth within the various states of existence and destinies, as well as the unfortunate realms and unfavorable conditions—can all be extinguished and exhausted without remainder, such that no further retribution is experienced.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

For example, when the calamity of water arises in the world, this trichiliocosm—including all the minor worlds, the various four great continents, the eighty thousand small islands, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all other mountains—is entirely dissolved and consumed by the ashen waters until nothing remains."

In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the great armor-wheel of the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which brings forth immeasurable, boundless, and vast requisites that pervade space, as well as all Buddha-dharmas, all samādhis, and all dhāraṇīs; furthermore, he is able to abide in the great armor-wheel of skillful means consisting of all the samādhis and dhāraṇīs of the "Eye of Space" and the "Crown of the Head."

All past drawn-out, yet unexhausted, evil and unwholesome karma—whether pertaining to the states of non-leisure, the evil destinies, the various modes of existence, the various realms of rebirth, or the karma of death and birth—all such karma can be eliminated and brought to total exhaustion without remainder, so that no further retribution is experienced.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as when the bright sun rises, it can completely dispel the darkness that pervades space, so too does this bodhisattva accomplish the great armor-wheel of firm patience and great dhāraṇīs, which brings forth all Buddha-dharmas, immeasurable and boundless vast requisites, and the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language that pervades space; furthermore, he is able to abide in the great armor-wheel of skillful means and dhāraṇīs, which brings forth all the 'Space-Eye' and 'Crown' samādhis."
One gives rise to the sun of wisdom of infinite space, which can forever eliminate the darkness of ignorance and the four inversions within oneself.

All past drawn-out, yet unexhausted, evil and unwholesome karmas—including those leading to the unfortunate realms, the various states of existence, the various destinies, and the karma of birth and death—are all able to be extinguished and brought to total exhaustion without remainder, such that no further retribution is received.
Furthermore, by virtue of this, one attains increasing mastery over all Buddha-dharmas and remains forever without regression; one no longer follows the forceful practices of evil friends.
One constantly never fails to see all Buddhas, as well as bodhisattvas and śrāvaka disciples, never fails to hear the Dharma, and never fails to draw near to and make offerings to the Saṃgha.

Regarding all meritorious qualities, their minds are never weary; they remain constant and uninterrupted until reaching bodhi. Furthermore, they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha and contemplation thereof, not even for a moment, even within their dreams.
"Furthermore, noble son!

How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva bring forth the great wheel of the armor of firm great patience, which encompasses all Buddha-dharmas, samādhis, and dhāraṇīs, as well as the unhindered analytical knowledge of vast and immeasurable words that pervades space and is infinite and boundless?"
That is to say:

when bodhisattvas enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, enter the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; while abiding in these attainments, all three types of sensation, the three types of mental formations, are severed and extinguished; the mind is devoid of movement, and all sensations, perceptions, volitions, contacts, and acts of attention are entirely severed and extinguished.
Abiding in this meditative concentration for one day and night, or even for as long as seven times seven days and nights, he partakes of the food that is the flavor of concentration.
Upon arising from this concentration, his mind is tranquil, free from grasping and attachment, and he dwells in serene composure.
He further entered the samādhi of ultimate emptiness of the supreme meaning; abiding within this concentration, his mind was equanimous, free from grasping or attachment, like empty space.
From all the pores of his body there issued a dew-like fluid, appearing like the Pleiades constellation, which extinguished all oppressive heat and fetters.
Emerging from this meditative absorption, he attains right mindfulness, and a most supreme joy and bliss pervade his entire body.
It is like the Great Lord Deva entering the "Samādhi that Manifests All Bliss," wherein all the pores of his body universally experience bliss.
"In this way, when the Bodhisattva’s body experiences a pleasant touch, he immediately brings the Buddha to mind; because he brings the Buddha to mind, he sees only the Buddha and no other signs.
At that time, if the Bodhisattva thinks of one Buddha, he sees one Buddha;
if he thinks of many Buddhas, he sees many Buddhas."
If one contemplates the Buddha with a small body, one sees the Buddha with a small body;
if one contemplates the Buddha with a large body, one sees the Buddha with a large body;
if one contemplates the Buddha with an immeasurable body, one sees the Buddha with an immeasurable body.
If one contemplates one’s own body as having the marks and signs of a Buddha’s body, then one sees one’s own body as identical to a Buddha’s body, with all marks fully perfected;
if one contemplates the bodies of others as having the marks and signs of a Buddha’s body, then one sees the bodies of others as identical to a Buddha’s body, with all marks fully perfected;

if one contemplates all forms and images, whether sentient or insentient, as having the marks and signs of a Buddha’s body, then one sees all forms and images, whether sentient or insentient, as being identical to a Buddha’s body with all marks fully perfected, and no other forms or images are seen.
At that time, the bodhisattva forms this thought:
"All dharmas and all forms and appearances are like illusions and the like; they are ultimately real and not false."
"I should now further bring to complete cessation all three types of sensation, the three types of formations, and so forth, leaving nothing remaining.

Having formed this thought, he entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); while dwelling in this absorption, everything was brought to total cessation exactly as his mind had intended.

“Good son! They shall always be able to never be separated from seeing all Buddhas, as well as bodhisattvas and śrāvaka disciples; they shall never be separated from hearing the Dharma, nor from attending upon and making offerings to the Saṃgha.

Regarding all meritorious qualities, his mind is never weary; until he reaches enlightenment, they are constant and uninterrupted. Furthermore, he is never separated from mindfulness of the Buddha and his contemplation thereof, not even for a moment, even within his dreams.
